title: The Martian Tripod: Walking a Fighting-Machine in MuJoCo
text:
“A monstrous tripod, higher than many houses, striding over the young pine trees, and smashing them aside in its career; a walking engine of glittering metal … Can you imagine a milking stool tilted and bowled violently along the ground?”
H. G. Wells, The War of the Worlds (1898), Book I, chapter X
Wells gives us a three-legged walking machine and almost nothing about how it walks. This post takes him at his word and builds one. The machine is a 257-tonne, 30-metre tripod simulated in MuJoCo, the physics engine that now underpins a large part of robot-learning research. It walks into a Surrey village, rears up to look round, and burns what it finds with a Heat-Ray.
On the way the post covers:
The video below is the simulation itself, seen from eye height in the village, with a soundtrack synthesised from the simulated motors, footfalls and fires.

title: The Martian Tripod: Walking a Fighting-Machine in MuJoCo
section: MuJoCo: the physics engine of robot learning
text:
MuJoCo: the physics engine of robot learning
MuJoCo (Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact) was written by Emanuel Todorov, with Tom Erez and Yuval Tassa, at the University of Washington. It was introduced in the 2012 paper “MuJoCo: A physics engine for model-based control”. As the title says, it was built for control: for computing what an articulated body will do, quickly and accurately, so that an optimiser could plan its movements.

How it works
Game physics engines usually simulate each rigid body separately and hold them together with joint constraints. MuJoCo instead works in generalised coordinates, the joint angles themselves, and writes the dynamics of the whole mechanism as
\[
M(q)\,\dot v + c(q, v) = \tau + J^\top(q)\, f,
\]
where \(q\) and \(v\) are joint positions and velocities, \(M\) is the mass matrix, \(c\) collects gravity, Coriolis and centrifugal terms, \(\tau\) the motor torques, and \(f\) the contact and constraint forces acting through their Jacobian \(J\).
The distinctive part is contact. MuJoCo treats contacts as soft constraints and finds the contact forces by solving a small convex optimisation at each step, a modern form of Gauss’s principle of least constraint. The method is fast, stable at large timesteps, and well-defined in both directions. Given a motion, it can recover the forces that produced it, and that inverse dynamics is what model-based controllers need.
Models are written in an XML format, MJCF. The tripod’s model file is generated from a single Python parameter file, so changing a leg length changes everything consistently.


From research tool to AI infrastructure
MuJoCo’s speed made it the default simulator for a new kind of AI.

Deep reinforcement learning (2015 onward). Learning to control a body by trial and error needs millions of simulated episodes. The continuous-control benchmarks that became standard (HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker, Ant, Humanoid in OpenAI Gym, and later the DeepMind Control Suite) were all MuJoCo models. Algorithms such as TRPO, PPO, DDPG and SAC were developed and compared on them.
Sim-to-real robotics. OpenAI’s Dactyl hand learned to manipulate a cube in simulation before doing it on a real robot hand. DeepMind trained small humanoid robots to play football in MuJoCo and transferred the policies to hardware.
DeepMind’s acquisition (2021). DeepMind, where Tassa and others now worked, bought MuJoCo in October 2021 and made it free. In 2022 it was released as open source under the Apache 2.0 licence. That removed the licence cost that had kept it out of many labs and classrooms.
Scaling up. MuJoCo 3 added MJX, a re-implementation in JAX that runs thousands of simulations in parallel on GPUs and TPUs. The point is the same as with large language models: learning is limited by how much experience you can generate. Later work extended this further, including a GPU version built with NVIDIA (MuJoCo Warp).

In short, MuJoCo is to robot learning roughly what large text datasets are to language models: the source of experience. The control methods in this post are classical rather than learned, but they lean on the same features. These are an exact, fast forward model, cheap inverse dynamics and Jacobians, ray casting (used for the Heat-Ray) and easy access to every internal quantity.


Show code
import sys, math, warnings
from pathlib import Path
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve().parents[1] / "martian-tripod"
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import mujoco
from scipy.optimize import brentq
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

from tripod.build import write
from tripod.params import DEFAULT as P, leg_ik, planar_ik
from tripod.control import BodyController
from tripod.kinematics import rotz
from tripod.gait import PredictiveGait, PredictiveConfig

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.25,
                     "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
BRASS, STEEL, RED, BLUE, GREEN, GREY = "#b8860b", "#4a5a6a", "#c0392b", "#2c7fb8", "#2ca25f", "#7f8c8d"

model = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path(str(write()))
def fresh():
    d = mujoco.MjData(model)
    mujoco.mj_resetDataKeyframe(model, d, model.key("stand").id)
    mujoco.mj_forward(model, d)
    return d

HOOD = model.body("hood").id
MASS = float(model.body_subtreemass[HOOD])
print(f"MuJoCo {mujoco.__version__}: {model.nbody} bodies, {model.njnt} joints, "
      f"{model.nu} motors, timestep {model.opt.timestep*1e3:.0f} ms")
print(f"machine mass {MASS/1e3:.1f} t")

title: The Martian Tripod: Walking a Fighting-Machine in MuJoCo
text:
Leg kinematics
Each leg hangs from the underside of the hood at azimuth \(a_i \in \{0^\circ, 120^\circ, 240^\circ\}\), on a circle of radius \(r_h = 2.6\) m, \(d_h = 2\) m below the hood’s centre. It has three joints: a yaw \(\psi\) that swings the leg’s plane round, then a hip pitch \(q_h\) and knee \(q_k\) that work in that plane like a two-link arm.






Explainer series



This section and the gait planning below are covered in more depth in a four-part explainer series: forward kinematics, inverse kinematics, statics and the Jacobian and planning the falling walk.



Forward kinematics
Within the leg plane, measure the thigh and shin by their elevation angles \(\phi_1 = -q_h\) and \(\phi_2 = -(q_h + q_k)\). The foot, relative to the hip, is at
\[
\mathbf{p}_\text{plane} = \begin{pmatrix} L_1\cos\phi_1 + L_2\cos\phi_2 \\ 0 \\ L_1\sin\phi_1 + L_2\sin\phi_2 \end{pmatrix},
\]
and in the world it is
\[
\mathbf{p}_\text{foot} = \mathbf{p}_\text{hood} + R_\text{hood}\left(\mathbf{m}_i + R_z(a_i)\,R_z(\psi)\,\mathbf{p}_\text{plane}\right),
\]
where \(\mathbf{m}_i = (r_h\cos a_i,\ r_h\sin a_i,\ -d_h)\) is the hip mount.


Inverse kinematics
Going the other way, to find joint angles that put the foot at a given point, is what every gait needs. Transform the target into the hip’s frame to get \((x, y, z)\). Then the yaw is \(\psi = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x)\), which leaves a planar problem with horizontal reach \(\rho = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) and height \(z\). The law of cosines gives the knee bend:
\[
\cos\beta = \frac{\rho^2 + z^2 - L_1^2 - L_2^2}{2L_1L_2}, \qquad
\phi_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(z, \rho) - \operatorname{atan2}(L_2\sin\beta,\ L_1 + L_2\cos\beta),
\]
with \(\phi_2 = \phi_1 + \beta\). There are two solutions, \(\pm\beta\). The model takes the knee-up one, with knees above the line from hip to foot. That is how a spider or a harvestman stands, and it is the silhouette everyone draws for Wells’s machines. A solution exists only if the foot lies in the annulus \(|L_1 - L_2| \le \sqrt{\rho^2 + z^2} \le L_1 + L_2\), between 12 m and 44 m from the hip.


Show code
L1, L2 = P.leg.thigh, P.leg.shin
hip_z = P.stance_height - P.hip_drop
def leg_pts(dx, dz):
    qh, qk = planar_ik(L1, L2, dx, dz, True)
    p1, p2 = -qh, -(qh + qk)
    knee = np.array([L1*math.cos(p1), L1*math.sin(p1)])
    foot = knee + np.array([L2*math.cos(p2), L2*math.sin(p2)])
    return np.array([[0, 0], knee, foot])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.6))
th = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 400)
for rr, fc in [(L1 + L2, "#e8eef3"), (L2 - L1, "white")]:
    ax.fill(P.hip_radius + rr*np.cos(th), hip_z + rr*np.sin(th), color=fc, zorder=0)
ax.axhline(0, color="#7a6a4f", lw=2)
reach = P.stance_radius - P.hip_radius
for dz, ls, lab in [(-(hip_z - P.leg.foot_radius), "-", "walking stance (hood 30 m)"),
                    (-(hip_z + 7.0 - P.leg.foot_radius), "--", "reared up (hood 37 m)")]:
    pts = leg_pts(reach, dz)
    base = np.array([P.hip_radius, hip_z if ls == "-" else hip_z + 7.0])
    pts = pts + base
    ax.plot(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], ls, color=STEEL, lw=3, label=lab)
    ax.plot(*pts[1], "o", color=BRASS, ms=7); ax.plot(*pts[2], "o", color="k", ms=6)
    hood = plt.matplotlib.patches.Ellipse((0, base[1] + P.hip_drop), 2*P.hood_radius, 2*P.hood_height,
                                          color=BRASS, alpha=0.8 if ls == "-" else 0.25)
    ax.add_patch(hood)
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlim(-8, 50); ax.set_ylim(-3, 48)
ax.set_xlabel("horizontal distance from body axis (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("height (m)")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False)
plt.show()
qh0, qk0 = leg_ik(P)
print(f"stance joint angles: hip pitch {math.degrees(qh0):.1f} deg, knee {math.degrees(qk0):.1f} deg")








Figure 2: One leg in its own plane. The shaded annulus is everywhere the foot can reach. The solid leg is the walking stance; the dashed leg is the machine reared up to look round, with the hood raised 7 m and the legs near the edge of their reach.





stance joint angles: hip pitch -3.2 deg, knee 86.2 deg


In the walking stance the thigh is almost level and the shin drops nearly vertically, like a harvestman’s leg. Rearing up to look round takes the foot to about 90% of full reach. That is why the machine has to stop to do it: from there it cannot take a full stride.


Statics: what the motors must hold
A leg pushing on the ground with force \(\mathbf{f}\) at the foot needs joint torques
\[
\boldsymbol\tau = J^\top(q)\,\mathbf{f},
\]
where \(J\) is the foot’s Jacobian, the matrix that maps joint velocities to foot velocity. This is the principle of virtual work: power in at the joints equals power out at the foot, \(\boldsymbol\tau\cdot\dot{\mathbf q} = \mathbf f\cdot\dot{\mathbf p}\). For a vertical foot force \(F_z\), the hip-pitch torque is just \(F_z\) times the foot’s horizontal distance from the hip, less the moment of the leg’s own weight:
\[
\tau_\text{hip} = F_z\,\rho_\text{foot} - \sum_\text{parts} m_j g\, \rho_j .
\]
Here is that estimate against what MuJoCo’s balance controller actually commands while the machine stands still.


Show code
d = fresh()
ctl = BodyController(P, model)
goal, _ = ctl.com_state(d)
while d.time < 6.0:
    ctl(d, [0, 1, 2], goal, np.zeros(3), rotz(0.0)); mujoco.mj_step(model, d)

# hand calculation for leg 1, from the stance geometry
qh, qk = leg_ik(P)
p1, p2 = -qh, -(qh + qk)
x_knee = L1*math.cos(p1); x_foot = x_knee + L2*math.cos(p2)
leg = P.leg
weight_moment = 9.81*(leg.thigh_mass*x_knee/2 + leg.knee_mass*x_knee
                      + leg.shin_mass*(x_knee + x_foot)/2 + leg.foot_mass*x_foot)
Fz = ctl.last_forces[1][2]
tau_hip_hand = Fz*x_foot - weight_moment
tau_knee_hand = Fz*(x_foot - x_knee) - 9.81*(leg.shin_mass*(x_foot - x_knee)/2 + leg.foot_mass*(x_foot - x_knee))
tau_sim = d.ctrl[3:6]
print(f"foot load (leg 1)          {Fz/1e6:6.2f} MN   (weight / 3 = {MASS*9.81/3/1e6:.2f} MN)")
print(f"foot reach from hip        {x_foot:6.1f} m, knee {x_knee:.1f} m out")
print(f"hip torque   hand {tau_hip_hand/1e6:6.2f} MN m,  MuJoCo {abs(tau_sim[1])/1e6:6.2f} MN m")
print(f"knee torque  hand {tau_knee_hand/1e6:6.2f} MN m,  MuJoCo {abs(tau_sim[2])/1e6:6.2f} MN m")
print(f"motor limit  {P.max_torque/1e6:.0f} MN m = {P.max_torque/abs(tau_sim[1]):.1f} x the standing hip torque")


foot load (leg 1)            0.85 MN   (weight / 3 = 0.84 MN)
foot reach from hip          19.4 m, knee 16.0 m out
hip torque   hand  13.20 MN m,  MuJoCo  13.20 MN m
knee torque  hand   2.68 MN m,  MuJoCo   2.68 MN m
motor limit  40 MN m = 3.0 x the standing hip torque


The hand calculation and the simulation agree. The hip carries most of the load because the foot is almost 20 m out from it. The knee, sitting nearly above the foot, carries much less. That is the advantage of the spider stance: the shin stands almost vertical, so the knee works little, and the hip motor does most of the work.

title: The Martian Tripod: Walking a Fighting-Machine in MuJoCo
section: Can a tripod roll? The milking-stool problem
text:
Can a tripod roll? The milking-stool problem
Wells’s image, a milking stool “tilted and bowled violently along the ground”, suggests the machine rolls over its legs like a wheel without a rim. That is a classic model in walking research, the rimless wheel (McGeer, 1990): \(N\) rigid spokes of length \(L\) around a hub of mass \(M\) and radius of gyration \(kL\).
Between footfalls the wheel pivots over the stance spoke. When the next spoke strikes the ground, the collision is instantaneous, so angular momentum about the new contact point is conserved. Two spokes are \(2\alpha = 2\pi/N\) apart, which gives
\[
\frac{\omega^+}{\omega^-} = \frac{k^2 + \cos 2\alpha}{1 + k^2}.
\]
For a three-spoke wheel, \(\cos 2\alpha = \cos 120^\circ = -\tfrac12\). Unless \(k^2 > \tfrac12\), the ratio is negative, which would need the trailing foot to pull on the ground. It can’t, so the footfall stops the roll dead. The milking stool only bowls along if most of its inertia is out in its legs. The tripod’s isn’t, as MuJoCo’s mass properties show.


Show code
d = fresh()
com = d.subtree_com[HOOD].copy()
I = np.zeros((3, 3)); M = 0.0
for b in range(model.nbody):
    if model.body_rootid[b] != HOOD:
        continue
    mb = model.body_mass[b]; R = d.ximat[b].reshape(3, 3)
    rvec = d.xipos[b] - com
    I += R @ np.diag(model.body_inertia[b]) @ R.T + mb*(rvec @ rvec*np.eye(3) - np.outer(rvec, rvec))
    M += mb
foot = d.site_xpos[model.site("foot1").id].copy(); foot[2] -= P.leg.foot_radius
L_spoke = math.hypot(foot[0] - com[0], com[2] - foot[2])     # in the plane of the roll over the 1-2 edge
k2 = I[1, 1]/(M*L_spoke**2)

k2s = np.linspace(0, 1.5, 300)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8))
for n, col in [(3, RED), (4, BRASS), (6, BLUE), (12, GREEN)]:
    ax.plot(k2s, (k2s + math.cos(2*math.pi/n))/(1 + k2s), color=col, lw=2, label=f"N = {n}")
ax.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8); ax.axvline(k2, color=GREY, ls="--")
ax.text(k2 + 0.03, 0.3, f"tripod\nk² = {k2:.2f}", color=GREY)
ax.set_xlabel("k²  (radius of gyration / spoke length, squared)"); ax.set_ylabel("ω⁺ / ω⁻")
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=4, loc="lower right"); plt.show()
print(f"spoke length {L_spoke:.1f} m, k^2 = {k2:.3f}, three-spoke footfall ratio = {(k2 - 0.5)/(1 + k2):.2f}")








Figure 3: Fraction of angular velocity that survives a footfall for an N-spoked rimless wheel, against how far out the mass is (k²). Below zero, the wheel stops dead. The vertical line is the tripod with its legs locked, computed from the MuJoCo model.





spoke length 29.3 m, k^2 = 0.110, three-spoke footfall ratio = -0.35


So the legs must carry the body over every step. The project’s rimless_wheel.py checks the impact law against MuJoCo contact simulations: the six-spoke wheel’s steady rolling speed down a 15° slope matches theory to about 1%, and a three-spoke wheel stops at the first footfall.

title: The Martian Tripod: Walking a Fighting-Machine in MuJoCo
section: Balance: the support triangle and the hinge
text:
Balance: the support triangle and the hinge
A body standing on point feet is statically balanced when its centre of mass lies above the support polygon, the convex hull of the feet. For a tripod that is a triangle. With all three feet down the machine is stable, but it cannot step: lifting any foot shrinks the support polygon to the line between the other two.
On two feet the machine is a hinge. Nothing the motors do can produce a moment about the line through two point feet, so across that line the body simply falls. Treat it as an inverted pendulum with the centre of mass at height \(h\). If \(y\) is the horizontal distance of the centre of mass from the hinge line,
\[
\ddot y = \frac{g}{h}\,y \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y(t) = y_0\cosh\omega t + \frac{\dot y_0}{\omega}\sinh\omega t, \qquad \omega = \sqrt{g/h}.
\]


Show code
h_com = 26.5
w = math.sqrt(9.81/h_com)
print(f"omega = {w:.3f} 1/s, so the fall e-folds every {1/w:.2f} s")
print(f"over a 1.2 s swing a lean of 1 m grows to {math.cosh(w*1.2):.2f} m (starting at rest)")


omega = 0.608 1/s, so the fall e-folds every 1.64 s
over a 1.2 s swing a lean of 1 m grows to 1.28 m (starting at rest)


The fall is slow because the machine is tall, but it cannot be stopped from two feet. The swinging leg must land in time to catch it. The tumble is therefore part of the gait itself: Wells’s bowled milking stool, in three dimensions.

title: The Martian Tripod: Walking a Fighting-Machine in MuJoCo
text:
Walking by planning the fall
The project’s first gait waited out the topple. It moved the centre of mass to just inside the edge of the next two-foot support, lifted a leg, let the body fall onto it, and settled. That works, but slowly: in the project’s tests, about 1.1 mph, with the hood tilting by up to 17°.
The faster gait plans the fall instead, using the standard model from humanoid robotics: the linear inverted pendulum with a zero-moment point (ZMP). Hold the centre of mass at constant height \(h\). Then its horizontal position \(\mathbf c\) obeys
\[
\ddot{\mathbf c} = \omega^2(\mathbf c - \mathbf z),
\]
where \(\mathbf z\) is the ZMP, the point on the ground through which the net ground force acts. The ZMP is what the legs control, and it must stay inside the support polygon. With three feet down, it can go anywhere in the triangle. With one leg swinging, it is confined to the line between the other two, which is the hinge again, seen from the planner’s side.
Over a timestep \(\Delta t\) with \(\mathbf z\) held fixed, the pendulum’s motion is exact:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf c\\ \dot{\mathbf c}\end{pmatrix}_{k+1} =
\begin{pmatrix}\cosh\omega\Delta t & \omega^{-1}\sinh\omega\Delta t\\ \omega\sinh\omega\Delta t & \cosh\omega\Delta t\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf c\\ \dot{\mathbf c}\end{pmatrix}_k +
\begin{pmatrix}1 - \cosh\omega\Delta t\\ -\omega\sinh\omega\Delta t\end{pmatrix}\mathbf z_k .
\]
Given the footstep rhythm, the planner chooses \(\mathbf z_0, \dots, \mathbf z_{N-1}\) over a 14-second horizon to minimise a quadratic cost:
\[
\sum_k w_v\|\dot{\mathbf c}_k - \mathbf v_\text{ref}\|^2 + w_p\|\mathbf c_k - \mathbf c^\text{nom}_k\|^2 + w_{\Delta z}\|\mathbf z_k - \mathbf z_{k-1}\|^2 + w_z\|\mathbf z_k - \bar{\mathbf p}_k\|^2.
\]
The terms keep the walking speed, keep up with the footstep schedule, smooth the ZMP and centre it in the support (\(\bar{\mathbf p}_k\) is the centroid of the planted feet). The constraints are the pendulum dynamics and linear inequalities keeping each \(\mathbf z_k\) inside its support triangle or on its hinge line. It is a quadratic programme, solved with OSQP, and re-solved from the measured state at every change of support and every 0.4 s. Re-planning from the measured state is what makes this model-predictive control.
A whole-body controller then turns the plan into joint torques. It computes the ground force and moment that keep the centre of mass and hood on plan, and shares them among the planted feet by least squares, never pulling on the ground and staying within friction. It maps each foot’s share to joint torques through \(J^\top\), the statics formula from earlier.


Show code
d = fresh()
gait = PredictiveGait(P, model, d, PredictiveConfig())
start = gait.centroid().copy(); t_start = d.time
log = {k: [] for k in ("t", "cx", "cy", "vx", "zx", "zy", "tilt", "two")}
landings = [[f.copy() for f in gait.planted]]
steps_seen = 0
while gait.steps_done < 15 and d.time < 60:
    info = gait(d)
    mujoco.mj_step(model, d)
    c, v = gait.ctl.com_state(d)
    R = d.xmat[HOOD].reshape(3, 3)
    z = gait.planner.reference(d.time)[3] if gait.planner.X is not None else c[:2]
    for k, val in zip(log, (d.time, c[0], c[1], v[0], z[0], z[1],
                            math.degrees(math.acos(min(1.0, R[2, 2]))), info["two_legged"])):
        log[k].append(val)
    if gait.steps_done != steps_seen:
        steps_seen = gait.steps_done
        landings.append([f.copy() for f in gait.planted])
log = {k: np.array(v) for k, v in log.items()}
T_walk = d.time - t_start
moved = float((gait.centroid() - start) @ gait.dir)
speed = moved/T_walk
print(f"{gait.steps_done} steps in {T_walk:.1f} s: {moved:.0f} m at {speed:.2f} m/s = {speed*2.237:.1f} mph")
print(f"on two feet {log['two'].mean():.0%} of the time, max hood tilt {log['tilt'].max():.1f} deg")
print(f"planner failures: {gait.plan_failures}")


15 steps in 30.6 s: 77 m at 2.52 m/s = 5.6 mph
on two feet 59% of the time, max hood tilt 2.7 deg
planner failures: 0




Show code
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 6.6), gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.1, 1]})
for i, feet in enumerate(landings):
    tri = np.array([f[:2] for f in feet] + [feet[0][:2]])
    a1.fill(tri[:, 0], tri[:, 1], color=GREY, alpha=0.08)
    a1.plot(tri[:, 0], tri[:, 1], color=GREY, lw=0.6, alpha=0.6)
    for f in feet:
        a1.plot(f[0], f[1], "o", color="k", ms=3)
a1.plot(log["zx"][::40], log["zy"][::40], ".", color=RED, ms=3, label="planned ZMP")
a1.plot(log["cx"], log["cy"], color=BLUE, lw=2, label="centre of mass")
a1.set_aspect("equal"); a1.set_xlabel("x (m)"); a1.set_ylabel("y (m)")
a1.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left", ncol=2)
t = log["t"] - log["t"][0]
two = log["two"].astype(bool)
for a in (a2,):
    edges = np.flatnonzero(np.diff(two.astype(int)))
    starts = list(t[edges[two[edges + 1]] + 1]) if len(edges) else []
    ends = list(t[edges[~two[edges + 1]] + 1]) if len(edges) else []
    if two[0]: starts = [t[0]] + starts
    if two[-1]: ends = ends + [t[-1]]
    for s0, s1 in zip(starts, ends):
        a.axvspan(s0, s1, color=GREY, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
a2.plot(t, log["vx"], color=BLUE, lw=1.6, label="forward speed (m/s)")
a2.plot(t, log["tilt"], color=BRASS, lw=1.6, label="hood tilt (deg)")
a2.set_xlabel("time (s)"); a2.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Figure 4: Five gait cycles seen from above (top) and over time (bottom). Grey triangles are the support polygon after each footfall; the line is the centre of mass and the dots are the planned zero-moment point. Shading marks the times on two feet, when the machine is a hinge.





The centre of mass never stops. It swings from side to side as each two-foot hinge appears in a different direction, which is the 3-D version of the bowled stool. The hood stays within a few degrees of level, and the machine walks at about 5.5 mph, five times the speed of the wait-and-topple gait with a sixth of its tilt.
How fast could it go? Animals of very different sizes walk in dynamically similar ways at the same Froude number \(\mathrm{Fr} = v^2/(g\ell)\), where \(\ell\) is leg length. People switch from walking to running near \(\mathrm{Fr} \approx 0.5\).


Show code
ell = P.stance_height - P.hip_drop
print(f"leg length ~{ell:.0f} m; this gait: Fr = {speed**2/(9.81*ell):.3f}")
print(f"a person walking at 1.4 m/s: Fr = {1.4**2/(9.81*0.9):.2f}")
print(f"Fr = 0.5 would be {math.sqrt(0.5*9.81*ell):.1f} m/s = {math.sqrt(0.5*9.81*ell)*2.237:.0f} mph")


leg length ~28 m; this gait: Fr = 0.023
a person walking at 1.4 m/s: Fr = 0.22
Fr = 0.5 would be 11.7 m/s = 26 mph


By that measure the simulated machine is strolling, at a tenth of a person’s dynamic pace. Its speed is limited by the 40 MN·m motors and by the planner, not by geometry. Faster rhythms manage 6–7 mph for a dozen steps and then fall, as the swing legs saturate. A machine that strode at Wells’s evident pace would need much stronger joints, or a planner that also chooses where to put its feet.

title: The Martian Tripod: Walking a Fighting-Machine in MuJoCo
text:
The road from Mars
The fighting-machines are the end of a much longer journey. Wells describes it in his first chapter: astronomers see “a huge outbreak of incandescent gas upon the planet”, then another, “and so for ten nights, a flame each night”. The Martians are firing a vast gun, one shot a night, and each shot is a cylinder about thirty yards across that will land in Surrey. How hard is that?

Launching from the surface
To leave Mars and still be moving at speed \(v_\infty\) relative to it once far away, energy conservation gives the speed needed at the surface:
\[
v_\text{muzzle} = \sqrt{v_\text{esc}^2 + v_\infty^2}, \qquad v_\text{esc} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM_\text{Mars}}{R_\text{Mars}}} \approx 5.0\ \text{km/s}.
\]
A gun has no burn time: all of that speed must be given inside the barrel. For a barrel of length \(L\) and constant acceleration \(a\), \(v^2 = 2aL\), so the acceleration the passengers feel is
\[
a = \frac{v_\text{muzzle}^2}{2L}.
\]
The atmosphere then slows the cylinder on the way out. For a body with ballistic coefficient \(\beta = m/(C_D A)\) crossing an exponential atmosphere of surface density \(\rho_0\) and scale height \(H\) at angle \(\gamma\), the speed falls by a factor \(\exp\!\left(-\rho_0 H / (2\beta\sin\gamma)\right)\). Mars helps here too: its column of air, \(\rho_0 H\), is about 40 times smaller than Earth’s.


Show code
MU_MARS, R_MARS = 42828.37, 3389.5                      # km^3/s^2, km
MU_EARTH, R_EARTH = 398600.4, 6371.0
v_esc_m = math.sqrt(2*MU_MARS/R_MARS); v_esc_e = math.sqrt(2*MU_EARTH/R_EARTH)
D_cyl = 30*0.9144                                        # "about thirty yards" diameter (m)
A_cyl = math.pi*(D_cyl/2)**2
def beta(mass_t, cd=1.0): return mass_t*1e3/(cd*A_cyl)
print(f"escape speed: Mars {v_esc_m:.2f} km/s, Earth {v_esc_e:.2f} km/s")
print(f"air column rho0*H: Mars {0.020*11100:.0f} kg/m^2, Earth {1.225*7200:.0f} kg/m^2")
for mass in (1000, 3000):
    b = beta(mass)
    print(f"{mass:>5} t cylinder (beta = {b:,.0f} kg/m^2): speed kept through the air, fired vertically: "
          f"Mars {math.exp(-0.020*11100/(2*b)):.0%}, Earth {math.exp(-1.225*7200/(2*b)):.0%}")


escape speed: Mars 5.03 km/s, Earth 11.19 km/s
air column rho0*H: Mars 222 kg/m^2, Earth 8820 kg/m^2
 1000 t cylinder (beta = 1,692 kg/m^2): speed kept through the air, fired vertically: Mars 94%, Earth 7%
 3000 t cylinder (beta = 5,076 kg/m^2): speed kept through the air, fired vertically: Mars 98%, Earth 42%


This is why the gun is on Mars and not on Earth. Jules Verne’s moon gun would lose a large part of its speed to the air, while a Martian gun gives up only a few per cent.


Choosing the moment: porkchops and oppositions
Which \(v_\infty\)? That depends on when the gun fires and how long the trip takes. Model Mars and Earth on circular, coplanar orbits (1.524 AU and 1 AU). Then fix the departure time and the flight time. The cylinder’s path between Mars’s position at departure and Earth’s position at arrival is the solution of Lambert’s problem: the Keplerian orbit through two points in a given time. It is solved here with the universal-variable method. Plotting the required speeds over a grid of departure dates and flight times gives the mission designer’s porkchop plot.


Show code
MU_SUN = 1.32712440018e11; AU = 1.495978707e8
rE, rM = AU, 1.523679*AU
nE, nM = math.sqrt(MU_SUN/rE**3), math.sqrt(MU_SUN/rM**3)
DAY = 86400.0

def stumpff(z):
    if z > 1e-8:
        s = math.sqrt(z); return (1 - math.cos(s))/z, (s - math.sin(s))/s**3
    if z < -1e-8:
        s = math.sqrt(-z); return (math.cosh(s) - 1)/(-z), (math.sinh(s) - s)/s**3
    return 0.5, 1/6

def lambert(r1v, r2v, tof, mu=MU_SUN):
    """Prograde single-revolution Lambert solution (universal variables)."""
    r1, r2 = np.linalg.norm(r1v), np.linalg.norm(r2v)
    dth = math.acos(np.clip(r1v @ r2v/(r1*r2), -1, 1))
    if r1v[0]*r2v[1] - r1v[1]*r2v[0] < 0:
        dth = 2*math.pi - dth
    A = math.sin(dth)*math.sqrt(r1*r2/(1 - math.cos(dth)))
    def y(z):
        C, S = stumpff(z); return r1 + r2 + A*(z*S - 1)/math.sqrt(C)
    def F(z):
        C, S = stumpff(z); yz = y(z)
        return (yz/C)**1.5*S + A*math.sqrt(yz) - math.sqrt(mu)*tof
    zl, zh = -4*math.pi**2, 4*math.pi**2 - 1e-6
    while y(zl) < 0 or F(zl) > 0:
        zl += 0.05
        if zl >= zh: raise ValueError("no bracket")
    z = brentq(F, zl, zh, xtol=1e-12)
    yz = y(z); C, S = stumpff(z)
    f, g, gd = 1 - yz/r1, A*math.sqrt(yz/mu), 1 - yz/r2
    return (r2v - f*r1v)/g, (gd*r2v - r1v)/g

def planet(r, n, t):
    th = n*t
    return r*np.array([math.cos(th), math.sin(th)]), math.sqrt(MU_SUN/r)*np.array([-math.sin(th), math.cos(th)])

def transfer(t_dep, tof):
    """t_dep in days relative to opposition (both planets at longitude 0 at t = 0)."""
    r1, vM = planet(rM, nM, t_dep*DAY)
    r2, vE = planet(rE, nE, (t_dep + tof)*DAY)
    v1, v2 = lambert(r1, r2, tof*DAY)
    return np.linalg.norm(v1 - vM), np.linalg.norm(v2 - vE), v1, r1

# Hohmann reference
a_h = (rE + rM)/2
tof_h = math.pi*math.sqrt(a_h**3/MU_SUN)/DAY
vinf_dep_h = math.sqrt(MU_SUN/rM) - math.sqrt(MU_SUN*(2/rM - 1/a_h))
vinf_arr_h = math.sqrt(MU_SUN*(2/rE - 1/a_h)) - math.sqrt(MU_SUN/rE)
lead_h = (math.pi - nE*tof_h*DAY) % (2*math.pi)                 # Earth's angle ahead of Mars at departure
days_before_opp = (2*math.pi - lead_h)/(nE - nM)/DAY

dep = np.linspace(-320, 40, 121); tofs = np.linspace(60, 420, 121)
VD = np.full((len(tofs), len(dep)), np.nan); VA = VD.copy()
for j, td in enumerate(dep):
    for i, tf in enumerate(tofs):
        # skip the degenerate 180-degree transfers of the coplanar model
        r1, _ = planet(rM, nM, td*DAY); r2, _ = planet(rE, nE, (td + tf)*DAY)
        ang = math.degrees(math.acos(np.clip(r1 @ r2/(np.linalg.norm(r1)*np.linalg.norm(r2)), -1, 1)))
        if abs(ang - 180) < 4:
            continue
        try:
            VD[i, j], VA[i, j], _, _ = transfer(td, tf)
        except Exception:
            pass
print(f"Hohmann transfer: {tof_h:.0f} days, v_inf leaving Mars {vinf_dep_h:.2f} km/s, "
      f"arriving at Earth {vinf_arr_h:.2f} km/s")
print(f"it departs {days_before_opp:.0f} days before opposition")


Hohmann transfer: 259 days, v_inf leaving Mars 2.65 km/s, arriving at Earth 2.94 km/s
it departs 163 days before opposition




Show code
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.6))
cs = a1.contourf(dep, tofs, np.clip(VD, 0, 20), levels=np.arange(2.5, 20.5, 1.0), cmap="viridis_r")
a1.contour(dep, tofs, VA, levels=[3, 5, 8, 12], colors="w", linewidths=0.8, linestyles="--")
fig.colorbar(cs, ax=a1, label="v∞ leaving Mars (km/s)")
a1.plot(-days_before_opp, tof_h, "*", color=BRASS, ms=14, mec="k")
a1.axvline(0, color=RED, lw=1)
a1.text(-4, 395, "opposition", color=RED, fontsize=9, ha="right")
a1.set_xlabel("departure, days relative to opposition"); a1.set_ylabel("flight time (days)")
a1.set_title("dashed: arrival v∞ at Earth (km/s)", fontsize=9)

def propagate(r0, v0, days):
    f = lambda t, s: np.r_[s[2:], -MU_SUN*s[:2]/np.linalg.norm(s[:2])**3]
    sol = solve_ivp(f, (0, days*DAY), np.r_[r0, v0], rtol=1e-9, atol=1, max_step=DAY)
    return sol.y[:2]/AU
th = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 300)
a2.plot(np.cos(th), np.sin(th), color=BLUE, lw=1); a2.plot(1.524*np.cos(th), 1.524*np.sin(th), color=RED, lw=1)
a2.plot(0, 0, "o", color="#f4c430", ms=12, mec="k")
for td, tf, col in [(-days_before_opp, tof_h, BRASS), (0.0, 120.0, RED)]:
    if col == BRASS:    # Hohmann: start at Mars on the transfer ellipse's aphelion
        r1, vM = planet(rM, nM, td*DAY)
        v1 = vM*(1 - vinf_dep_h/np.linalg.norm(vM))
    else:
        _, _, v1, r1 = transfer(td, tf)
    path = propagate(r1, v1, tf)
    a2.plot(*path, color=col, lw=2.2)
    a2.plot(*path[:, 0], "o", color=col); a2.plot(*path[:, -1], "s", color=col)
a2.set_aspect("equal"); a2.set_xlabel("AU"); a2.set_ylabel("AU"); a2.set_xlim(-1.8, 1.8); a2.set_ylim(-1.8, 1.8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Figure 5: Left: porkchop plot of the speed the gun must leave Mars with (v∞, km/s), against departure date relative to opposition and flight time. The star is the Hohmann minimum-energy transfer; the white band is 180° transfers, where the flat circular-orbit model is degenerate. Right: that transfer (brass) and a fast 120-day shot fired at opposition (red), with Mars’s and Earth’s orbits.





The cheapest shot is the Hohmann transfer, half an ellipse touching both orbits. It takes eight and a half months and must be fired about five months before opposition, while Earth is still well behind Mars, so that Earth arrives at the meeting point at the same time as the cylinder. Wells has his astronomers see the flashes as Mars approaches opposition, which is the right season. Firing at opposition, when the planets are closest, is not cheapest: Earth is already pulling ahead, and catching it quickly costs much more speed.


Show code
rows = []
for name, td, tf in [("Hohmann (minimum energy)", None, tof_h),
                     ("fired at opposition, 250 days", 0.0, 250.0),
                     ("fired at opposition, 120 days", 0.0, 120.0)]:
    if td is None:      # exactly 180 degrees: use the closed form, not Lambert
        vd, va = vinf_dep_h, vinf_arr_h
    else:
        vd, va, _, _ = transfer(td, tf)
    rows.append((name, tf, vd, math.sqrt(v_esc_m**2 + vd**2), va, math.sqrt(v_esc_e**2 + va**2)))
print(f"{'trajectory':32s}{'days':>6s}{'v_inf Mars':>12s}{'muzzle':>9s}{'v_inf Earth':>13s}{'entry':>8s}  (km/s)")
for r_ in rows:
    print(f"{r_[0]:32s}{r_[1]:6.0f}{r_[2]:12.2f}{r_[3]:9.2f}{r_[4]:13.2f}{r_[5]:8.2f}")
v_muzzle = rows[0][3]; v_entry = rows[0][5]
print("\nbarrel length needed for the Hohmann shot:")
for gees in (10, 100, 1000):
    print(f"  {gees:>5} g  ->  {(v_muzzle*1e3)**2/(2*gees*9.81)/1e3:8.1f} km")


trajectory                        days  v_inf Mars   muzzle  v_inf Earth   entry  (km/s)
Hohmann (minimum energy)           259        2.65     5.68         2.94   11.57
fired at opposition, 250 days      250        5.11     7.17         9.73   14.82
fired at opposition, 120 days      120       13.68    14.58         9.14   14.44

barrel length needed for the Hohmann shot:
     10 g  ->     164.6 km
    100 g  ->      16.5 km
   1000 g  ->       1.6 km


Even the gentlest shot needs a muzzle speed of almost 6 km/s. Accelerating to that at a survivable 10 g would need a barrel well over a hundred kilometres long. A barrel of a kilometre or so, closer to anything one might call a gun, means more than a thousand g. Wells’s Martians are, in his description, little more than great heads with hands. Perhaps a body built like that, raised in Mars’s 0.38 g, packs well for a violent ride.


Ten nights, ten shots
Why one shot a night? A gun built into the ground turns with the planet. Mars’s day (the sol) lasts 24 h 37 min, almost the same as Earth’s, so the gun points along its firing line once per sol. Each cylinder follows nearly the same path, so they arrive about a day apart, as they do in the novel: the first lands in the early hours of a Friday, the second around Friday midnight, the third on Saturday night. Near opposition Mars is highest in the sky around midnight, so watchers on Earth would see each flash at nearly the same hour, drifting about 40 minutes later each night: Wells’s “a flame each night”.


Arriving: entry and impact
The cylinder reaches Earth’s atmosphere at the entry speed in the table, at least 11.6 km/s. It is a ballistic body with no wings or parachute in Wells, so its descent follows the equations of planar atmospheric flight:
\[
\dot v = -\frac{\rho(h)\,v^2}{2\beta} + g\sin\gamma, \qquad
\dot\gamma = \left(\frac{g}{v} - \frac{v}{R_\oplus + h}\right)\cos\gamma, \qquad
\dot h = -v\sin\gamma,
\]
with \(\gamma\) the angle below horizontal and \(\rho(h) = \rho_0 e^{-h/H}\). For a steep, fast entry the classic Allen–Eggers result gives the peak deceleration in closed form, independent of the body’s mass,
\[
a_\text{max} = \frac{v_E^2\sin\gamma}{2eH},
\]
so the passengers’ worst moment depends only on how fast and how steeply they come in. The impact speed, by contrast, depends strongly on mass. The cylinder’s mass is not given, so the calculation sweeps it from a few hundred tonnes (light, for a craft carrying several Martians and the parts of fighting-machines) to many thousands.


Show code
H, RHO0, G0 = 7200.0, 1.225, 9.81
gamma0 = math.radians(30)
def entry(mass_t, v0=v_entry*1e3, h0=120e3, g0=gamma0):
    b = beta(mass_t)
    def rhs(t, s):
        v, gam, h = s
        g = G0*(R_EARTH*1e3/(R_EARTH*1e3 + h))**2
        rho = RHO0*math.exp(-h/H)
        return [-rho*v*v/(2*b) + g*math.sin(gam),
                (g/v - v/(R_EARTH*1e3 + h))*math.cos(gam),
                -v*math.sin(gam)]
    hit = lambda t, s: s[2]; hit.terminal = True; hit.direction = -1
    sol = solve_ivp(rhs, (0, 3000), [v0, g0, h0], events=hit, max_step=0.05, rtol=1e-8)
    v, gam, h = sol.y
    rho = RHO0*np.exp(-h/H)
    decel = rho*v*v/(2*b)
    return sol.t, v, h, decel

masses = [300, 1000, 3000, 10000, 30000]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
results = []
for mass, col in zip(masses, ["#6baed6", BLUE, GREEN, BRASS, RED]):
    t_, v_, h_, dec = entry(mass)
    ax.plot(v_/1e3, h_/1e3, color=col, lw=2, label=f"{mass:,} t")
    ke = 0.5*mass*1e3*v_[-1]**2/4.184e9          # tonnes of TNT
    results.append((mass, v_[-1], dec.max()/9.81, ke))
ax.set_xlabel("speed (km/s)"); ax.set_ylabel("altitude (km)"); ax.set_ylim(0, 80)
ax.legend(title="cylinder mass", frameon=False); plt.show()

print(f"Allen-Eggers peak deceleration at {math.degrees(gamma0):.0f} deg: "
      f"{(v_entry*1e3)**2*math.sin(gamma0)/(2*math.e*H)/9.81:.0f} g")
print(f"{'mass (t)':>9s}{'impact speed':>15s}{'peak decel':>12s}{'impact energy':>20s}")
for mass, vi, gmax, ke in results:
    print(f"{mass:9,d}{vi:12.0f} m/s{gmax:10.0f} g{ke:14,.0f} t of TNT")








Figure 6: A thirty-yard cylinder entering Earth’s atmosphere at the Hohmann arrival speed, 30° below horizontal, for several masses. Heavy cylinders reach the ground at kilometres per second; only light ones are slowed to the speed of a falling meteorite.





Allen-Eggers peak deceleration at 30 deg: 174 g
 mass (t)   impact speed  peak decel       impact energy
      300          93 m/s       173 g             0 t of TNT
    1,000         192 m/s       173 g             4 t of TNT
    3,000        1985 m/s       173 g         1,412 t of TNT
   10,000        6829 m/s       172 g        55,725 t of TNT
   30,000        9757 m/s       117 g       341,318 t of TNT


A heavy cylinder barely notices the air. It would reach Horsell Common at several kilometres per second and release the energy of a small nuclear weapon, leaving a crater rather than Wells’s “enormous hole” in a sand pit, with a cylinder still intact enough to unscrew. A light cylinder is slowed to a few hundred metres per second, which is survivable for a strong hull and fits the novel’s sandy pit and the “still so hot” metal much better. Either way, the occupants ride through a peak deceleration of well over a hundred g, set by the entry speed and angle, not by the hull. A shallower entry or a parachute would help. Wells, writing five years before the Wright brothers flew, gives his cylinders neither, and the arithmetic suggests the Martians were tougher than they looked.

title: The Martian Tripod: Walking a Fighting-Machine in MuJoCo
text:
Takeaways

MuJoCo grew from a 2012 research engine for model-based control into the standard simulator for robot learning. Its fast, convex contact model and generalised-coordinate dynamics make it suited to both classical control and reinforcement learning, and DeepMind’s 2021 purchase and open-sourcing made it free to everyone.
A tripod’s leg is a two-link arm on a yaw joint. Inverse kinematics is the law of cosines; the knee-up spider stance puts the load on the hips; and statics is \(\boldsymbol\tau = J^\top\mathbf f\), which the simulation confirms by hand.
A three-legged machine cannot roll passively. The rimless-wheel impact law, \(\omega^+/\omega^- = (k^2 + \cos 2\alpha)/(1 + k^2)\), is negative for a tripod unless most of its mass is in its legs.
Walking on three legs means repeatedly falling about a hinge. Planning that fall with a linear inverted pendulum and a model-predictive ZMP planner gives a steady 5.5 mph with the hood within a few degrees of level.
The cylinders are the hard part. A gun on Mars works, because Mars has little air. The cheapest shot leaves about five months before opposition, needs almost 6 km/s, a barrel of tens or hundreds of kilometres to keep the g-load down, and ends in an entry of more than a hundred g. Wells’s ten nightly flashes fit a gun that turns with the planet.

title: The Martian Tripod: Walking a Fighting-Machine in MuJoCo
text:
Further reading

H. G. Wells, The War of the Worlds (1898), free at Project Gutenberg.
E. Todorov, T. Erez and Y. Tassa, “MuJoCo: A physics engine for model-based control”, IROS (2012); the MuJoCo documentation.
T. McGeer, “Passive dynamic walking”, International Journal of Robotics Research (1990), for the rimless wheel.
S. Kajita et al., “Biped walking pattern generation by using preview control of zero-moment point”, ICRA (2003), for ZMP planning.
H. D. Curtis, Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students, for Lambert’s problem and porkchop plots.
H. J. Allen and A. J. Eggers, “A study of the motion and aerodynamic heating of ballistic missiles entering the earth’s atmosphere at high supersonic speeds”, NACA Report 1381 (1958).

title: Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole
text:
“Interstellar is the first Hollywood movie to attempt depicting a black hole as it would actually be seen by somebody nearby.”
Oliver James, Eugénie von Tunzelmann, Paul Franklin and Kip Thorne, Classical and Quantum Gravity (2015)
Show code
import sys, math, time, warnings
from pathlib import Path
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve().parents[1] / "gargantua"
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from blackhole import kerr, render as R, sky as SK, disk as D, schwarzschild as S
from blackhole.colour import tonemap, bloom

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})

def show(ax, img, title=None):
    ax.imshow(np.clip(img, 0, 1), interpolation="lanczos")
    ax.set_axis_off()
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)

def hero(img, name=None, w=11):
    h = w * img.shape[0] / img.shape[1]
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(w, h))
    ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
    show(ax, img)
    if name:
        plt.imsave(name, np.clip(img, 0, 1))
    plt.show()

milky = SK.Sky(SK.milky_way(2048))
stars = SK.star_catalogue()

# the film's geometry: spin 0.6, camera at r = 74.1 M, 3.44 degrees above the disk
# (Figures 13-16 of James et al. 2015)
A_FILM, R_CAM, TH_CAM, R_OUT = 0.6, 74.1, 86.56, 20.0
Show code
NX, NY, SS = 1600, 800, 2
tr_film = R.trace_image(R_CAM, TH_CAM, A_FILM, NX, NY, 30, ss=SS, disk=True, r_out=R_OUT)
film, film_lin = R.compose(tr_film, A_FILM, SS, sky=milky, stars=stars, star_gain=0.6,
                           disk=dict(model="film", T=4500, shift="none", r_out=R_OUT), exposure=0.35)
hero(film, "thumbnail.png")








Figure 1: Gargantua as Interstellar showed it, recreated here from the equations: a black hole spinning at 0.6 of the maximum, its thin accretion disk glowing at a uniform 4500 K, seen from 74 M away and 3.4° above the disk, without the Doppler and gravitational frequency shifts (which the film left out) and with a soft lens glare (which the film added).
The black hole in Christopher Nolan’s Interstellar (2014) is one of the most recognisable images in modern cinema: a black disk with a band of glowing gas across its middle and the same band arched over its top and curled under its bottom. It is also one of the very few images in any film that was computed from general relativity rather than designed. The physicist Kip Thorne wrote down the equations, and a team at the visual-effects company Double Negative turned them into a renderer.
This post rebuilds that image from scratch: the spacetime of a spinning black hole, the paths of light rays through it, a camera, a star field and an accretion disk. All of it is in a few hundred lines of Python. It also renders what the film chose not to show, the same disk as it would really appear, with its light shifted in colour and brightness by the motion of the gas and the pull of the hole.
The mathematics is covered properly in a four-part explainer series, and this post links to it as it goes:

title: Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole
section: Kip Thorne and the Double Negative Gravitational Renderer
text:
Kip Thorne and the Double Negative Gravitational Renderer
Kip Thorne is a theoretical physicist at Caltech who has spent his career on black holes, gravitational waves and the strange corners of general relativity. He co-wrote Gravitation, the standard graduate text, and co-founded LIGO, which detected gravitational waves from colliding black holes in 2015. For that he shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics with Rainer Weiss and Barry Barish. Interstellar grew out of a film treatment he developed with the producer Lynda Obst, and he served as the film’s scientific adviser and an executive producer.
According to the 2015 paper, work on the black hole began in May 2013, when Nolan asked Double Negative to build realistic images of a spinning black hole and its disk at IMAX resolution. Thorne wrote a step-by-step prescription for mapping light from the sky, or from a disk, onto a camera near a spinning hole, and checked it in Mathematica. A Double Negative team including Oliver James, Eugénie von Tunzelmann and the visual-effects supervisor Paul Franklin turned it into a production renderer, the Double Negative Gravitational Renderer (DNGR):

about 40,000 lines of C++, running on Double Negative’s render farm of 1,633 blade servers;
23 million pixels per IMAX frame, each traced as a ray bundle, a narrow beam whose cross-section is evolved through curved spacetime, so that stars stay sharp and smooth without flickering;
from 30 minutes to several hours per frame on 10 CPU cores;
the camera’s motion, relativistic aberration, Doppler shifts and gravitational redshift all built in.

Then came the film-making decisions, and they matter for what follows:

Spin. Gargantua’s story needs an almost maximally spinning hole: that is what lets an hour on Miller’s planet cost seven years on Earth. At that spin the shadow is flattened on one side, the disk’s images pile up along the flat edge, and the disk looks off-centre. Nolan and Franklin judged that too confusing for a mass audience, so the images use spin \(a = 0.6\) (in units of the hole’s mass) instead.
Doppler shifts. Gas in the disk orbits at a good fraction of the speed of light. A real observer would see the approaching side blue-shifted and blazing and the receding side red-shifted and dim. The film left these shifts out.
The disk. It is an “anaemic” artist’s disk, not a real quasar disk, which would fry anyone nearby with X-rays. It is thin, it is not accreting, and it shines as a blackbody at a uniform 4500 K.
Lens flare. Audiences expect images filmed through a real camera, so the final images were convolved with the measured point-spread function of an IMAX lens, which gives the soft “veiling flare” glow.

The recreation follows the same recipe, with the same numbers wherever the paper gives them.

title: Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole
text:
The mathematics in five steps
Everything rests on one idea. Light follows null geodesics, the straightest possible paths through curved spacetime with zero interval. Rendering means following those paths backwards, from the camera out to wherever the light came from.
1. The spacetime. A spinning black hole of mass \(M\) and angular momentum \(J = aM\) is described by the Kerr metric. In Boyer–Lindquist coordinates, with \(G = c = M = 1\),
\[
ds^2 = -\alpha^2\,dt^2 + \frac{\rho^2}{\Delta}\,dr^2 + \rho^2\,d\theta^2 + \varpi^2\,(d\phi - \omega\,dt)^2 .
\]
Here \(\alpha\) is the slowing of clocks, \(\omega\) the angular velocity at which space itself is dragged round, and \(\rho, \Delta, \varpi\) simple functions of \(r\) and \(\theta\) (part 3).
2. Three conserved quantities. A light ray in this spacetime carries three constants: its energy, its angular momentum about the spin axis, \(b\), and Carter’s constant, \(q\). Carter discovered \(q\) in 1968 from a hidden symmetry that lets the equations of motion separate (part 3). Together they fix a ray’s path completely.
3. The ray equations. DNGR integrates Hamilton’s equations for the Hamiltonian \(H = \tfrac12 g^{\mu\nu}p_\mu p_\nu\):
\[
\frac{dr}{d\zeta} = \frac{\Delta}{\rho^2}\,p_r, \quad
\frac{d\theta}{d\zeta} = \frac{p_\theta}{\rho^2}, \quad
\frac{d\phi}{d\zeta} = -\frac{\partial}{\partial b}\!\left(\frac{R + \Delta\Theta}{2\Delta\rho^2}\right), \quad
\frac{dp_{r,\theta}}{d\zeta} = \frac{\partial}{\partial(r,\theta)}\!\left[-\frac{\Delta p_r^2 + p_\theta^2}{2\rho^2} + \frac{R + \Delta\Theta}{2\Delta\rho^2}\right],
\]
with \(R(r)\) and \(\Theta(\theta)\) built from \(b\) and \(q\). Five coupled ODEs per pixel.
4. The camera. Each pixel’s direction is converted, by relativistic aberration, from the camera’s frame to that of a local “zero-angular-momentum” observer swept round by frame dragging, and from there into the ray’s initial momenta (part 2, part 3).
5. Shading. A ray that escapes shows the point of the sky it reaches. Lensing conserves surface brightness, by Liouville’s theorem, so that point keeps its true brightness (part 2). A ray that reaches the horizon is black. A ray that hits the disk shows the gas’s light, shifted in frequency by a factor \(g\) that combines Doppler shift and gravitational redshift (part 4).
The ray tracer behind this post integrates those equations with an adaptive Runge–Kutta method, compiled with numba, and checks itself against everything known exactly: the exact deflection angle for a non-spinning hole, Bardeen’s formula for the edge of a spinning hole’s shadow, the conservation of Carter’s constant (which the integrator never uses), and the camera speeds quoted in the DNGR paper. The details, and the checks, are in the explainers.

title: Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole
section: Step 1: a black hole in front of the stars
text:
Step 1: a black hole in front of the stars
Start with no disk at all: a non-spinning black hole and the night sky behind it, seen from a ship in orbit \(30\,M\) from the hole. This is the classic image of gravitational lensing, the one Alain Riazuelo’s film clip made famous and that opens the DNGR paper’s discussion.


Show code
r_cam = 30.0
tab = S.sky_angle_table(r_cam)
cam = kerr.Camera(r_cam, math.pi / 2, 0.0, beta="orbit", fov=90)
NX2, NY2, ss = 1000, 680, 2
N = cam.directions(NX2 * ss, NY2 * ss)
Ns = S.aberrate(N, cam.beta)

def render_sky(v, cap):
    fp = SK.footprint(v, ~cap)
    diffuse = R.downsample(np.where(cap[..., None], 0, milky.sample(v, fp)), ss)
    idx, x, y, mu, om = SK.lensed_stars(kerr.Camera.right_handed(N), v, ~cap, stars)
    pts = SK.paint_stars((NY2, NX2), stars, idx, (x + 0.5) / ss - 0.5, (y + 0.5) / ss - 0.5,
                         mu, 2 * np.abs(om) * ss * ss)
    return tonemap(bloom(diffuse + pts, weights=(0.03, 0.02, 0.01)), 2.0)

# no hole: each (aberrated) pixel sees the sky straight ahead
v_flat = np.stack([-Ns[..., 0], Ns[..., 1], Ns[..., 2]], -1)
img_flat = render_sky(v_flat, np.zeros(v_flat.shape[:2], bool))
v, cap = S.lens_directions(Ns, r_cam, cam.theta, tab)
img_hole = render_sky(v, cap)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.2))
show(ax[0], img_flat, "no black hole")
show(ax[1], img_hole, f"black hole, ship in orbit at r = {r_cam:g} M")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
psi_E = math.degrees(S.einstein_ring(r_cam, tab))
psi_sh = math.degrees(S.shadow_angle(r_cam))
print(f"orbital speed {cam.beta:.3f}c; for a hovering observer here: shadow radius {psi_sh:.1f}°, Einstein ring {psi_E:.1f}°")








Figure 2: The night sky seen from a ship orbiting a non-spinning black hole at 30 M (90° field of view). Left: the same sky with the hole removed. Right: with the hole. Light from behind the hole is bent round it: the Milky Way is split and wrapped round the Einstein ring, and a second, inverted image of the entire sky is squeezed into the bright annulus against the shadow.





orbital speed 0.189c; for a hovering observer here: shadow radius 9.6°, Einstein ring 23.7°


The hole bends every ray that passes it, by an angle that grows without limit as the ray grazes the photon sphere at \(r = 3M\). Rays that pass inside the critical impact parameter \(b = 3\sqrt3\,M\) fall in, which makes the shadow two and a half times wider than the horizon itself. Light from directly behind the hole arrives from every direction round the Einstein ring. Inside the ring sits a second image of the whole sky, and inside that a third, each about \(e^{\pi} \approx 23\) times thinner than the last (part 1).

title: Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole
text:
Step 2: spin
Now let the hole spin. Frame dragging carries light round with the hole: rays travelling with the rotation can skim closer before escaping, and rays travelling against it are captured further out. The shadow loses its circular symmetry.


Show code
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4.5))
for ax, a in zip(axs, [0.0, 0.6, 0.999]):
    tr = R.trace_image(R_CAM, TH_CAM, a, 600, 600, 12, ss=2, disk=False)
    img, _ = R.compose(tr, a, 2, sky=milky, stars=stars, star_gain=0.8, exposure=3.0)
    show(ax, img, f"a = {a}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 3: The sky round black holes of three spins, seen from the film’s camera position, 74.1 M away. The hole rotates so that its left side moves towards the camera. As the spin rises the shadow shifts to the right and its approaching edge flattens: at Gargantua’s story spin it is a ‘D’.





This is the shape Nolan and Franklin turned down. At the film’s \(a = 0.6\) the shadow is still nearly round and almost centred. At \(a = 0.999\) it is a D flattened on the approaching side, which is the first thing a viewer would notice about a fast-spinning black hole (part 3).

title: Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole
section: Step 3: Gargantua as the film showed it
text:
Step 3: Gargantua as the film showed it
Add the disk: a thin sheet of gas in the equatorial plane, orbiting on circular geodesics from the innermost stable orbit (\(3.83\,M\) for \(a = 0.6\)) out to about \(20\,M\), glowing like a 4500 K blackbody and seen from the film’s camera position. The disk is a flat ring, yet the image wraps it over and under the hole. Light leaving the top face of the far side of the disk passes over the hole and is bent down towards the camera, so the far side appears arched above the shadow. Light from the underside of the far side passes beneath the hole and is bent up, forming the ring below the shadow. A third, thin image of the top face hugs the shadow’s edge.
The difference spin makes is clearest with the disk in place. Here the same disk surrounds a hole at the film’s spin and at nearly the story’s spin (compare Figures 14 and 15a of the DNGR paper):


Show code
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 3.7))
for ax, a in zip(axs, [0.6, 0.999]):
    tr = R.trace_image(R_CAM, TH_CAM, a, 800, 400, 30, ss=2, disk=True, r_out=R_OUT, r_in=D.isco(A_FILM))
    img, _ = R.compose(tr, a, 2, sky=milky, stars=stars, star_gain=0.6,
                       disk=dict(model="film", T=4500, shift="none", r_out=R_OUT), exposure=0.35)
    show(ax, img, f"a = {a}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 4: The same disk (from 3.83 M to 20 M, no frequency shifts) round a hole spinning at a = 0.6 (left) and at a = 0.999 (right), seen from the same camera. At high spin the shadow flattens on its left, approaching side, extra thin images of the disk crowd along the flat edge, and the disk looks off-centre: the confusion the film-makers avoided.

title: Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole
section: Step 4: switching on the physics the film left out
text:
Step 4: switching on the physics the film left out
The gas does not sit still. At the inner edge of the disk it orbits at more than half the speed of light, so its light is Doppler shifted: up in frequency on the approaching side and down on the receding side. Everywhere, it is also gravitationally redshifted as it climbs out of the hole’s well. Both are captured by one factor per ray,
\[
g = \frac{\nu_\text{camera}}{\nu_\text{emitted}} = \frac{E_\text{camera}}{u^t\,(1 - \Omega\,b)},
\]
where \(u^t\) and \(\Omega\) describe the orbiting gas and \(b\) is the ray’s angular momentum (part 4). The shift changes the colour, and through Liouville’s theorem (\(I_\nu/\nu^3\) is the same for every observer) it changes the brightness too. A blackbody at temperature \(T\), seen through a shift \(g\), is exactly a blackbody at \(gT\), so its total brightness scales as \(g^4\).


Show code
hit = tr_film["outcome"] == kerr.DISK
g = tr_film["g"][hit]
print(f"rays hitting the disk: {hit.sum():,} of {hit.size:,}")
print(f"frequency shift g: {g.min():.2f} (receding side) to {g.max():.2f} (approaching side)")
print(f"apparent temperature of the 4500 K gas: {4500*g.min():.0f} K to {4500*g.max():.0f} K")
print(f"total brightness, g^4: from {g.min()**4:.3f} to {g.max()**4:.2f} times the unshifted value")
g_lo, g_hi = g.min(), g.max()


rays hitting the disk: 1,725,377 of 5,120,000
frequency shift g: 0.33 (receding side) to 1.51 (approaching side)
apparent temperature of the 4500 K gas: 1476 K to 6805 K
total brightness, g^4: from 0.012 to 5.23 times the unshifted value


The 4500 K gas appears anywhere from 1476 K to 6805 K. The DNGR paper quotes shift factors of “order 1.5 and 0.4” for its version of this disk, and the range here is 0.33 to 1.51. The paper also shows the effect in two steps, colour first and then brightness. Here are the same two steps:


Show code
for shift in ["colour", "full"]:
    img, _ = R.compose(tr_film, A_FILM, SS, sky=milky, stars=stars, star_gain=0.6,
                       disk=dict(model="film", T=4500, shift=shift, r_out=R_OUT), exposure=0.35)
    hero(img)











(a) Gargantua’s disk with the frequency shifts switched on. Top: the colour shift only, with brightness held at its unshifted value (the step shown in Figure 15b of the DNGR paper): the approaching left side shifts towards white (at 6800 K its gas is almost exactly the display’s white point), and the receding right side towards orange. Bottom: colour and brightness together. This is what an observer at the camera would actually see.











(b)






Figure 5




The true image is lopsided. The approaching side is white-hot and the receding side dims to a dull red-brown, up to 86 times fainter in total light and far fainter still to the eye. The DNGR paper calls the fully realistic disk “exceedingly lopsided, with the hole’s shadow barely discernible”, and it was never a candidate for the film. Nature does not share Hollywood’s concerns. The asymmetry is real, and it is why the Event Horizon Telescope’s 2019 image of the black hole in M87 is a ring brighter on one side.
Here is the film’s version beside the physical one:


Show code
_, lin_full = R.compose(tr_film, A_FILM, SS, sky=milky, stars=stars, star_gain=0.6,
                        disk=dict(model="film", T=4500, shift="full", r_out=R_OUT), exposure=0.35)
full = tonemap(bloom(lin_full), 0.35)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 3.5))
show(ax[0], film, "as in the film")
show(ax[1], full, "with Doppler and gravitational shifts")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 6: The same black hole, disk and camera. Left: as Interstellar showed it, without frequency shifts. Right: as it would really look, with Doppler and gravitational shifts in colour and brightness.

title: Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole
text:
How long it takes
Computing power has moved on since 2014, and a still image at blog resolution is far less demanding than a 23-million-pixel IMAX frame traced as ray bundles.


Show code
n_rays = tr_film["outcome"].size
print(f"film-geometry image: {n_rays:,} rays ({NX}x{NY} pixels, {SS}x{SS} samples each)")
print(f"geodesic integration: {float(tr_film['seconds']):.1f} s on this machine "
      f"({n_rays/float(tr_film['seconds'])/1e3:.0f} thousand rays per second)")
print(f"integration steps per ray: median {np.median(tr_film['steps']):.0f}, "
      f"99th percentile {np.percentile(tr_film['steps'], 99):.0f}")
counts = np.bincount(tr_film["outcome"].ravel(), minlength=4)
print(f"rays escaping to the sky {counts[0]:,}; into the hole {counts[1]:,}; onto the disk {counts[2]:,}")


film-geometry image: 5,120,000 rays (1600x800 pixels, 2x2 samples each)
geodesic integration: 21.2 s on this machine (242 thousand rays per second)
integration steps per ray: median 130, 99th percentile 353
rays escaping to the sky 2,962,609; into the hole 432,014; onto the disk 1,725,377


Each ray takes on the order of a hundred adaptive Runge–Kutta steps. Once a ray map is traced, shading it with a different disk model or a different set of frequency shifts takes a second or two, which is how the film, colour-shift and full versions above all come from one trace.

title: Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole
text:
What this leaves out
A few things that DNGR did, and this recreation does not:

Ray bundles. DNGR evolved the cross-section of a narrow beam around each pixel’s ray using the equation of geodesic deviation, which gives exact magnifications and smooth, flicker-free motion. Here, the same information comes from differences between neighbouring rays: stars are placed by mapping triangles of the image grid onto the sky (part 2), and extended light is filtered with a mip-map.
The disk. The film used a thin disk, a 17-million-voxel volumetric disk and procedurally textured close-ups. Here it is an infinitely thin, opaque disk with a simple streak texture.
The lens and the film stock. DNGR convolved images with an IMAX lens’s measured point-spread function and computed colours with the sensitivity curves of motion-picture film. Here a generic glare and the human eye’s colour response (CIE 1931) stand in.
Motion. In the film the camera moves, so stars stream round the critical curves and the images are motion-blurred. These are stills.

title: Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole
text:
Thorne’s other image
The DNGR paper ends by noting that the same code produced Interstellar’s wormhole, described in a companion paper (James, von Tunzelmann, Franklin and Thorne 2015, American Journal of Physics). The paper’s own assessment is that its work on the disk “retreads largely known ground”, which goes back to Jean-Pierre Luminet’s 1979 image of a disk round a non-spinning hole, computed and then drawn by hand. Its lensing of a star field by a camera close to a fast-spinning hole, with the caustics and critical curves that structure it, was new. A Hollywood film paid for research in general relativity, and the equations to reproduce it fit in a few hundred lines of Python.

text:
