title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
Every statistics course repeats that correlation is not causation. Almost none of them say what causation is, or how to get from data to a causal answer when you can’t run an experiment. Judea Pearl spent forty years building the missing machinery: a language for causal assumptions (diagrams), an algebra for answering causal questions (the do-calculus), and a hierarchy that says which questions each kind of data can answer (the ladder of causation).
This post is a tour of that machinery. It covers the person, the three rungs, the mathematics, working R checks of each idea, and why the work matters for artificial intelligence, both in how modern AI began and in what it is still missing.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
Who is Judea Pearl?
Judea Pearl was born in Tel Aviv in 1936 and trained as an electrical engineer at the Technion, later taking graduate degrees in the United States, including a PhD from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn. After industrial research work on electronic devices he joined UCLA in 1970, where he built the Cognitive Systems Laboratory and has worked ever since.
His career has two distinct halves, and the second grew out of the limits of the first.

Probabilistic reasoning for AI (1980s). At the time, AI reasoned with logic rules and ad-hoc “certainty factors”. Pearl argued that uncertainty should be handled by probability theory, and made that practical by representing a joint distribution as a Bayesian network: a directed graph in which each variable depends only on its parents. His 1982 paper on message passing in trees and his 1988 book Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems introduced belief propagation, an efficient way to compute posteriors by passing local messages along the graph.
Causality (1990s onward). Pearl came to think that a Bayesian network, however good at prediction, says nothing reliable about what happens when you act. His 1995 Biometrika paper “Causal diagrams for empirical research” introduced the do-calculus, and his book Causality (2000, second edition 2009) set out the full theory. The Book of Why (2018, written with Dana Mackenzie) is the popular version and the source of the “ladder of causation”.

He received the ACM Turing Award for 2011 “for fundamental contributions to artificial intelligence through the development of a calculus for probabilistic and causal reasoning”. The citation names both halves.
Pearl is also known beyond science. His son Daniel, a Wall Street Journal reporter, was kidnapped and murdered in Pakistan in 2002, and the family set up the Daniel Pearl Foundation in his memory.

What came before
Pearl did not invent causal thinking from nothing. The pieces he unified were scattered across fields that barely spoke to each other.

Sewall Wright (1921) drew path diagrams for guinea-pig coat colours, the first causal graphs, but the method stayed inside genetics and econometrics.
R. A. Fisher gave the randomised experiment its modern form in the 1920s and 30s. Randomisation works because it deletes the arrows into treatment, which we’ll see is exactly what Pearl’s \(do(\cdot)\) operator does to a diagram.
Jerzy Neyman (1923) and Donald Rubin (1970s) developed potential outcomes, the other major formalism, in which each unit has an outcome under each treatment.
Trygve Haavelmo (1940s) argued that structural equations in economics describe how a system responds to intervention, not just how it is distributed.
Statisticians such as Simpson (1951) documented paradoxes, but statistics had no vocabulary to say which of the two conflicting answers was right.

Pearl’s contribution was to put these into one framework with a precise graphical language, and to prove which causal quantities can be computed from which data.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
The ladder of causation
Pearl sorts all causal reasoning into three levels, which he calls rungs. Each rung asks a qualitatively different question, and, crucially, data on a lower rung can never answer a higher-rung question without extra assumptions.


Show code
rungs <- tibble(
  ymin = c(0, 1.1, 2.2),
  ymax = c(1, 2.1, 3.2),
  fill = c("#9ecae1", "#6baed6", "#2171b5"),
  txt  = c("#08306b", "#08306b", "white"),
  title = c("1. Seeing  (association)",
            "2. Doing  (intervention)",
            "3. Imagining  (counterfactuals)"),
  q = c("What does observing X tell me about Y?",
        "What happens to Y if I set X?",
        "What would Y have been, had X been different?"),
  sym = c("P(y | x)", "P(y | do(x))", "P(y_x | x', y')"),
  ex = c("Do people who take aspirin have fewer headaches?",
         "If I take aspirin, will my headache go?",
         "My headache went after aspirin. Was it the aspirin?")
)
ggplot(rungs) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0, xmax = 10, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, fill = fill)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.3, y = ymax - 0.2, label = title, colour = txt),
            hjust = 0, vjust = 1, fontface = "bold", size = 4.6) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.3, y = ymax - 0.52, label = q, colour = txt),
            hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 3.6) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.3, y = ymin + 0.18, label = ex, colour = txt),
            hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3.3, fontface = "italic") +
  geom_text(aes(x = 9.7, y = (ymin + ymax) / 2, label = sym, colour = txt),
            hjust = 1, size = 5, family = "mono") +
  scale_fill_identity() + scale_colour_identity() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 3.2), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void()








Figure 1: The three rungs of the ladder of causation. Each rung needs strictly more causal knowledge than the one below it.





Rung 1, seeing. Pure statistics lives here: conditional probabilities, regression, and today most of machine learning. Bayes’ theorem, as in the prosecutor’s fallacy, is a rung-1 tool. It tells you how to update beliefs on evidence, but not what would happen if you changed something.
Rung 2, doing. Here we ask about the consequences of deliberate action. The key notation is \(P(y \mid do(x))\): the distribution of \(Y\) in a world where \(X\) has been forced to \(x\), not merely observed there. A randomised trial measures it directly. Observational data can too, if the causal structure is known.
Rung 3, imagining. Counterfactuals concern a specific individual and a specific alternative history: “Would this patient have recovered had they not been treated?” The quantity \(P(y_x \mid x', y')\) reads “the probability that \(Y\) would have been \(y\) had \(X\) been \(x\), given that we actually saw \(x'\) and \(y'\)”. Responsibility, blame, regret and explanation all live here.
A tidy way to remember the difference: the rooster’s crow predicts sunrise (rung 1) but silencing the rooster doesn’t stop the sun (rung 2), and “had the rooster not crowed, would the sun still have risen?” is a counterfactual (rung 3) with an obvious answer that no dataset contains.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
Same data, different worlds
Why can’t rung-1 data reach rung 2? Because very different causal worlds can produce identical observational distributions. Here are two models with the same joint distribution of \((X, Y)\).

Model A: \(X\) is a fair coin; \(Y\) depends on \(X\): \(P(Y{=}1 \mid X) = 0.3 + 0.4X\).
Model B: a hidden coin \(U\); \(X\) is just a copy of \(U\); \(Y\) depends on \(U\) with the same formula, and \(X\) has no effect on \(Y\).



Show code
n <- 1e6
# Model A: X causes Y
xa <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
ya <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.4 * xa)
# Model B: hidden U drives both; X is a copy of U
ub <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
xb <- ub
yb <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.4 * ub)

# intervening: set X by an outside coin
do_a <- function(x) mean(rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.4 * x))
do_b <- function(x) mean(rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.4 * ub))   # X has no arrow into Y

tibble(
  model = c("A: X causes Y", "B: X is a copy of a hidden cause"),
  `P(Y=1 | X=1)` = c(mean(ya[xa == 1]), mean(yb[xb == 1])),
  `P(Y=1 | X=0)` = c(mean(ya[xa == 0]), mean(yb[xb == 0])),
  `P(Y=1 | do(X=1))` = c(do_a(1), do_b(1)),
  `P(Y=1 | do(X=0))` = c(do_a(0), do_b(0))
) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(v) round(v, 3))) |> knitr::kable()












model
P(Y=1 | X=1)
P(Y=1 | X=0)
P(Y=1 | do(X=1))
P(Y=1 | do(X=0))




A: X causes Y
0.700
0.300
0.700
0.299


B: X is a copy of a hidden cause
0.699
0.299
0.501
0.500





The observational columns are identical, and the interventional columns are not: in model A, forcing \(X\) moves \(Y\) by 0.4, and in model B it does nothing. No amount of rung-1 data separates them. You need to say which model you believe, and that is what a causal diagram does.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
section: Causal diagrams and the three basic structures
text:
Causal diagrams and the three basic structures
A structural causal model (SCM) assigns each variable a function of its direct causes (its parents) plus independent noise:
\[
X_i := f_i(\mathrm{pa}_i,\, U_i).
\]
Drawing an arrow from each parent to its child gives a directed acyclic graph (DAG). The graph is the qualitative content of the model: it encodes which variables listen to which, and, just as importantly, which don’t.
Every DAG is built from three elementary patterns, and each carries a different statistical signature.


Show code
# --- graph utilities (edges: data.frame with columns from, to) -----------
parents_of  <- function(e, v) e$from[e$to == v]
children_of <- function(e, v) e$to[e$from == v]

closure <- function(e, vs, step) {
  out <- vs
  repeat {
    new <- setdiff(unlist(lapply(out, \(v) step(e, v))), out)
    if (!length(new)) break
    out <- c(out, new)
  }
  out
}
ancestors_of   <- function(e, vs) closure(e, vs, parents_of)
descendants_of <- function(e, vs) closure(e, vs, children_of)

cut_in  <- function(e, nodes) e[!(e$to   %in% nodes), ]   # delete arrows INTO nodes
cut_out <- function(e, nodes) e[!(e$from %in% nodes), ]   # delete arrows OUT OF nodes

# d-separation via the moralised ancestral graph
d_sep <- function(e, x, y, z = character()) {
  anc <- ancestors_of(e, c(x, y, z))
  sub <- e[e$from %in% anc & e$to %in% anc, ]
  und <- data.frame(a = sub$from, b = sub$to)
  for (v in anc) {
    p <- sub$from[sub$to == v]
    if (length(p) > 1) {
      cm <- t(combn(p, 2))
      und <- rbind(und, data.frame(a = cm[, 1], b = cm[, 2]))
    }
  }
  und <- und[!(und$a %in% z | und$b %in% z), ]
  reach <- setdiff(x, z)
  frontier <- reach
  repeat {
    nb <- setdiff(unique(c(und$b[und$a %in% frontier], und$a[und$b %in% frontier])), reach)
    if (!length(nb)) break
    reach <- c(reach, nb)
    frontier <- nb
  }
  !any(y %in% reach)
}

# backdoor criterion: Z has no descendant of X, and blocks every path
# that starts with an arrow INTO X
backdoor_ok <- function(e, x, y, z) {
  !any(z %in% descendants_of(e, x)) && d_sep(cut_out(e, x), x, y, z)
}

# all minimal valid adjustment sets drawn from observed variables
adjustment_sets <- function(e, x, y, latent = character()) {
  cand <- setdiff(unique(c(e$from, e$to)), c(x, y, latent))
  ok <- list()
  for (k in 0:length(cand)) {
    combs <- if (k == 0) list(character()) else combn(cand, k, simplify = FALSE)
    for (s in combs) if (backdoor_ok(e, x, y, s)) ok[[length(ok) + 1]] <- s
  }
  Filter(\(s) !any(vapply(ok, \(t) length(t) < length(s) && all(t %in% s), logical(1))), ok)
}
fmt_sets <- function(s) {
  if (!length(s)) return("none")
  paste(vapply(s, \(v) if (length(v)) paste0("{", paste(v, collapse = ", "), "}") else "{} (nothing)",
               ""), collapse = "; ")
}

# --- drawing -------------------------------------------------------------
draw_dag <- function(nodes, edges) {
  lv <- unique(nodes$graph)
  seg <- edges |>
    left_join(select(nodes, graph, from = name, x, y), by = c("graph", "from")) |>
    left_join(select(nodes, graph, to = name, xend = x, yend = y), by = c("graph", "to")) |>
    mutate(len = sqrt((xend - x)^2 + (yend - y)^2),
           x2 = x + (xend - x) * (len - 0.22) / len, y2 = y + (yend - y) * (len - 0.22) / len,
           x1 = x + (xend - x) * 0.22 / len,         y1 = y + (yend - y) * 0.22 / len,
           graph = factor(graph, levels = lv))
  nodes <- mutate(nodes, graph = factor(graph, levels = lv))
  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = seg, aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed"), linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x, y, fill = latent), shape = 21, size = 12, stroke = 0.8) +
    geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = name), size = 4) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "white", `TRUE` = "grey80"), guide = "none") +
    facet_wrap(~graph, nrow = 1) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = c(-0.3, 2.3), ylim = c(-0.3, 1.3)) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, margin = margin(b = 6)))
}




Show code
motif_nodes <- bind_rows(
  tibble(graph = "Chain", name = c("X", "M", "Y"), x = c(0, 1, 2), y = 0.5),
  tibble(graph = "Fork", name = c("X", "M", "Y"), x = c(0, 1, 2), y = c(0, 1, 0)),
  tibble(graph = "Collider", name = c("X", "M", "Y"), x = c(0, 1, 2), y = c(1, 0, 1))
) |> mutate(latent = FALSE)
motif_edges <- bind_rows(
  tibble(graph = "Chain", from = c("X", "M"), to = c("M", "Y")),
  tibble(graph = "Fork", from = c("M", "M"), to = c("X", "Y")),
  tibble(graph = "Collider", from = c("X", "Y"), to = c("M", "M"))
)
draw_dag(motif_nodes, motif_edges)








Figure 2: The three building blocks of every causal diagram: a chain (mediator), a fork (common cause) and a collider (common effect).







Show code
motif_tab <- lapply(c("Chain", "Fork", "Collider"), \(g) {
  e <- motif_edges |> filter(graph == g) |> select(from, to)
  tibble(structure = g,
         `X, Y independent?` = d_sep(e, "X", "Y"),
         `X, Y independent given M?` = d_sep(e, "X", "Y", "M"))
}) |> bind_rows()
knitr::kable(motif_tab)





structure
X, Y independent?
X, Y independent given M?




Chain
FALSE
TRUE


Fork
FALSE
TRUE


Collider
TRUE
FALSE






In a chain (\(X \to M \to Y\)) the association flows through \(M\). Conditioning on \(M\) blocks it.
In a fork (\(X \leftarrow M \to Y\)) \(M\) is a common cause (a confounder), which creates a spurious association between \(X\) and \(Y\). Conditioning on \(M\) removes it.
In a collider (\(X \to M \leftarrow Y\)) the two causes are independent, but conditioning on the common effect \(M\) creates a dependence between them.

The last is the surprising one, and it is the rule that Pearl’s d-separation criterion generalises: a path is blocked by a set \(Z\) if it contains a non-collider in \(Z\), or a collider that is neither in \(Z\) nor has a descendant in \(Z\). The d_sep function above implements it by the standard moralised-ancestral-graph test.

Colliders in action
Suppose talent and looks are independent in the general population, but a casting director only hires people whose combination of the two is high enough. Among those hired, the two are negatively correlated: someone with modest talent must be good-looking to have got the job.


Show code
N <- 1e5
talent <- rnorm(N); looks <- rnorm(N)
hired <- (talent + looks) > quantile(talent + looks, 0.9)
c(everyone = cor(talent, looks), hired_only = cor(talent[hired], looks[hired]))


    everyone   hired_only 
 0.001020544 -0.717057871 


This selection effect, also called Berkson’s paradox, is a standard source of spurious findings (“why are the cleverest students so clumsy?”) and a good reason not to “control for everything”. It also has a cosmological cousin: Martin Rees’s fine-tuning argument is a statement about the universes in which observers exist, so any inference from “we observe these constants” conditions on the collider “observers exist”.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
Simpson’s paradox, resolved
Here is the classic reversal, using the figures usually quoted for a 1980s comparison of two treatments for kidney stones: open surgery (A) and percutaneous nephrolithotomy (B).


Show code
ks <- tibble(
  treatment = rep(c("A: open surgery", "B: percutaneous"), each = 2),
  size      = rep(c("small", "large"), 2),
  n         = c(87, 263, 270, 80),
  recovered = c(81, 192, 234, 55)
) |> mutate(rate = recovered / n)

by_size <- ks |> mutate(rate = sprintf("%.1f%%  (%d/%d)", 100 * rate, recovered, n)) |>
  select(treatment, size, rate) |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = size, values_from = rate)

overall <- ks |> group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(overall = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * sum(recovered) / sum(n)))

knitr::kable(left_join(by_size, overall, by = "treatment"))





treatment
small
large
overall




A: open surgery
93.1% (81/87)
73.0% (192/263)
78.0%


B: percutaneous
86.7% (234/270)
68.8% (55/80)
82.6%





Treatment A does better for small stones, better for large stones, and yet B looks better overall. Whether the paradox is a paradox, or which table to trust, depends on the causal story. Doctors give the harder open surgery to the harder cases, so stone size \(Z\) influences both treatment \(X\) and recovery \(Y\): \(Z\) is a confounder.


Show code
pz <- ks |> group_by(size) |> summarise(n = sum(n)) |> mutate(pz = n / sum(n))
adj <- ks |> left_join(select(pz, size, pz), by = "size") |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(`naive P(recover | treatment)` = sum(recovered) / sum(n),
            `adjusted P(recover | do(treatment))` = sum(rate * pz))
knitr::kable(adj, digits = 3)










treatment
naive P(recover | treatment)
adjusted P(recover | do(treatment))




A: open surgery
0.780
0.833


B: percutaneous
0.826
0.779





Adjusting for stone size, weighting each treatment’s within-size rates by how common each size is in the whole population, reverses the naive ranking and favours A. The formula used is the backdoor adjustment:
\[
P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_z P(y \mid x, z)\, P(z).
\]
This answer is only right because the diagram says size is a confounder. If instead the “\(Z\)” were a post-treatment variable (say, a measured side effect of the treatment), adjusting for it would be the wrong move, and the aggregated table would be the right one. The same numbers can give opposite advice. The graph decides, and the data cannot.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
Interventions as graph surgery
Pearl’s central idea is that an intervention is a local change to the model. Setting \(X\) to \(x\) replaces the equation for \(X\) with the constant \(x\), which deletes every arrow into \(X\) and leaves all other equations alone. The result is the truncated factorisation: if the joint distribution factorises over the DAG as \(P(v) = \prod_i P(v_i \mid \mathrm{pa}_i)\), then
\[
P(v \mid do(x)) = \prod_{i:\,V_i \notin X} P(v_i \mid \mathrm{pa}_i)\quad\text{(for $v$ consistent with $x$)},
\]
with the factors for the intervened variables dropped. This is exactly what randomisation does: it makes treatment independent of everything upstream.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
The backdoor criterion
When can we express \(P(y \mid do(x))\) using only observational quantities? The simplest sufficient condition is the backdoor criterion: a set \(Z\) satisfies it relative to \((X, Y)\) if

no member of \(Z\) is a descendant of \(X\), and
\(Z\) blocks every path from \(X\) to \(Y\) that starts with an arrow into \(X\) (the “back doors”).

Then the adjustment formula above is valid. Checking condition 2 is a d-separation test on the graph with \(X\)’s outgoing arrows removed, which is how backdoor_ok is written. Here it is on three graphs with different causes of trouble.


Show code
dag_nodes <- bind_rows(
  tibble(graph = "Confounder", name = c("Z", "X", "Y"), x = c(1, 0, 2), y = c(1, 0, 0), latent = FALSE),
  tibble(graph = "M-bias", name = c("U1", "U2", "Z", "X", "Y"),
         x = c(0, 2, 1, 0, 2), y = c(1.1, 1.1, 0.55, 0, 0),
         latent = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)),
  tibble(graph = "Front-door", name = c("U", "X", "M", "Y"),
         x = c(1, 0, 1, 2), y = c(1.1, 0, 0, 0), latent = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE))
)
dag_edges <- bind_rows(
  tibble(graph = "Confounder", from = c("Z", "Z", "X"), to = c("X", "Y", "Y")),
  tibble(graph = "M-bias", from = c("U1", "U1", "U2", "U2", "X"), to = c("X", "Z", "Z", "Y", "Y")),
  tibble(graph = "Front-door", from = c("U", "U", "X", "M"), to = c("X", "Y", "M", "Y"))
)
draw_dag(dag_nodes, dag_edges)








Figure 3: Three diagrams. Grey nodes are unobserved. Left: a simple confounder. Middle: ‘M-bias’, where the observed Z is a collider. Right: the front-door graph, where the confounder U is never observed.







Show code
latent <- list(Confounder = character(), `M-bias` = c("U1", "U2"), `Front-door` = "U")
adj_tab <- lapply(names(latent), \(g) {
  e <- dag_edges |> filter(graph == g) |> select(from, to)
  tibble(graph = g, `valid adjustment sets` = fmt_sets(adjustment_sets(e, "X", "Y", latent[[g]])))
}) |> bind_rows()
knitr::kable(adj_tab)





graph
valid adjustment sets




Confounder
{Z}


M-bias
{} (nothing)


Front-door
none






Confounder: adjust for \(Z\), as in the kidney-stone example.
M-bias: the empty set is valid. \(Z\) is not a confounder; it is a collider on the path \(X \leftarrow U_1 \to Z \leftarrow U_2 \to Y\), which is already blocked. Adjusting for it would open the path and introduce bias. Habitually controlling for every pre-treatment variable is not safe.
Front-door: there is no valid set among the observed variables, since the only observed candidate \(M\) is a descendant of \(X\). The backdoor route is closed to us. This is where the do-calculus earns its keep.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
The do-calculus
The backdoor criterion is a special case of something more general. Pearl’s do-calculus consists of three rules for transforming expressions containing \(do(\cdot)\). Write \(G_{\overline{X}}\) for the graph with arrows into \(X\) deleted, and \(G_{\underline{Z}}\) for the graph with arrows out of \(Z\) deleted. For disjoint sets of variables \(X, Y, Z, W\):
Rule 1: insert or delete an observation. \[
P(y \mid do(x), z, w) = P(y \mid do(x), w) \quad\text{if } (Y \perp Z \mid X, W)_{G_{\overline{X}}}.
\]
Rule 2: exchange an action for an observation. \[
P(y \mid do(x), do(z), w) = P(y \mid do(x), z, w) \quad\text{if } (Y \perp Z \mid X, W)_{G_{\overline{X}\,\underline{Z}}}.
\]
Rule 3: insert or delete an action. \[
P(y \mid do(x), do(z), w) = P(y \mid do(x), w) \quad\text{if } (Y \perp Z \mid X, W)_{G_{\overline{X}\,\overline{Z(W)}}},
\] where \(Z(W)\) is the set of \(Z\)-nodes that are not ancestors of any \(W\)-node in \(G_{\overline{X}}\).
Each rule says that when a certain d-separation holds in a surgically modified graph, two interventional or observational expressions are equal. Rule 1 is d-separation itself; Rule 2 is the licence to treat “seeing” as “doing” once confounding is cut away; Rule 3 says some interventions have no effect at all.
The results that make this more than a curiosity are:

Soundness: every equality derived with the rules is true in every model compatible with the graph.
Completeness (Shpitser & Pearl, and independently Huang & Valtorta, 2006): if a causal effect can be identified from the graph and the observational distribution at all, then some sequence of do-calculus steps will derive it. An algorithm, the ID algorithm, finds one automatically, and returns “not identifiable” otherwise.

So whether a causal question is answerable from your data is a decidable property of the diagram.

The backdoor formula, derived
Let \(Z\) satisfy the backdoor criterion. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(y \mid do(x)) &= \sum_z P(y \mid do(x), z)\,P(z \mid do(x)) && \text{(probability)}\\
&= \sum_z P(y \mid x, z)\,P(z \mid do(x)) && \text{(Rule 2: } Y \perp X \mid Z \text{ once back doors are cut)}\\
&= \sum_z P(y \mid x, z)\,P(z) && \text{(Rule 3: } Z \perp X \text{ in } G_{\overline{X}}\text{, since } Z \text{ is not a descendant)}.
\end{aligned}
\]


The front-door formula
Now the harder case: \(U\) is never observed, so we can’t adjust for it, but we have a mediator \(M\) that is shielded from \(U\). A (hypothetical) example: genotype \(U\) affects both smoking \(X\) and cancer \(Y\) and cannot be measured; smoking acts on cancer only through tar deposits \(M\). Three applications of the rules give
\[
P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_m P(m \mid x) \sum_{x'} P(y \mid x', m)\, P(x').
\]
The reasoning has three steps, each licensed by a rule. Here the graph conditions are checked by machine.


Show code
fd <- dag_edges |> filter(graph == "Front-door") |> select(from, to)
tibble(
  step = c("1. P(m | do(x)) = P(m | x)       [Rule 2: X's own effect on M is unconfounded]",
           "2. P(y | do(m)) = sum_x' P(y | m, x') P(x')   [backdoor via X]",
           "3. P(y | do(x), do(m)) = P(y | do(m))   [Rule 3: once M is set, X is irrelevant]"),
  `graph condition holds?` = c(
    d_sep(cut_out(fd, "X"), "X", "M"),
    backdoor_ok(fd, "M", "Y", "X"),
    d_sep(cut_in(fd, c("X", "M")), "X", "Y", "M")
  )
) |> knitr::kable()









step
graph condition holds?




1. P(m | do(x)) = P(m | x) [Rule 2: X’s own effect on M is unconfounded]
TRUE


2. P(y | do(m)) = sum_x’ P(y | m, x’) P(x’) [backdoor via X]
TRUE


3. P(y | do(x), do(m)) = P(y | do(m)) [Rule 3: once M is set, X is irrelevant]
TRUE





Now the numerical test. Simulate a world with a genuine hidden confounder, so we know the true answer, and see whether the front-door formula recovers it from only the observed \((X, M, Y)\).


Show code
# SCM:  U -> X, U -> Y, X -> M -> Y     (U hidden)
n <- 2e6
sim <- function(do_x = NULL) {
  u <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
  x <- if (is.null(do_x)) rbinom(n, 1, 0.2 + 0.6 * u) else rep(do_x, n)
  m <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.1 + 0.7 * x)
  y <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.1 + 0.5 * m + 0.3 * u)
  data.frame(x, m, y)
}
d <- sim()

# ground truth: actually intervene in the simulator
truth <- c(`do(X=0)` = mean(sim(0)$y), `do(X=1)` = mean(sim(1)$y))
# naive: just condition on X
naive <- c(`do(X=0)` = mean(d$y[d$x == 0]), `do(X=1)` = mean(d$y[d$x == 1]))
# front-door formula using only observed x, m, y
front <- function(d, x) {
  px <- prop.table(table(d$x))
  sum(sapply(0:1, \(m) {
    pm <- mean(d$m[d$x == x] == m)
    inner <- sum(sapply(0:1, \(xp) mean(d$y[d$x == xp & d$m == m]) * px[as.character(xp)]))
    pm * inner
  }))
}
fdoor <- c(`do(X=0)` = front(d, 0), `do(X=1)` = front(d, 1))

res <- rbind(`True (simulated intervention)` = truth,
             `Naive conditioning on X` = naive,
             `Front-door formula` = fdoor)
res <- cbind(res, `effect (do1 - do0)` = res[, 2] - res[, 1])
knitr::kable(round(res, 3))






do(X=0)
do(X=1)
effect (do1 - do0)




True (simulated intervention)
0.300
0.650
0.350


Naive conditioning on X
0.210
0.740
0.530


Front-door formula
0.299
0.651
0.352





The naive contrast overstates the effect, because people with high \(U\) are both more likely to have \(X = 1\) and more likely to have \(Y = 1\). The front-door formula, which never sees \(U\), lands on the interventional truth.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
Rung 3: counterfactuals
Rungs 1 and 2 describe populations. Counterfactuals describe one unit. Pearl’s recipe has three steps, given a fully specified SCM and an observed outcome:

Abduction: update the noise terms \(U\) to be consistent with what was observed.
Action: apply the intervention \(do(X = x')\) to the model.
Prediction: compute the outcome in the modified model, using the updated \(U\).

The result is the counterfactual \(Y_{x'}(u)\). Counterfactuals are defined inside a model, as a mutilated model plus the unit’s own unobserved background, rather than as events in other physical worlds. That is a useful contrast with the many-worlds interpretation, where the alternative branches are taken to be real. Pearl’s counterfactuals are a way of reasoning, whatever one thinks about branching universes.

Probability of necessity
A very practical rung-3 quantity is the probability of necessity,
\[
\mathrm{PN} = P(Y_{x'} = 0 \mid X = x,\, Y = 1),
\]
“given that the treated patient recovered, the chance they would not have recovered without treatment”. It is what a court means by “but for” causation, and it is not identified by experiments alone. Tian and Pearl (2000) showed that experimental and observational data nevertheless bound it:
\[
\max\!\left\{0,\ \frac{P(y) - P(y_{x'})}{P(x, y)}\right\} \;\le\; \mathrm{PN} \;\le\; \min\!\left\{1,\ \frac{P(y'_{x'}) - P(x', y')}{P(x, y)}\right\}.
\]
We can test this because we can build a population in which each person’s response type is known. There are four types: doomed (never recovers), immune (always recovers), causal (recovers only if treated) and preventive (recovers only if untreated). Doctors tend to treat the people most likely to benefit, so treatment is confounded.


Show code
types <- tibble(
  type = c("doomed", "immune", "causal", "preventive"),
  p    = c(0.30, 0.25, 0.35, 0.10),    # population share
  y0   = c(0, 1, 0, 1),                # recovery without treatment
  y1   = c(0, 1, 1, 0),                # recovery with treatment
  px   = c(0.30, 0.50, 0.70, 0.40)     # P(treated | type): confounded
) |> mutate(
  p_x1 = p * px,           # P(type, X = 1)
  p_x0 = p * (1 - px)      # P(type, X = 0)
)

# observational probabilities
P_x1y1 <- sum(types$p_x1 * types$y1)
P_x0y0 <- sum(types$p_x0 * (1 - types$y0))
P_y1   <- sum(types$p_x1 * types$y1) + sum(types$p_x0 * types$y0)
# interventional (experimental) probabilities
P_y_do0 <- sum(types$p * types$y0)
P_y_do1 <- sum(types$p * types$y1)

lower <- max(0, (P_y1 - P_y_do0) / P_x1y1)
upper <- min(1, ((1 - P_y_do0) - P_x0y0) / P_x1y1)

# ground truth PN, available only because we know each person's type
pn_true <- sum(types$p_x1[types$type == "causal"]) /
           sum(types$p_x1 * types$y1)

tibble(
  quantity = c("Naive risk difference  P(y|x) - P(y|x')",
               "Causal effect  P(y|do(x)) - P(y|do(x'))",
               "PN lower bound", "PN true value (needs the types)", "PN upper bound"),
  value = c(P_x1y1 / sum(types$p_x1) - sum(types$p_x0 * types$y0) / sum(types$p_x0),
            P_y_do1 - P_y_do0, lower, pn_true, upper)
) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)





quantity
value




Naive risk difference P(y|x) - P(y|x’)
0.370


Causal effect P(y|do(x)) - P(y|do(x’))
0.250


PN lower bound
0.554


PN true value (needs the types)
0.662


PN upper bound
0.905





The true probability of necessity lies inside the bounds, as the theory requires, but the bounds are not tight: experiments and observations together say it is somewhere in an interval, and only extra assumptions (for example, no preventive types, called monotonicity) or knowledge of the mechanism can pin it down. That is the content of “rung 3 needs more than rung 2”.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
Why it matters for AI

Genesis: how Pearl shaped early modern AI
Before the late 1980s, the dominant AI approach to uncertainty was to attach ad-hoc “certainty factors” to rules, as in the medical expert system MYCIN, or to avoid numbers altogether. Probability was dismissed as intractable: a joint distribution over \(n\) binary variables has \(2^n\) entries.
Pearl’s insight was that real domains have structure, since most variables are directly relevant to only a few others, and that a DAG captures that structure and makes inference local. Belief propagation computes exact marginals on trees by passing messages between neighbours, in time linear in the number of variables. The same machinery spread through the field:

Probabilistic graphical models, developed by Lauritzen and Spiegelhalter, Jordan, Koller and Friedman and many others, built a whole toolkit (junction trees, variational inference, structure learning) on Bayesian networks.
Hidden Markov models and Kalman filters, the workhorses of speech recognition and tracking, turned out to be special cases of belief propagation on chains.
Error-correcting codes: the decoders for turbo and LDPC codes, used in mobile networks and satellite links, were recognised in the late 1990s as loopy belief propagation (McEliece, MacKay and Cheng’s paper “Turbo decoding as an instance of Pearl’s belief propagation algorithm”). Pearl’s message-passing idea is inside the phone in your pocket.
Statistical physics: belief propagation has deep ties to mean-field theory and the Bethe approximation. Fixed points of belief-propagation maps and mean-field theory with annealed disorder are discussed elsewhere on this blog, and they are the same mathematics.

The 1980s revolution made reasoning under uncertainty a respectable engineering discipline, and set the stage for the data-driven AI that followed.


Ongoing: what modern AI is missing
Pearl’s later complaint is that the field took the first half of his work and mostly ignored the second. In a 2018 essay (Theoretical impediments to machine learning with seven sparks from the causal revolution) he characterised deep learning as, in effect, sophisticated curve fitting: powerful, but confined to rung 1. The issues are concrete.

Distribution shift and robustness. A model that learns \(P(y \mid x)\) is correct only while the data-generating process stays put. Causal mechanisms are the parts that tend to stay stable under change, which is the motivation for invariant risk minimisation (Arjovsky et al.) and for causal representation learning (Schölkopf et al.).
Decisions, not predictions. Recommendation, pricing and treatment systems are used to intervene. Evaluating a new policy from logs of an old one is a rung-2 question, handled by off-policy evaluation and counterfactual reasoning in advertising and reinforcement learning (Bottou et al. and others).
Fairness. “Would this loan decision have been different had the applicant been of another group, all else causally equal?” is a counterfactual, and counterfactual fairness (Kusner et al.) formalises it. Purely associational fairness metrics can be satisfied by models that are plainly discriminatory, and vice versa.
Explanation. Counterfactual explanations (“you would have been approved with an income £3,000 higher”) are rung-3 statements. Regulators increasingly want them.
Large language models. Models trained to predict text have absorbed enormous amounts of causal talk, and can often answer causal questions correctly, but they can also fail in fluent and confident ways. Benchmarks such as CLadder and Corr2Cause were built to separate genuine causal reasoning from pattern recall. Whether next-token prediction can climb the ladder, or only mimic having climbed it, is an open and live debate, and Pearl has been a prominent sceptic.
Agents. An AI agent acts, and every action is an intervention on a system whose logs were generated by other behaviour. Judging whether an agent’s intervention caused an outcome, rather than coincided with it, is a rung-2 and rung-3 problem. The instrumentation ideas in Instrumenting Agent Cybernetics are about observing agent behaviour, and the do-calculus is the natural language for asking what those observations imply.



Caveats and critics
Pearl’s framework is not universally embraced, and honest accounts note the disagreements.

Identification results depend on the diagram being right. The calculus tells you what follows from your assumptions, but cannot validate them from observational data. Sensitivity analysis and domain knowledge remain essential.
The potential-outcomes school (Rubin, Imbens and others) reaches many of the same results by different means, and some statisticians prefer it for its focus on estimation. The two frameworks are formally equivalent in the cases they both cover, and the long-running debate has been more about style and emphasis than about disagreement on the mathematics.
Pearl is known for strong opinions, including about the field’s slowness to adopt graphical methods. Whatever one thinks of his tone, the technical results (soundness, completeness, the front-door and backdoor criteria) are not in dispute.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
Takeaways

Pearl has two legacies: Bayesian networks and belief propagation, which gave AI a workable theory of uncertainty in the 1980s, and causal inference, which gave science a formal language for intervention and counterfactuals.
The ladder of causation (seeing, doing, imagining) organises questions by what knowledge they require. Data at one rung cannot answer a question at a higher rung without causal assumptions.
A causal diagram is the assumption set. d-separation reads independence off it, graph surgery models an intervention, and the backdoor and front-door formulas are corollaries of the three do-calculus rules.
The do-calculus is complete: whether a causal effect is identifiable from observational data is a decidable property of the graph.
Counterfactuals need more than experiments, but experiments and observations together can bound them, as with the probability of necessity.
For AI, the lesson is that prediction is not the same as understanding what happens when you act. Robustness, policy evaluation, fairness, explanation and agent oversight are all causal questions, which is why Pearl’s frameworks keep reappearing in current research.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
Further reading

Judea Pearl and Dana Mackenzie, The Book of Why (2018). The accessible introduction and source of the ladder.
Judea Pearl, Causality: Models, Reasoning and Inference (2nd ed., 2009). The full theory.
Judea Pearl, Madelyn Glymour and Nicholas Jewell, Causal Inference in Statistics: A Primer (2016). A short textbook.
Judea Pearl, “Causal diagrams for empirical research”, Biometrika (1995). The origin of the do-calculus.
Ilya Shpitser and Judea Pearl, “Identification of joint interventional distributions in recursive semi-Markovian causal models” (2006). Completeness.
Bernhard Schölkopf et al., “Toward causal representation learning”, Proceedings of the IEEE (2021). The machine-learning view.

title: The Birthday Paradox
text: Put 23 people in a room and the chance that two of them share a birthday is better than 50%. It feels wrong, which is why it’s called a paradox, but it’s a true statement and the arithmetic is short.

title: The Birthday Paradox
text:
Count the complement
Assume 365 equally likely birthdays (ignore 29 February and seasonal effects). Computing “at least one match” directly is messy, so compute the opposite: no one shares a birthday.
Person 1 can have any birthday. Person 2 must avoid 1 day, so has probability \(364/365\). Person 3 must avoid 2 days, so \(363/365\), and so on. For \(n\) people,
\[
P(\text{no match}) = \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{365-k}{365} = \frac{365!}{(365-n)!\,365^n},
\]
and the answer we want is
\[
P(\text{match}) = 1 - \frac{365!}{(365-n)!\,365^n}.
\]

p_match <- function(n, d = 365) {
  1 - sapply(n, function(m) prod((d - seq_len(m) + 1) / d))
}
tibble(n = c(10, 20, 23, 30, 50, 70)) |>
  mutate(P_match = round(p_match(n), 4))

# A tibble: 6 × 2
      n P_match
  <dbl>   <dbl>
1    10   0.117
2    20   0.411
3    23   0.507
4    30   0.706
5    50   0.970
6    70   0.999


The probability crosses 50% at \(n = 23\) and passes 99% by \(n = 57\).

df <- tibble(n = 1:80, p = p_match(1:80))
ggplot(df, aes(n, p)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 23, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Number of people", y = "P(at least one shared birthday)")







Figure 1: Exact probability of at least one shared birthday as the group grows. The 50% line is crossed at n = 23.

title: The Birthday Paradox
section: Why it feels wrong: pairs, not people
text:
Why it feels wrong: pairs, not people
The intuition says “23 is small next to 365”. But we aren’t asking whether someone matches my birthday. We’re asking whether any pair matches, and the number of pairs grows quadratically:
\[
\binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}, \qquad \binom{23}{2} = 253.
\]
Each pair matches with probability \(1/365\), so with 253 pairs a match is no longer surprising. (Pairs aren’t independent, so this is only a heuristic, but it points at the right scaling.)

title: The Birthday Paradox
text:
An approximation
Use \(1 - x \approx e^{-x}\) for small \(x\):
\[
P(\text{no match}) = \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{365}\right) \approx \exp\!\left(-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{k}{365}\right) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{n(n-1)}{2\cdot 365}\right).
\]
Setting this equal to \(1/2\) and solving for \(n\) gives
\[
n \approx \sqrt{2\ln 2\; d}\;\approx\; 1.18\sqrt{d},
\]
which for \(d = 365\) is about \(22.5\). So the threshold scales as \(\sqrt{d}\) rather than \(d\). That square-root law is what makes hash collisions arrive so much sooner than people expect: a 64-bit hash has \(d = 2^{64}\) values, yet collisions become likely after only about \(2^{32}\) items.

df <- df |> mutate(approx = 1 - exp(-n * (n - 1) / (2 * 365)))
df |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(p, approx), names_to = "which", values_to = "prob") |>
  mutate(which = recode(which, p = "Exact", approx = "Approximation")) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, prob, colour = which, linetype = which)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Number of people", y = "P(match)", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")







Figure 2: The exponential approximation tracks the exact curve closely over the whole range.






n50 <- min(which(df$p >= 0.5))
c(exact_threshold = n50, sqrt_formula = sqrt(2 * log(2) * 365))

exact_threshold    sqrt_formula 
       23.00000        22.49439

title: The Birthday Paradox
text:
Monte Carlo check
Simulate it directly: draw \(n\) random birthdays many times and count how often a duplicate appears.

sim_match <- function(n, trials = 20000) {
  mean(replicate(trials, anyDuplicated(sample.int(365, n, replace = TRUE)) > 0))
}
ns <- seq(5, 70, by = 5)
mc <- tibble(n = ns, p = sapply(ns, sim_match))

ggplot(df, aes(n, p)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2c7fb8", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = mc, colour = "#d95f0e", size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Number of people", y = "P(match)")







Figure 3: Monte Carlo estimates (points, 20,000 trials each) against the exact curve.





The simulated points sit on the exact curve to within sampling noise (about \(\pm 0.007\) at 20,000 trials).

title: The Birthday Paradox
text:
Takeaways

Count the complement: “no shared birthday” is a clean product.
The surprise comes from \(\binom{n}{2}\) pairs, not \(n\) people.
Collision thresholds scale as \(\sqrt{d}\), a fact that shows up well beyond birthdays, in hashing and cryptographic collision attacks.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
text:
Note



This post’s comparative framing was originally drafted by an AI research assistant under my general direction, synthesizing my own 2022 dissertation and Sclocchi et al. (2024). The mathematics has been independently re-derived and computed in R below, rather than simply reproduced from that draft.
Two pieces of work on this blog turn out to share more mathematics than their subject headings suggest. My 2022 dissertation (Milne 2022) uses the renormalization group (RG) to describe critical phenomena in thermodynamics and financial markets. An earlier post reproduces Sclocchi, Favero & Wyart’s (2024) result (Sclocchi, Favero, and Wyart 2024) that denoising diffusion models undergo a sharp, hierarchy-dependent phase transition. Both are, underneath, the same story: a discrete iterated map, a critical parameter, and an unstable fixed point that separates two very different fates for the system.
This post makes that bridge concrete rather than just asserting it — implementing both maps in R, finding their fixed points numerically, and plotting the resulting cobweb diagrams side by side.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
text:
Two hierarchies, one structure
Both frameworks simplify a high-dimensional system into a multi-scale tree. In statistical mechanics, a 2D spin lattice is grouped recursively into blocks, each decimated down to a single block-spin variable — Kadanoff’s original coarse-graining move. In Sclocchi et al.’s Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), the same tree runs the other way: a class label at the root branches down through latent features to the pixels at the leaves. The parameters line up directly:







Statistical mechanics & RG
Hierarchical diffusion (RHM)




Microscopic spin configuration \(s_i \in \{-1, 1\}\)
Leaf / input variables \(X_i^{(0)}\)


Block-spin variable at level \(\ell\)
Latent feature node \(X_i^{(\ell)}\)


Lattice spacing / scale length
Tree branching factor \(s\)


Correlation length \(\xi\)
Correct reconstruction depth


Potts state dimension \(Q\)
Alphabet size \(v\)


Coupling strength \(K = J/kT\)
Belief in correct sequence \(p = 1 - \epsilon + \epsilon/v\)


Bond recursion under decimation
Production-rule density \(f\)



In both, one parameter controls order versus disorder: \(K\) above a critical value \(K_c\) gives spontaneous magnetic alignment; \(f < 1\) in the RHM gives structured, hierarchically-correlated data rather than unstructured noise.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
section: The RG side: Kadanoff decimation and the critical coupling
text:
The RG side: Kadanoff decimation and the critical coupling
For the Potts model on a hierarchical diamond lattice, decimating spin sites under a scale transformation gives an exact recurrence for the coupling strength \(K\):
\[
K_{\ell-1} = \phi(K_\ell) \equiv \left( \frac{K_\ell^2 + Q - 1}{2K_\ell + Q - 2} \right)^2
\]
The physical critical point — where the correlation length diverges — is the unstable fixed point of this map, \(K_c = \phi(K_c)\). I’ll use \(Q=3\) (a three-state Potts model): it avoids a singularity in the denominator that shows up at \(Q=2\), and it happens to give a clean, exact critical point.

phi <- function(K, Q) ((K^2 + Q - 1) / (2 * K + Q - 2))^2
Q <- 3

Kc <- uniroot(function(K) phi(K, Q) - K, interval = c(1.5, 10))$root

h <- 1e-6
dphi <- function(K) (phi(K + h, Q) - phi(K - h, Q)) / (2 * h)

curve_df <- data.frame(K = seq(0.5, 6, length.out = 400)) |>
  mutate(phiK = phi(K, Q))

fixed_points <- data.frame(
  K = c(1, Kc),
  stability = c("stable", "unstable")
)

cb_below <- cobweb_path(phi, x0 = 3.9, n = 12, Q = Q) |> mutate(traj = "K0 = 3.9")
cb_above <- cobweb_path(phi, x0 = 4.1, n = 6, Q = Q) |> mutate(traj = "K0 = 4.1")
cobweb_df <- bind_rows(cb_below, cb_above)

ggplot() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(data = curve_df, aes(K, phiK), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_path(data = cobweb_df, aes(x, y, group = traj, colour = traj), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(
    data = fixed_points, aes(K, K, shape = stability, colour = stability),
    size = 3, show.legend = c(shape = TRUE, colour = FALSE)
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(stable = 16, unstable = 4)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 6), ylim = c(0.5, 6)) +
  labs(
    x = expression(K[ell]), y = expression(K[ell - 1] == phi(K[ell])),
    colour = "trajectory", shape = "fixed point",
    title = "Kadanoff-Potts RG recursion (Q = 3)"
  )







Figure 1: Kadanoff-Potts RG recursion (Q = 3). The unstable critical coupling sits at K_c = 4; trajectories starting on either side flow away from it toward one of two very different fates.





Solving numerically: \(K_c = 4\), with derivative \(\phi'(K_c) \approx 1.778\) — greater than 1, confirming it’s unstable. A trajectory starting just below \(K_c\) (green line, \(K_0=3.9\)) flows down; one starting just above (orange, \(K_0=4.1\)) flows up and diverges.
One correction to the source material is worth flagging here. The original synthesis described the disordered basin as flowing toward \(K \to 0\). Checking the map directly: \(\phi(0, 3) = 4\), not \(0\) — so \(K=0\) isn’t a fixed point of this recursion at all. The actual trivial fixed point, true for every \(Q\), is \(K=1\): \(\phi(1, Q) \equiv 1\) identically, since numerator and denominator both reduce to \(Q\). It’s also superstable (\(\phi'(1) = 0\)), which is why the “K0 = 3.9” trajectory above collapses onto it so fast.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
section: The diffusion side: belief propagation and the class transition

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
text:
Same bifurcation, two dictionaries
Both maps are governed by the identical mechanism: a system crosses the basin boundary set by an unstable fixed point of a nonlinear discrete map, and the outcome on the other side is qualitatively different from where it started. A magnet losing its alignment, a market crashing, and a diffusion model’s reconstructed class flipping to something else entirely are, in this sense, the same event described in three different vocabularies.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
text:
Schröder’s equation: the linearizing bridge
Both works lean on the same piece of machinery for handling these maps analytically: Schröder’s functional equation (Curtright and Zachos 2011),
\[
\psi(\phi(x)) = \lambda\, \psi(x)
\]
where \(\lambda = \phi'(x^*)\) is the eigenvalue at a fixed point and \(\psi\) is the (unknown) conjugating function. It linearizes the messy nonlinear dynamics of \(\phi\) into simple scaling by \(\lambda\) near \(x^*\) — which is what lets you extend a discrete iteration into a continuous-time trajectory, \(x(t) = \psi^{-1}(\lambda^t \psi(x))\).

A brief aside: the Johansen–Ledoit–Sornette crash model
In my dissertation, applying this to the Johansen-Ledoit-Sornette model of financial bubbles — where the scaling factor \(\lambda\) is complex rather than real — gives the Log-Periodic Power Law:
\[
F(x) = x^\beta\, G(\omega \log x)
\]
with \(G\) periodic and \(x = |t_c - t|\) the distance from the crash time \(t_c\) (Johansen, Ledoit, and Sornette 1998). The oscillations get faster (in \(x\)) as the crash approaches, which is the model’s signature prediction of accelerating, log-periodic herding behaviour before a crash.

lppl <- function(x, beta = 0.3, A = 1, B = 0.3, omega = 6, phase = 0) {
  x^beta * (A + B * cos(omega * log(x) + phase))
}
data.frame(x = seq(0.001, 1, length.out = 2000)) |>
  mutate(Fx = lppl(x)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, Fx)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  labs(
    x = expression("|" * t[c] - t * "|" ~ "(time to crash, decreasing rightward)"),
    y = "F(x)  (illustrative index level)"
  )







Figure 3: Illustrative log-periodic power law approaching a critical time – not fitted to real market data, just the functional form.





Sclocchi et al. don’t solve an analogue of this — but they make a structural observation that plays a similar bridging role. The convolutional U-Net used for denoising naturally approximates belief propagation: the encoder path acts as the upward BP pass (coarse-graining noisy pixels into abstract features), and the decoder path with its skip connections acts as the downward pass, mixing global class belief back down with local detail to reconstruct clean pixels.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
section: Where the analogy breaks: scale invariance
text:
Where the analogy breaks: scale invariance
The two frameworks diverge on one point worth stating plainly rather than glossing over. In the RG picture, criticality brings true continuous scale invariance: the correlation length diverges, the lattice spacing becomes irrelevant, and the system is fractally self-similar — which is exactly why wildly different physical materials fall into the same universality class.
Diffusion models don’t have this. Scale invariance is broken during denoising: the macroscopic scale (the class label) undergoes a sharp, discontinuous transition at a critical noise level, while the microscopic scale (fine texture) changes smoothly and continuously straight through that transition — sometimes composing pieces of the old class with the new one (a wolf generated with leopard eyes, in Sclocchi et al.’s example). That’s a time-scale separation reflecting the discrete, compositional structure of real data, not the continuous scale invariance of a system at a genuine critical point. The mathematics of the fixed point is shared; the physical picture it’s describing isn’t quite the same.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
text:
Conclusion
Kadanoff’s block-spin decimation and Sclocchi et al.’s belief propagation on the Random Hierarchy Model turn out to be the same functional-equation machinery pointed at two different problems — one asking how magnetic order emerges from a spin lattice, the other how a diffusion model recovers (or loses) a semantic class from noise. See the dissertation for the full RG derivation, and the earlier post for the diffusion side reproduced end to end on real images.
Related: Mean-Field Theory and Annealed Disorder is a refresher on the annealed approximation this post’s belief-propagation map relies on, worked through the classical Curie-Weiss ferromagnet.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
text:

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
text: Third and final part of a series behind Reproducing a Phase Transition in Diffusion Models and Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models. This one assumes the first post’s closed-form jump \(q(x_t\mid x_0)\); the second is a self-contained detour and isn’t needed here.

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
text:
Noising a whole distribution
The first post applied the forward chain to a single starting point, \(x_0=2\). Real data isn’t a point, it’s a distribution — so apply the same closed-form jump to a batch of samples instead. Take something with actual structure to destroy: a two-component mixture, two bumps at \(-2\) and \(+2\).

mu1 <- -2; mu2 <- 2; sd0 <- 0.4; w1 <- 0.5; w2 <- 0.5
r_data <- function(n) {
  is_mode2 <- rbinom(n, 1, w2)
  ifelse(is_mode2 == 1, rnorm(n, mu2, sd0), rnorm(n, mu1, sd0))
}

set.seed(7)
n <- 4000
x0_data <- r_data(n)

T_steps <- 400
beta <- seq(1e-4, 0.02, length.out = T_steps)
alpha <- 1 - beta
alpha_bar <- cumprod(alpha)

noise_to_t <- function(x0_vec, t) {
  sqrt(alpha_bar[t]) * x0_vec + sqrt(1 - alpha_bar[t]) * rnorm(length(x0_vec))
}
x_mid <- noise_to_t(x0_data, T_steps %/% 2)
x_T <- noise_to_t(x0_data, T_steps)

data.frame(
  x = c(x0_data, x_mid, x_T),
  t = factor(rep(c("t = 0", paste0("t = ", T_steps %/% 2), paste0("t = ", T_steps)),
                 each = n),
             levels = c("t = 0", paste0("t = ", T_steps %/% 2), paste0("t = ", T_steps)))
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, fill = t)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") +
  facet_wrap(~t, ncol = 1) +
  labs(y = "density", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







Figure 1: The bimodal starting distribution collapsing to N(0,1) as t increases, under the same schedule shape as Ho et al. (2020).





By \(t=400\), mean \(-0.0108\) and sd \(1.0414\) — the two bumps have merged into plain \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), no trace of where they started.

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
section: What a denoiser actually needs: the score
text:
What a denoiser actually needs: the score
Reversing this requires knowing which direction “more like the data” is, at every noise level. That direction is the score, \(\nabla_x \log p_t(x)\) — the gradient of the log-density of the noisy marginal at time \(t\). Tweedie’s formula relates it directly to the optimal denoiser: the best single-step estimate of the clean signal given a noisy \(x_t\) is a simple function of the score. This is the modern way to think about what a diffusion model’s network is trained to produce — not “the clean image” directly, but a time-indexed family of score estimates, one per noise level.

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
section: The one case you don’t need a network for
text:
The one case you don’t need a network for
For almost any real data distribution, the score has no closed form and has to be learned. But a Gaussian mixture is a rare exception: convolving a Gaussian mixture with Gaussian noise gives another Gaussian mixture, so the noised marginal at every \(t\) — and hence its score — stays exactly computable:
\[
p_t(x) = \sum_k w_k\, \mathcal{N}\!\left(x;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mu_k,\ \ \bar\alpha_t \sigma_0^2 + (1-\bar\alpha_t)\right)
\]

exact_score <- function(x, t) {
  abar <- alpha_bar[t]
  v <- abar * sd0^2 + (1 - abar)
  m1 <- sqrt(abar) * mu1
  m2 <- sqrt(abar) * mu2
  d1 <- dnorm(x, m1, sqrt(v))
  d2 <- dnorm(x, m2, sqrt(v))
  p <- w1 * d1 + w2 * d2
  (w1 * d1 * (-(x - m1) / v) + w2 * d2 * (-(x - m2) / v)) / p
}

log_p_t <- function(x, t) {
  abar <- alpha_bar[t]
  v <- abar * sd0^2 + (1 - abar)
  m1 <- sqrt(abar) * mu1
  m2 <- sqrt(abar) * mu2
  log(w1 * dnorm(x, m1, sqrt(v)) + w2 * dnorm(x, m2, sqrt(v)))
}

h <- 1e-5
test_x <- c(-1, 0, 0.5, 1.5)
numeric_score <- (log_p_t(test_x + h, 100) - log_p_t(test_x - h, 100)) / (2 * h)
analytic_score <- exact_score(test_x, 100)

Checked against a numerical derivative of \(\log p_t(x)\) at \(t=100\), four test points: numeric gives -2.16329, 0, 3.52389, 0.7375, the closed form gives -2.16329, 0, 3.52389, 0.7375 — matching to the precision shown.

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
text:
Reversing it, exactly
The ancestral-sampling reverse update, written in terms of the score:
\[
x_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t + \beta_t\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x_t)\Big) + \sqrt{\beta_t}\, z, \qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \text{ for } t>1
\]
Ordinarily \(\nabla_x \log p_t\) is what a trained network approximates. Here it’s the closed form from the previous section — nothing learned, nothing approximate.

n_gen <- 4000
set.seed(11)
x_gen <- rnorm(n_gen)
for (t in T_steps:1) {
  score_val <- exact_score(x_gen, t)
  noise_term <- if (t > 1) rnorm(n_gen) else 0
  x_gen <- (x_gen + beta[t] * score_val) / sqrt(alpha[t]) + sqrt(beta[t]) * noise_term
}

ks_result <- ks.test(x0_data, x_gen)

data.frame(x = c(x0_data, x_gen), source = rep(c("original data", "reverse-generated"), each = n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, fill = source)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60, alpha = 0.55, position = "identity") +
  labs(y = "density", fill = NULL)







Figure 2: Samples generated by reverse diffusion from pure noise, using only the exact score, against the true starting distribution.





Generation recovers both modes: mean/sd of the lower cluster \(-1.9774\) / \(0.3953\) against a true \(-2\)/\(0.4\), and the upper cluster \(1.9727\) / \(0.3994\) against a true \(2\)/\(0.4\). A two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test against the original data gives \(D=0.023\), \(p=0.241\) — nowhere near rejecting “same distribution.”

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
text:
What this stands in for
The diffusion-phase-transition post does exactly this same procedure — forward-diffuse partway, then reverse — but on real ImageNet images, with a trained U-Net standing in for the score computed here in closed form (Ho, Jain, and Abbeel 2020). The abrupt class-flip reported there is a direct consequence of how that (learned, not closed-form) score behaves across noise levels for hierarchically-structured data — the same mechanics as this toy, just with a far richer \(p_0\) than two Gaussian bumps (Sclocchi, Favero, and Wyart 2024).

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
text:
Series wrap-up
Three explainers, one underlying machine: a Markov chain moves data toward noise and, run in reverse with the right score function, moves noise back toward data; mean-field/annealed averaging is how you get a tractable equation for when that reversal preserves the “shape” of the data versus loses it; and the toy model here makes both pieces concrete enough to check by hand. With all three in place, Reproducing a Phase Transition in Diffusion Models and Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models should read as engineering and analysis built on genuinely solid ground, rather than machinery taken on faith.

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
text:
References


Ho, Jonathan, Ajay Jain, and Pieter Abbeel. 2020. “Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2006.11239.


Sclocchi, Antonio, Alessandro Favero, and Matthieu Wyart. 2024. “A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models Reveals the Hierarchical Nature of Data.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2402.16991.

title: Mean-Field Theory and Annealed Disorder
text: Second of three short refreshers behind Reproducing a Phase Transition in Diffusion Models and Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models. The first covered Markov chains; read it first only if that material feels unfamiliar — this one stands alone.

title: Mean-Field Theory and Annealed Disorder
text:
The problem mean-field theory solves
A ferromagnet is a lattice of interacting spins: each one wants to align with its neighbours, but the neighbours are themselves fluctuating, coupled to their neighbours, and so on. Tracking the full joint distribution over every spin is intractable for anything but tiny systems.
The mean-field trick: replace each spin’s actual, fluctuating neighbours with their average value. A many-body problem becomes a single spin sitting in an effective field set by everybody else’s average behaviour — and that’s tractable, at the cost of ignoring fluctuation correlations between neighbours. Sclocchi et al. (2024) (Sclocchi, Favero, and Wyart 2024) use exactly this move — under a different name, “annealed” approximation — to get a closed-form description of belief propagation on their Random Hierarchy Model, and it’s worth seeing the classical version first.

title: Mean-Field Theory and Annealed Disorder
text:
Curie-Weiss, derived
Give each spin \(z\) neighbours, coupling strength \(J\), at inverse temperature \(\beta\). Averaging over its neighbours’ fluctuations, a spin’s effective field is proportional to the mean magnetization \(m\), and self-consistency (the average spin must reproduce the magnetization that produced its own field) gives:
\[
m = \tanh(Km), \qquad K \equiv \beta J z
\]
Folding \(\beta\), \(J\), \(z\) into the single parameter \(K\) is the standard textbook reduction — the actual critical temperature is \(\beta_c = 1/(Jz)\), i.e. \(K=1\) exactly. Below \(K=1\) the only solution is \(m=0\) (paramagnetic: no net alignment); above it, two new nonzero solutions appear (ferromagnetic: spontaneous alignment, sign chosen by symmetry breaking).

title: Mean-Field Theory and Annealed Disorder
text:
Solving it
\(m=0\) satisfies \(\tanh(K \cdot 0) = 0\) for every \(K\) — it’s always a trivial root, present whether or not the interesting nonzero one exists. Searching for the nonzero branch means excluding it explicitly: bracket uniroot away from zero.

nontrivial_root <- function(K, lower = 1e-6, upper = 1 - 1e-9) {
  if (K <= 1) return(0)
  self_consist_gap <- function(m) tanh(K * m) - m
  if (sign(self_consist_gap(lower)) == sign(self_consist_gap(upper))) return(NA_real_)
  uniroot(self_consist_gap, c(lower, upper))$root
}

Ks <- seq(0.05, 3, by = 0.01)
df <- data.frame(K = Ks)
df$m_stable <- sapply(Ks, nontrivial_root)

ggplot(df, aes(K)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = m_stable), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = -m_stable), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = expression(K == beta * J * z), y = "magnetization m",
       title = "Order emerges above the critical point")







Figure 1: Curie-Weiss magnetization vs. K. The nonzero branch only exists above the critical point K=1.





Below \(K=1\), only \(m=0\); above it, a genuine phase transition. Three independent checks on the nonzero branch agree: at \(K=2\), uniroot gives \(m=0.9575\), and simply iterating \(m \leftarrow \tanh(2m)\) a thousand times from \(m=0.5\) converges to \(0.957504\) — the same fixed point found two different ways. Near the critical point, mean-field theory predicts \(m \approx \sqrt{3(K-1)}\); at \(K=1.01\) that asymptotic gives \(0.1732\) against uniroot’s \(0.1717\) — agreement to about 1%, which is the classical mean-field critical exponent \(\beta=1/2\) showing up numerically.

title: Mean-Field Theory and Annealed Disorder
section: The same move, in belief propagation
text:
The same move, in belief propagation
The Random Hierarchy Model’s disordered production rules play the role of the Ising model’s disordered neighbour spins. Tracking every possible realization of the hierarchy’s rules exactly is just as intractable as tracking every spin’s actual neighbours. Sclocchi et al. take the identical shortcut: average over the ensemble of rule realizations (the “annealed” approximation) rather than conditioning on one specific (quenched) realization, and a complicated random recursion collapses into the single deterministic belief-propagation map
\[
p' = F(p)
\]
already implemented and solved in Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models — same recipe (disorder → ensemble average → deterministic self-consistency map), same qualitative payoff (a clean, analyzable bifurcation), different physical dressing. That post doesn’t re-derive the annealed approximation; this is the missing piece that justifies why \(F(p)\) is allowed to be written down as a plain deterministic function at all.
The same self-consistency structure — and the same \(\sqrt{K-1}\)-type critical scaling — also shows up throughout my own dissertation on renormalization-group critical phenomena, where the RG fixed point plays the role \(K=1\) plays here.

title: Mean-Field Theory and Annealed Disorder
text:
What’s next
The final post in this series builds a complete toy diffusion model from scratch — forward noising, the score function, and exact reverse sampling — using the closed-form Markov chain from the first post.

References

title: Bending Light Around a Black Hole
text:
This is the first of four explainers behind Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole. That post renders the black hole from Interstellar, with and without the Doppler shifts the film left out. These explainers work through the mathematics it rests on:
All the code is in the gargantua project alongside the blog, and every number below is computed when the page is built.
Show code
import sys, math, warnings
from pathlib import Path
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve().parents[1] / "gargantua"
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
from scipy.optimize import brentq

from blackhole import schwarzschild as S

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})

# physical constants (SI)
G, c, M_sun = 6.674e-11, 2.998e8, 1.989e30
AU, PC = 1.496e11, 3.086e16

title: Bending Light Around a Black Hole
text:
The Schwarzschild metric
In 1916, a few weeks after Einstein published his field equations, Karl Schwarzschild found their solution outside a spherical, non-rotating mass \(M\). In coordinates \((t, r, \theta, \phi)\) the spacetime interval is
\[
ds^2 = -\left(1 - \frac{2GM}{c^2 r}\right)c^2\,dt^2 + \frac{dr^2}{1 - 2GM/(c^2 r)} + r^2\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right).
\]
The radius \(r\) is defined so that a sphere at \(r\) has area \(4\pi r^2\), and \(t\) is the time kept by a clock at rest far away. The metric becomes singular at the Schwarzschild radius \(r_s = 2GM/c^2\). That singularity is a feature of the coordinates, not of spacetime, but the sphere at \(r_s\) is real: it is the event horizon, from inside which nothing escapes.
From here on we use geometrised units, \(G = c = 1\), and measure lengths in units of \(M\) (strictly \(GM/c^2\)). The metric is then
\[
ds^2 = -\left(1 - \frac{2}{r}\right)dt^2 + \frac{dr^2}{1 - 2/r} + r^2\,d\Omega^2,
\]
and the horizon is at \(r = 2\). To convert back, multiply lengths by \(GM/c^2\):


Show code
def length_unit(mass_suns):
    """GM/c^2 in metres."""
    return G * mass_suns * M_sun / c**2

for name, m in [("Sun", 1.0), ("Sagittarius A*", 4.3e6), ("Gargantua", 1e8), ("M87*", 6.5e9)]:
    L = length_unit(m)
    print(f"{name:15s}  M = {m:9.3g} suns   GM/c^2 = {L/1e3:12.4g} km = {L/AU:9.3g} AU")


Sun              M =         1 suns   GM/c^2 =        1.477 km =  9.87e-09 AU
Sagittarius A*   M =   4.3e+06 suns   GM/c^2 =    6.351e+06 km =    0.0425 AU
Gargantua        M =     1e+08 suns   GM/c^2 =    1.477e+08 km =     0.987 AU
M87*             M =   6.5e+09 suns   GM/c^2 =      9.6e+09 km =      64.2 AU


In the film, Gargantua has a mass of 100 million Suns, so one unit of length is about 1.5 × 10⁸ km, which is roughly the distance from the Earth to the Sun.

title: Bending Light Around a Black Hole
text:
Light rays are null geodesics
A free particle follows a geodesic, a path of extremal proper time. A geodesic \(x^\mu(\lambda)\) extremises the action of the Lagrangian
\[
\mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2} g_{\mu\nu}\,\dot{x}^\mu \dot{x}^\nu, \qquad \dot{x} = dx/d\lambda,
\]
where \(\lambda\) is an affine parameter along the path. For light the interval vanishes, \(g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu \dot x^\nu = 0\), so a light ray is a null geodesic.
The Schwarzschild metric depends on neither \(t\) nor \(\phi\), so the Euler–Lagrange equations for those coordinates give two conserved quantities:
\[
E = \left(1 - \frac{2}{r}\right)\dot t, \qquad L = r^2 \sin^2\theta\,\dot\phi .
\]
\(E\) is the photon’s energy as measured at infinity, and \(L\) is its angular momentum about the axis. Spherical symmetry lets us choose the orbital plane to be the equator, \(\theta = \pi/2\). The null condition is then
\[
-\frac{E^2}{1 - 2/r} + \frac{\dot r^2}{1 - 2/r} + \frac{L^2}{r^2} = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dot r^2 = E^2 - \left(1 - \frac{2}{r}\right)\frac{L^2}{r^2}.
\]
Rescaling the affine parameter rescales \(E\) and \(L\) together, so only their ratio matters for the shape of a ray. That ratio is the impact parameter
\[
b = \frac{L}{E},
\]
which, far from the hole, is the perpendicular distance between the incoming ray and a parallel line through the centre. Dividing by \(L^2\),
\[
\frac{\dot r^2}{L^2} = \frac{1}{b^2} - V(r), \qquad V(r) = \frac{1}{r^2}\left(1 - \frac{2}{r}\right).
\]
This is a one-dimensional problem. A ray coming in from infinity moves inwards while \(1/b^2 > V(r)\) and turns round where \(1/b^2 = V(r)\).

title: Bending Light Around a Black Hole
section: The photon sphere and the critical impact parameter
text:
The photon sphere and the critical impact parameter
\(V(r)\) has a single maximum. Setting \(V'(r) = -2/r^3 + 6/r^4 = 0\) gives
\[
r = 3, \qquad V_\text{max} = \frac{1}{27}.
\]
At \(r = 3M\), the photon sphere, light can travel on a circular orbit, an unstable one, balanced on top of the potential. A ray with
\[
b_c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{V_\text{max}}} = 3\sqrt{3} \approx 5.196
\]
spirals in towards that orbit forever. This splits all incoming rays into two families:

\(b > 3\sqrt 3\): the ray meets the potential barrier, turns round at a radius \(r_0 > 3\), and escapes back to infinity.
\(b < 3\sqrt 3\): the ray passes over the barrier and falls through the horizon.



Show code
r = np.linspace(2.0, 20, 1000)
V = (1 - 2 / r) / r**2
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.plot(r, V, "k", lw=2)
for b, col in [(4.5, "C3"), (S.B_CRIT, "C1"), (6.5, "C0"), (10, "C2")]:
    ax.axhline(1 / b**2, color=col, lw=1, ls="--")
    lab = "b = 3√3 (critical)" if abs(b - S.B_CRIT) < 1e-9 else f"b = {b:g}"
    ax.text(19.8, 1 / b**2 + 0.0008, lab, ha="right", color=col, fontsize=9)
    if b > S.B_CRIT:
        r0 = float(S.turning_point(b))
        ax.plot(r0, 1 / b**2, "o", color=col, ms=5)
ax.axvline(3, color="0.6", lw=0.8)
ax.text(3.1, 0.0005, "photon sphere r = 3", color="0.4", fontsize=9)
ax.axvspan(0, 2, color="k", alpha=0.85)
ax.set_xlim(1.5, 20)
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.055)
ax.set_xlabel("r  (units of M)")
ax.set_ylabel("V(r)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 1: The effective potential for light, V(r) = (1 - 2/r)/r². A ray with impact parameter b reaches the radius where 1/b² meets the curve and turns back. Only rays with b below the critical value 3√3 clear the peak at the photon sphere, r = 3, and fall in.





The turning point \(r_0\) and the impact parameter are related by \(1/b^2 = V(r_0)\), that is
\[
b = \frac{r_0}{\sqrt{1 - 2/r_0}},
\]
and inverting this means solving the cubic \(r_0^3 - b^2 r_0 + 2b^2 = 0\), whose largest root is \(r_0 = \tfrac{2b}{\sqrt 3}\cos\!\big[\tfrac13 \arccos(-3\sqrt3/b)\big]\). That is what S.turning_point evaluates.
The consequence for a picture is immediate. Look towards the hole from far away: every line of sight with impact parameter less than \(3\sqrt3\,M\) ends on the horizon, so the hole appears as a black disk of radius
\[
b_c = 3\sqrt{3}\,M \approx 2.6\,r_s,
\]
which is more than two and a half times the size of the horizon itself. This dark disk is the black hole’s shadow. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope imaged the ring of light around the shadow of M87*. For its mass and distance the formula predicts an angular diameter of


Show code
m87 = 2 * S.B_CRIT * length_unit(6.5e9) / (16.8e6 * PC) * 206264.806 * 1e6
print(f"2 b_c / D = {m87:.1f} micro-arcseconds")


2 b_c / D = 39.7 micro-arcseconds


which is close to the 42 ± 3 µas ring the collaboration reported. (The ring of emission sits slightly outside the shadow’s edge, so the agreement is as good as it should be.)

title: Bending Light Around a Black Hole
text:
The orbit equation
To get the shape of a ray, trade the affine parameter for the angle \(\phi\). Using \(\dot\phi = L/r^2\) and \(u = 1/r\),
\[
\left(\frac{dr}{d\phi}\right)^2 = \frac{\dot r^2}{\dot\phi^2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\left(\frac{du}{d\phi}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{b^2} - u^2 + 2u^3 \equiv P(u).
\]
Differentiating once with respect to \(\phi\) removes the constant:
\[
\boxed{\;\frac{d^2u}{d\phi^2} + u = 3u^2\;}
\]
Without the right-hand side this is the equation of a straight line, \(u = \sin\phi / b\). The term \(3u^2\) (in ordinary units \(3GMu^2/c^2\)) is all of the bending. It is the same correction that makes Mercury’s orbit precess, here acting on a particle with no rest mass.
Integrating it for a fan of parallel incoming rays shows the whole story at once:


Show code
def ray_xy(b, x0=-30.0, phi_max=4 * np.pi):
    """Integrate u'' + u = 3u^2 from a point far to the left."""
    # start on the line y = b at x = x0
    r0 = math.hypot(x0, b)
    phi0 = math.atan2(b, x0)
    u0 = 1 / r0
    # du/dphi from the straight-line approximation at the start, then exact
    du0 = -math.sqrt(max(1 / b**2 - u0**2 + 2 * u0**3, 0.0))
    def f(phi, y):
        return [y[1], -y[0] + 3 * y[0] ** 2]
    def horizon(phi, y):
        return y[0] - 0.5
    def away(phi, y):
        return y[0] - 1 / 40
    horizon.terminal = True
    away.terminal = True
    away.direction = -1
    sol = solve_ivp(f, [phi0, phi0 - phi_max], [u0, du0], events=[horizon, away],
                    max_step=0.01, rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-12)
    rr = 1 / sol.y[0]
    return rr * np.cos(sol.t), rr * np.sin(sol.t)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 6))
for b in np.concatenate([np.linspace(2, 5.0, 7), [5.2, 5.22, 5.3, 5.5], np.linspace(6, 9, 4)]):
    x, y = ray_xy(b)
    col = "C3" if b < S.B_CRIT else ("C1" if b < 5.6 else "C0")
    ax.plot(x, y, color=col, lw=1)
th = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 300)
ax.fill(2 * np.cos(th), 2 * np.sin(th), color="k")
ax.plot(3 * np.cos(th), 3 * np.sin(th), "k:", lw=0.8)
ax.plot(S.B_CRIT * np.cos(th), S.B_CRIT * np.sin(th), color="0.7", lw=0.6, ls="--")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlim(-16, 14)
ax.set_ylim(-10, 11)
ax.set_xlabel("x / M")
ax.set_ylabel("y / M")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 2: Light rays arriving from the left with impact parameters from 2 to 9 (units of M). Rays with b below 3√3 (red) fall into the hole. Those just above it (orange) wind round the photon sphere (dotted) before escaping, and the closer b is to the critical value, the more times they wind. Distant rays (blue) are bent only slightly.

title: Bending Light Around a Black Hole
text:
The exact deflection angle
A ray from infinity that turns round at \(u_0 = 1/r_0\) sweeps out an angle \(\int_0^{u_0} du/\sqrt{P(u)}\) on the way in and the same on the way out. A straight line would sweep exactly \(\pi\), so the deflection is
\[
\alpha(b) = 2\int_0^{u_0}\frac{du}{\sqrt{1/b^2 - u^2 + 2u^3}} - \pi .
\]
Two ways to evaluate this are worth having, because each checks the other.
Quadrature. The integrand blows up like \((u_0 - u)^{-1/2}\) at the turning point. The substitution \(u = u_0 - s^2\) removes this, since \(du = -2s\,ds\) and \(\sqrt{P} \approx s\sqrt{-P'(u_0)}\), which leaves a smooth integrand for adaptive quadrature.
Elliptic integrals. \(P(u)\) is a cubic, \(2(u - u_1)(u - u_2)(u - u_3)\), with roots \(u_1 < 0 < u_2 = u_0 < u_3\) when \(b > 3\sqrt3\). A standard reduction (Byrd and Friedman, formula 233.00) gives, for any starting point \(y\),
\[
\int_y^{u_2}\frac{du}{\sqrt{P(u)}} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{u_3 - u_1}}\;F(\varphi, k),
\qquad k^2 = \frac{u_2 - u_1}{u_3 - u_1},
\qquad \sin^2\varphi = \frac{(u_3 - u_1)(u_2 - y)}{(u_2 - u_1)(u_3 - y)},
\]
where \(F\) is the incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind. With \(y = 0\) this is half the swept angle, in closed form.

Show code
bs = [5.2, 5.3, 5.5, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0, 30.0, 100.0, 1e4]
rows = []
for b in bs:
    aq = 2 * S.sweep_quad(b) - math.pi
    ae = float(S.deflection(b))
    rows.append((b, float(S.turning_point(b)), aq, ae, abs(aq - ae)))

    print(f"{b:8g} {r0:9.4f} {aq:14.10f} {ae:14.10f} {d:11.1e}")
max_diff = max(r[-1] for r in rows)

Far from the hole: Einstein’s 1.75 arcseconds
For \(b \gg 1\), expanding the integral in powers of \(1/b\) gives
\[
\alpha(b) = \frac{4}{b} + \frac{15\pi}{4b^2} + \frac{128}{3b^3} + O(b^{-4}).
\]
Restoring units, the leading term is \(\alpha = 4GM/(c^2 b)\), twice what you get by treating light as a Newtonian particle, because space is curved as well as time. For a ray grazing the Sun this is


Show code
R_sun = 6.957e8
alpha_sun = 4 * G * M_sun / (c**2 * R_sun) * 206264.806

4GM/(c^2 R) = 1.752 arcseconds


which is the deflection the 1919 eclipse expeditions led by Eddington and Dyson set out to measure.


Close to the photon sphere: winding without limit
As \(b \to b_c\) from above, the turning point approaches the photon sphere and the ray winds round it more and more times. Near the critical value the deflection diverges logarithmically. Bozza (2002) derived the strong-field limit
\[
\alpha(b) \approx -\ln\!\left(\frac{b}{b_c} - 1\right) + \ln\!\big[216\,(7 - 4\sqrt3)\big] - \pi .
\]


Show code

ms = b < 1.3 * S.B_CRIT
