Figure 3: The exact deflection angle (black) against impact parameter, with the weak-field series to first and third order and the strong-field logarithm. The weak-field series fails below about b = 10, while the strong-field formula, plotted against the distance from the critical value on the right, holds over many decades close to it.





The coefficient of the logarithm, exactly 1 for Schwarzschild, carries a physical meaning. Each extra half-turn round the hole adds \(\pi\) to \(\alpha\). To add \(\pi\), the distance from the critical value, \(b - b_c\), must shrink by a factor of \(e^{-\pi} \approx 0.0432\). Solving \(\alpha(b) = n\pi\) exactly confirms it:

The same number reappears in a picture: next to the shadow’s edge sits a stack of ever-thinner rings, the second, third and later images of the whole sky, each about 23 times thinner than the last. Only the first one or two are ever visible, but they are there.

title: Inverse Kinematics: Putting the Foot Where You Want It
text:
Second of four explainers behind The Martian Tripod. Part 1 built the forward map from joint angles to foot position, \(\mathbf p = f(\mathbf q)\). Every gait needs the reverse: the planner decides where the feet and the hood should be, and something has to turn that into joint angles. That is inverse kinematics (IK): solve \(f(\mathbf q) = \mathbf p^\ast\) for \(\mathbf q\).
FK always has exactly one answer. IK can have none (the target is out of reach), several (the leg can bend either way), or infinitely many (the robot has more joints than the task needs). This post works through each case on the tripod.
Show code
import sys, math, warnings
from pathlib import Path
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve().parents[1] / "martian-tripod"
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import mujoco

from tripod.build import write
from tripod.params import DEFAULT as P, leg_ik, planar_ik
from tripod.kinematics import foot_fk, foot_ik, rotz

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.25,
                     "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
BRASS, STEEL, RED, BLUE, GREEN, GREY = "#b8860b", "#4a5a6a", "#c0392b", "#2c7fb8", "#2ca25f", "#7f8c8d"

model = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path(str(write()))
L1, L2 = P.leg.thigh, P.leg.shin
LIM = {j: model.jnt_range[model.joint(f"leg0_{j}").id].copy() for j in ("yaw", "hip", "knee")}
def within_limits(q):
    return all(LIM[j][0] <= v <= LIM[j][1] for j, v in zip(("yaw", "hip", "knee"), q))
print(f"L1 = {L1:.0f} m, L2 = {L2:.0f} m; reach between {abs(L2 - L1):.0f} and {L1 + L2:.0f} m from the hip")


L1 = 16 m, L2 = 28 m; reach between 12 and 44 m from the hip

title: Inverse Kinematics: Putting the Foot Where You Want It
section: Divide and conquer: the yaw first
text:
Divide and conquer: the yaw first
The tripod’s leg is yaw, then pitch, then pitch. The yaw turns a vertical plane; the hip and knee then work entirely inside that plane. So the 3-D problem splits in two.

Express the target in the hip’s own frame (undo the hood’s pose, the mount offset and the mount’s azimuth), giving \((x, y, z)\).
The leg’s plane must contain the target, so the yaw is \[\psi = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x),\] and within that plane the foot must reach horizontal distance \(\rho = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) and height \(z\).
Solve the planar two-link problem for \((q_h, q_k)\).

Step 2 already hides a choice. \(\psi + \pi\) with reach \(-\rho\) points the plane the other way and reaches back through the body. It is a valid solution of the equations, but it is far outside the yaw limit of ±0.8 rad, so it is discarded. Step 2 also has a singularity: when the target is directly below the hip (\(\rho = 0\)), every yaw works. A tripod never puts its foot there, but a humanoid’s hip faces exactly this problem when the foot passes under it.

title: Inverse Kinematics: Putting the Foot Where You Want It
text:
The planar two-link problem
Put the hip at the origin and the foot target at \((\rho, z)\), a distance \(d = \sqrt{\rho^2 + z^2}\) away. The thigh, the shin and the line from hip to foot make a triangle with sides \(L_1\), \(L_2\) and \(d\). The law of cosines gives the angle at the knee, and so the knee bend \(\beta\) (the shin’s direction relative to the thigh’s):
\[
d^2 = L_1^2 + L_2^2 + 2L_1L_2\cos\beta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\cos\beta = \frac{d^2 - L_1^2 - L_2^2}{2L_1L_2}.
\]
A solution exists only if \(-1 \le \cos\beta \le 1\), that is \(|L_1 - L_2| \le d \le L_1 + L_2\): the reachable annulus from part 1. When it exists there are two solutions, \(\pm\beta\), mirror images across the hip–foot line.
The thigh’s elevation \(\phi_1\) is then the direction to the foot, corrected by the angle between the thigh and that line:
\[
\phi_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(z, \rho) - \operatorname{atan2}(L_2\sin\beta,\; L_1 + L_2\cos\beta), \qquad \phi_2 = \phi_1 + \beta .
\]
The second term is the angle at the hip in the hip–knee–foot triangle. Writing it with \(\operatorname{atan2}\) rather than an \(\arccos\) keeps the right sign for both branches and stays accurate near the edge of reach. Finally the joint angles are \(q_h = -\phi_1\) and \(q_k = -(\phi_2 - \phi_1)\), using part 1’s convention that a positive rotation about \(+y\) swings a link downward.


Show code
def ik2(rho, z, knee_up=True):
    """Planar two-link IK, written out in full. Returns (q_hip, q_knee) or None if out of reach."""
    c = (rho*rho + z*z - L1*L1 - L2*L2)/(2*L1*L2)
    if abs(c) > 1:
        return None
    beta = -math.acos(c) if knee_up else math.acos(c)
    phi1 = math.atan2(z, rho) - math.atan2(L2*math.sin(beta), L1 + L2*math.cos(beta))
    return -phi1, -beta

def fk2(qh, qk):
    p1, p2 = -qh, -(qh + qk)
    return np.array([L1*math.cos(p1) + L2*math.cos(p2), L1*math.sin(p1) + L2*math.sin(p2)])

foot = (P.stance_radius - P.hip_radius, -(P.stance_height - P.hip_drop - P.leg.foot_radius))
for up in (True, False):
    q = ik2(*foot, up)
    print(f"{'knee-up  ' if up else 'knee-down'}: q_hip = {math.degrees(q[0]):+7.2f} deg, q_knee = {math.degrees(q[1]):+7.2f} deg,"
          f" FK error {np.linalg.norm(fk2(*q) - foot):.1e} m, within limits: {within_limits((0, *q))}")
print("agrees with the project's planar_ik:", np.allclose(ik2(*foot), planar_ik(L1, L2, *foot, True)))


knee-up  : q_hip =   -3.19 deg, q_knee =  +86.16 deg, FK error 0.0e+00 m, within limits: True
knee-down: q_hip = +111.59 deg, q_knee =  -86.16 deg, FK error 0.0e+00 m, within limits: False
agrees with the project's planar_ik: True




Show code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5))
th = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 300)
ax.plot(L1*np.cos(th), L1*np.sin(th), color=GREY, lw=0.8, alpha=0.5)
ax.plot(foot[0] + L2*np.cos(th), foot[1] + L2*np.sin(th), color=GREY, lw=0.8, alpha=0.5)
for up, ls, col in ((True, "-", STEEL), (False, "--", RED)):
    qh, qk = ik2(*foot, up)
    knee = np.array([L1*math.cos(-qh), L1*math.sin(-qh)])
    pts = np.array([[0, 0], knee, foot])
    ax.plot(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], ls, color=col, lw=3, label="knee-up" if up else "knee-down")
    ax.plot(*knee, "o", color=BRASS, ms=8)
ax.plot([0, foot[0]], [0, foot[1]], ":", color="k", lw=1)
ax.plot(0, 0, "ks"); ax.plot(*foot, "ko")
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlim(-20, 50); ax.set_ylim(-45, 20)
ax.set_xlabel("ρ (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("z (m)"); ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right"); plt.show()








Figure 1: The two solutions for the standing foot. Knee-up (solid) is the spider stance the model uses; knee-down (dashed) reaches the same point with the knee bent backwards, which the knee’s joint limit forbids. The faint circles are the loci of the knee: within L1 of the hip and within L2 of the foot. The two knee positions are where those circles cross.





Geometrically the knee must lie on a circle of radius \(L_1\) round the hip and on a circle of radius \(L_2\) round the foot. Two circles cross in zero, one or two points, which is the whole existence-and-uniqueness story in one picture. The joint limits then choose between the branches: the model’s knee range \([-0.3, 2.6]\) rad allows the knee-up solution and forbids the knee-down one. The IK solver needs no special logic to choose; the limits make the choice.

Checking it everywhere
A closed-form IK should invert FK exactly wherever a solution exists. Throwing 50,000 random targets at it, in and out of the annulus, tests every branch of the code.


Show code
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
pts = rng.uniform([-50, -50], [50, 50], (50000, 2))
worst, n_ok, n_out, n_lim = 0.0, 0, 0, 0
for rho, z in pts:
    q = ik2(rho, z)
    if q is None:
        d = math.hypot(rho, z); assert d > L1 + L2 - 1e-9 or d < L2 - L1 + 1e-9
        n_out += 1; continue
    worst = max(worst, np.linalg.norm(fk2(*q) - (rho, z)))
    n_ok += 1; n_lim += not within_limits((0, *q))
print(f"{n_ok} reachable targets: worst round-trip error {worst:.1e} m")
print(f"{n_out} targets correctly reported out of reach")
print(f"{n_lim} reachable in principle but needing a joint outside its limits")


28085 reachable targets: worst round-trip error 2.6e-14 m
21915 targets correctly reported out of reach
17396 reachable in principle but needing a joint outside its limits


Every reachable target round-trips to rounding error, and every unreachable one is reported as such. Most of the geometrically reachable points in this square, about three in five, need a joint beyond its limit. They are behind the hip, above it, or curled under it. So a real IK solver must check limits as well as reach.

title: Inverse Kinematics: Putting the Foot Where You Want It
text:
Singularities: where IK becomes ill-conditioned
At the edge of reach, \(d \to L_1 + L_2\), the leg is straight and the two branches merge. The knee angle depends on \(d\) through an arccos, whose derivative is infinite at \(\pm 1\):
\[
\frac{\partial q_k}{\partial d} = \frac{d}{L_1L_2\sin\beta} \;\to\; \infty \quad\text{as}\quad \beta \to 0 .
\]
Near a straight leg, moving the foot a centimetre outward demands a large knee rotation. Past the rim it demands an impossible one. That is a kinematic singularity, and it is the same thing as the Jacobian losing rank (part 3 computes \(\det J = \rho\,L_1L_2\sin q_k\)). It matters in practice: a controller that tracks a foot target near full reach will command huge joint velocities.


Show code
d = np.linspace(12.05, 43.995, 2000)
cb = (d**2 - L1**2 - L2**2)/(2*L1*L2)
qk = np.arccos(cb)
dqk = d/(L1*L2*np.sin(qk))
d_stand = math.hypot(*foot)
d_rear = math.hypot(foot[0], foot[1] - 7.0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
ax[0].plot(d, np.degrees(qk), color=STEEL, lw=2); ax[0].set_ylabel("knee angle (deg)")
ax[1].semilogy(d, np.degrees(dqk), color=RED, lw=2); ax[1].set_ylabel("d(knee)/d(reach)  (deg per m)")
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlabel("hip-to-foot distance d (m)")
    for x, lab in ((d_stand, "stand"), (d_rear, "reared")):
        a.axvline(x, color=GREY, ls="--", lw=1)
        a.text(x, a.get_ylim()[1]*0.95 if a is ax[0] else 300, lab, rotation=90, va="top", ha="right", color=GREY)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for x, lab in ((d_stand, "standing"), (d_rear, "reared up 7 m")):
    q = math.acos((x*x - L1*L1 - L2*L2)/(2*L1*L2))
    print(f"{lab:14s}: d = {x:.1f} m ({x/(L1 + L2):.0%} of full reach), {math.degrees(x/(L1*L2*math.sin(q))):.1f} deg of knee per metre")








Figure 2: Left: knee angle needed to put the foot a distance d from the hip. Right: how fast it changes, in degrees of knee per metre of foot travel. It blows up as the leg straightens at 44 m. The dashed lines mark the standing pose and the reared-up pose from the main post.





standing      : d = 33.2 m (75% of full reach), 4.3 deg of knee per metre
reared up 7 m : d = 39.1 m (89% of full reach), 5.9 deg of knee per metre


Standing, the leg is at 75% of full reach and well conditioned: about 4° of knee per metre of foot travel. Reared up to look round, it is at 89% of reach and the sensitivity is up by a third. The steep part of the curve is not far beyond. That is one reason the machine in the main post’s video stops to rear up rather than walking tall.

title: Inverse Kinematics: Putting the Foot Where You Want It
text:
Whole-body IK: posing the hood
A walking machine rarely thinks about one foot at a time. With all three feet planted, the question is: where can the hood go? Give the hood a pose (position \(\mathbf p_\text{hood}\) and orientation \(R_\text{hood}\)), keep the feet fixed, and solve IK for each leg separately. Each leg sees its foot target transformed into its own hip frame,
\[
\mathbf p_\text{local} = R_z(a_i)^\top\Big(R_\text{hood}^\top(\mathbf p_\text{foot} - \mathbf p_\text{hood}) - \mathbf m_i\Big),
\]
which is the project’s foot_ik. The hood’s pose has six degrees of freedom and the three legs have nine joints between them, but with the three feet pinned (nine constraints) the nine joints are fully determined by the six numbers of the hood pose. The legs form a parallel mechanism, like a flight simulator’s Stewart platform. In a serial arm, FK is easy and IK is hard; in a parallel mechanism it is the other way round. Here, IK of the hood is just three independent leg IKs.
The useful question is which hood poses are feasible: every foot within reach and every joint within its limits.


Show code
feet = [np.array([P.stance_radius*math.cos(math.radians(a)), P.stance_radius*math.sin(math.radians(a)), P.leg.foot_radius])
        for a in P.leg_azimuths_deg]
def hood_ok(pos, R=np.eye(3)):
    try:
        return all(within_limits(foot_ik(P, i, pos, R, feet[i])) for i in range(3))
    except ValueError:
        return False

xs = np.linspace(-26, 26, 181)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 6))
for h, col in ((16, GREEN), (30, STEEL), (38, RED)):
    ok = np.array([[hood_ok(np.array([x, y, h])) for x in xs] for y in xs])
    ax.contour(xs, xs, ok.astype(float), levels=[0.5], colors=[col], linewidths=2)
    ax.plot([], [], color=col, lw=2, label=f"hood at {h} m: {ok.mean()*(xs[-1]-xs[0])**2:.0f} m²")
tri = np.array([f[:2] for f in feet] + [feet[0][:2]])
ax.plot(tri[:, 0], tri[:, 1], color=GREY, lw=1); ax.plot(tri[:, 0], tri[:, 1], "ko")
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("x (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("y (m)"); ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower left")
plt.show()

top = max(h for h in np.arange(20, 46, 0.1) if hood_ok(np.array([0, 0, h])))
low = min(h for h in np.arange(5, 46, 0.1) if hood_ok(np.array([0, 0, h])))
print(f"centred and level, the hood can go from {low:.1f} m to {top:.1f} m with the feet planted")








Figure 3: Where the hood centre can go with the three feet planted at the standing positions (black dots), at three hood heights, with the hood kept level. Inside each outline every leg has an IK solution within its joint limits. The machine stands at 30 m.





centred and level, the hood can go from 12.7 m to 42.5 m with the feet planted




Show code
hs = np.arange(low, top, 0.05)
qs = np.array([foot_ik(P, 0, np.array([0, 0, h]), np.eye(3), feet[0]) for h in hs])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.4))
ax.plot(hs, np.degrees(qs[:, 1]), color=STEEL, lw=2, label="hip pitch")
ax.plot(hs, np.degrees(qs[:, 2]), color=BRASS, lw=2, label="knee")
for j, col in (("hip", STEEL), ("knee", BRASS)):
    for v in LIM[j]:
        if np.degrees(qs).min() - 10 < math.degrees(v) < np.degrees(qs).max() + 10:
            ax.axhline(math.degrees(v), color=col, ls=":", lw=1)
ax.axvline(30, color=GREY, ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("hood height (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("angle (deg)"); ax.legend(frameon=False); plt.show()








Figure 4: Joint angles of leg 0 as the hood rises straight up, feet planted. Going up, the hip lifts and the knee opens until the leg runs out of reach at 42.5 m. Going down, the hip drops until it hits its −69° limit at 12.7 m. Dotted lines are the joint limits in range; the dashed line is the standing height.





Three different limits shape the region. At the standing height it is a rounded triangle set by the yaw limits: move the hood too far sideways and some leg has to swing more than 46° from its radial direction. The region is the same from about 20 m to 30 m. Above that, reach takes over and the region shrinks fast, from about 720 m² at 30 m to 230 m² at 38 m: a tall machine can lean less far before a leg runs out of length. Below about 20 m, the knee and hip limits start to cut pieces out of it as the legs fold up (the green outline at 16 m). Notice too that the region pokes outside the support triangle. Kinematically the hood can lean beyond its feet; whether it stays up is a question of statics and dynamics, taken up in parts 3 and 4. The planning explainer moves the centre of mass several metres from side to side every step, and this map shows how much room it has to do so.

title: Inverse Kinematics: Putting the Foot Where You Want It
section: Numerical IK: Newton’s method on the Jacobian
text:
Numerical IK: Newton’s method on the Jacobian
The closed form works because this leg is simple. A general chain, such as a seven-joint arm or a humanoid with a flexible spine, usually has no closed form, and IK is solved numerically. The workhorse is Newton’s method. Linearise FK about the current guess using the Jacobian \(J = \partial f/\partial\mathbf q\):
\[
f(\mathbf q + \Delta\mathbf q) \approx f(\mathbf q) + J(\mathbf q)\,\Delta\mathbf q ,
\]
and choose the step that zeroes the error \(\mathbf e = \mathbf p^\ast - f(\mathbf q)\):
\[
\Delta\mathbf q = J^{-1}\mathbf e \qquad\text{(Newton–Raphson)}.
\]
Near a singularity \(J^{-1}\) explodes. When the target is unreachable it doesn’t exist at all. The standard fix is damped least squares, also called Levenberg–Marquardt. It minimises \(\|J\Delta\mathbf q - \mathbf e\|^2 + \lambda^2\|\Delta\mathbf q\|^2\), which gives
\[
\Delta\mathbf q = J^\top\big(JJ^\top + \lambda^2 I\big)^{-1}\mathbf e .
\]
The damping \(\lambda\) trades accuracy for step size. Far from singularities it behaves like Newton. Near one, it refuses to take huge steps and settles for the closest point it can reach. A third, cruder option is the Jacobian transpose step, \(\Delta\mathbf q = \alpha J^\top\mathbf e\). It never inverts anything and always moves downhill on \(\|\mathbf e\|^2\), but it converges slowly.


Show code
def fk3(q):
    return foot_fk(P, 0, np.zeros(3), np.eye(3), q)
def jac3(q, eps=1e-7):
    p0 = fk3(q)
    return np.column_stack([(fk3(q + eps*np.eye(3)[j]) - p0)/eps for j in range(3)])

def solve(target, method, q0=(0.3, 0.3, 0.5), iters=40, lam=3.0, alpha=1e-3):
    q = np.array(q0, float); hist = []
    for _ in range(iters):
        e = target - fk3(q); hist.append(np.linalg.norm(e))
        J = jac3(q)
        if method == "Newton":
            dq = np.linalg.solve(J, e)
        elif method == "damped LS":
            dq = J.T @ np.linalg.solve(J @ J.T + lam**2*np.eye(3), e)
        else:
            dq = alpha*J.T @ e
        q = q + dq
    return q, np.array(hist)

q_true = np.array([0.2, *leg_ik(P)])
target_ok = fk3(q_true)
m0 = np.array([P.hip_radius, 0, -P.hip_drop])
far = m0 + (target_ok - m0)/np.linalg.norm(target_ok - m0)*(L1 + L2 + 5)
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6), sharey=True)
for ax, tgt, title, lam in ((axs[0], target_ok, "reachable target", 3.0), (axs[1], far, "target 5 m out of reach", 10.0)):
    for method, col in (("Newton", RED), ("damped LS", BLUE), ("J transpose", BRASS)):
        q, h = solve(tgt, method, lam=lam)
        ax.semilogy(np.maximum(h, 1e-15), color=col, lw=2, label=method)
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("iteration")
axs[0].set_ylabel("foot position error (m)"); axs[0].legend(frameon=False); axs[0].set_ylim(1e-15, 1e3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

q_n, h_n = solve(target_ok, "Newton")
print("Newton from (17, 17, 29) deg: error by iteration", " ".join(f"{x:.0e}" for x in h_n[:9]))
print("   lands on", np.round(np.degrees(q_n), 2), "deg; closed form", np.round(np.degrees(q_true), 2))
q_b, _ = solve(target_ok, "Newton", q0=(0.5, -0.5, 0.3))
print("Newton from (29, -29, 17) deg lands on", np.round(np.degrees(q_b), 2), "deg: the knee-down branch,",
      "within limits" if within_limits(q_b) else "outside the joint limits")
for lam in (3.0, 10.0):
    q_d, h_d = solve(far, "damped LS", lam=lam, iters=300)
    print(f"damped LS (lambda = {lam:.0f}), unreachable: stops {h_d[-1]:.2f} m from the target, knee {math.degrees(q_d[2]):.1f} deg")








Figure 5: Numerical IK for one leg in 3-D, Left: a reachable target (the standing foot, with 11.5° of yaw), starting from a poor guess. Newton and damped least squares (λ = 3) converge in a handful of iterations; the transpose method crawls. Right: a target 5 m beyond reach. Newton thrashes; damped least squares (λ = 10) settles 5 m short, at the nearest reachable point, with the leg straight.





Newton from (17, 17, 29) deg: error by iteration 2e+01 2e+01 1e+01 8e+00 2e+00 2e-01 8e-04 2e-08 5e-15
   lands on [11.46 -3.19 86.16] deg; closed form [11.46 -3.19 86.16]
Newton from (29, -29, 17) deg lands on [ 11.46 111.59 -86.16] deg: the knee-down branch, outside the joint limits
damped LS (lambda = 3), unreachable: stops 5.83 m from the target, knee -23.2 deg
damped LS (lambda = 10), unreachable: stops 5.00 m from the target, knee 0.0 deg


Newton converges quadratically: once it is close, the number of correct digits roughly doubles each iteration, which is the plunge in the left panel. From this guess it recovers the closed-form joint angles exactly. From a different guess, with the hip raised and the knee nearly straight, it converges just as fast to the knee-down branch, which breaks the joint limits. Numerical IK finds a solution, usually the one nearest the starting guess, and knows nothing about branches or limits unless they are added. That is why walking controllers warm-start it from the previous timestep’s answer.
With the target out of reach, Newton has nothing to converge to, and its steps blow up near the straight-leg singularity. Damped least squares with enough damping does what you would want: it straightens the leg towards the target and stops exactly 5 m short. With too little damping it can stall at a bent-knee configuration, where the error is perpendicular to every direction the foot can move: a local minimum of \(\|\mathbf e\|^2\). Choosing \(\lambda\) is a real engineering decision, and practical solvers adapt it as they go. Every serious IK library uses some form of damping for this reason.

title: Inverse Kinematics: Putting the Foot Where You Want It
section: Moving the foot: task space vs joint space
text:
Moving the foot: task space vs joint space
IK is rarely solved for one point; a swing leg needs a whole path. There are two ways to get from the lift-off configuration to the touch-down one.

Interpolate the joints: blend the joint angles from start to finish. This is cheap and smooth for the motors, but the foot traces whatever curve FK makes of it.
Interpolate the foot: design the foot’s path in space (the gait uses a smooth forward motion plus a \(\sin\)-shaped lift), and solve IK at every instant.



Show code
def smoothstep(x): return x*x*(3 - 2*x)
hood = np.array([0.0, 0, 30])
start = feet[0] + [-7.0, 0, 0]; end = feet[0] + [7.0, 0, 0]
s = np.linspace(0, 1, 120)
path = np.array([start + smoothstep(v)*(end - start) + [0, 0, 4*math.sin(math.pi*v)] for v in s])
q_task = np.array([foot_ik(P, 0, hood, np.eye(3), p) for p in path])
qa, qb = q_task[0], q_task[-1]
q_joint = np.array([qa + smoothstep(v)*(qb - qa) for v in s])
p_joint = np.array([foot_fk(P, 0, hood, np.eye(3), q) for q in q_joint])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.3, 1]})
ax[0].plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 2] - P.leg.foot_radius, color=STEEL, lw=2, label="task-space path")
ax[0].plot(p_joint[:, 0], p_joint[:, 2] - P.leg.foot_radius, "--", color=RED, lw=2, label="joint interpolation")
ax[0].axhline(0, color="#7a6a4f", lw=2); ax[0].set_xlabel("x (m)"); ax[0].set_ylabel("foot height (m)")
ax[0].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")
for j, (lab, col) in enumerate((("hip", STEEL), ("knee", BRASS))):
    ax[1].plot(s, np.degrees(q_task[:, j + 1]), color=col, lw=2, label=lab)
ax[1].set_xlabel("swing phase"); ax[1].set_ylabel("angle (deg)"); ax[1].legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"joint interpolation: foot goes {-(p_joint[:, 2] - P.leg.foot_radius).min():.2f} m below the ground mid-swing")








Figure 6: One step of leg 0 seen from the side, with the hood fixed. Solid: the foot follows the planned path (smoothstep forward, sine lift of 4 m) and the joint angles come from IK at each instant. Dashed: the joint angles are interpolated directly between the same start and end poses; the foot sags below the ground mid-swing. Right: the joint angles for the task-space path.





joint interpolation: foot goes 0.90 m below the ground mid-swing


For a walking machine the foot’s path is what matters: it must clear obstacles and must not scuff the ground. So the gaits in the main post plan in task space and call IK at every control step, a few hundred times a second. Closed-form IK is cheap enough for that. A numerical solver warm-started from the last step converges in one or two Newton iterations.

title: Inverse Kinematics: Putting the Foot Where You Want It
text:
Summary

IK solves \(f(\mathbf q) = \mathbf p^\ast\). It may have no solution, a finite number, or a continuum.
The tripod’s leg decouples: yaw by \(\operatorname{atan2}\), then a planar two-link problem solved by the law of cosines, with two mirror-image branches; the joint limits pick the knee-up one.
Near full reach the solution becomes ill-conditioned: a kinematic singularity, where the Jacobian loses rank.
Hood poses are found by three independent leg IKs, because the planted legs form a parallel mechanism. The feasible region shrinks as the hood rises.
Numerical IK uses Newton’s method on the Jacobian; damped least squares keeps it sane near singularities and out of reach.

Next: Statics and the Jacobian, the same matrix put to work on forces.

title: Inverse Kinematics: Putting the Foot Where You Want It
text:
Further reading

K. M. Lynch and F. C. Park, Modern Robotics (2017), chapter 6 (inverse kinematics).
S. R. Buss, “Introduction to inverse kinematics with Jacobian transpose, pseudoinverse and damped least squares methods” (2004). A short, clear survey of the numerical methods.
C. W. Wampler, “Manipulator inverse kinematic solutions based on vector formulations and damped least-squares methods”, IEEE Trans. SMC (1986). The origin of damped least squares in robotics.

title: Forward Kinematics: Where Is the Foot?
text:
This is the first of four explainers behind The Martian Tripod: Walking a Fighting-Machine in MuJoCo. That post moved quickly through the mathematics of making a three-legged machine walk. These explainers slow down and work through it properly:
Every formula is checked against the same MuJoCo model the main post uses, a 257-tonne tripod with 16 m thighs and 28 m shins.
Show code
import sys, math, warnings
from pathlib import Path
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve().parents[1] / "martian-tripod"
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import mujoco
from scipy.linalg import expm

from tripod.build import write
from tripod.params import DEFAULT as P, leg_ik
from tripod.kinematics import foot_fk

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.25,
                     "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
BRASS, STEEL, RED, BLUE, GREEN, GREY = "#b8860b", "#4a5a6a", "#c0392b", "#2c7fb8", "#2ca25f", "#7f8c8d"

model = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path(str(write()))
data = mujoco.MjData(model)
mujoco.mj_resetDataKeyframe(model, data, model.key("stand").id)
mujoco.mj_forward(model, data)
L1, L2 = P.leg.thigh, P.leg.shin
print(f"thigh L1 = {L1:.0f} m, shin L2 = {L2:.0f} m, hips on a {P.hip_radius} m circle, {P.hip_drop} m below the hood centre")


thigh L1 = 16 m, shin L2 = 28 m, hips on a 2.6 m circle, 2.0 m below the hood centre

title: Forward Kinematics: Where Is the Foot?
text:
Joint space and task space
A robot is described in two ways. Its configuration is the list of joint angles, \(\mathbf q = (q_1, \dots, q_n)\); that is what the motors and encoders know. Its task is described in space: where the foot is, which way the hood points. Kinematics is the map between them, ignoring forces and masses entirely.
Forward kinematics (FK) goes from joints to space, \(\mathbf p = f(\mathbf q)\). It is always easy: there is exactly one answer, found by composing one rigid motion per link. Inverse kinematics goes the other way and is harder: there may be no answer, one, several or infinitely many. That is the subject of part 2. This post builds the tools for FK and applies them to the tripod’s leg.

title: Forward Kinematics: Where Is the Foot?
text:
Rotations
A rotation is a \(3\times 3\) matrix \(R\) whose columns are the rotated frame’s axes, written in the original frame. Those axes stay unit length and mutually perpendicular, so
\[
R^\top R = I, \qquad \det R = +1 .
\]
Matrices with these two properties form the special orthogonal group \(SO(3)\). The inverse of a rotation is just its transpose, which is why \(R^\top\) appears so often below. The three basic rotations about the coordinate axes are
\[
R_x(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\0&\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix},\quad
R_y(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&0&\sin\theta\\0&1&0\\-\sin\theta&0&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix},\quad
R_z(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta&0\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Two facts matter for legs.

Rotations do not commute. \(R_y(a)R_z(b) \ne R_z(b)R_y(a)\) in general, so the order of joints along the chain matters.
A positive rotation about \(+y\) tips the \(x\)-axis down. \(R_y(\theta)\) sends \((1,0,0)\) to \((\cos\theta, 0, -\sin\theta)\). The tripod’s hip and knee hinges both turn about their local \(+y\) axis, so a positive hip angle swings the thigh downward. This sign convention trips up almost everyone the first time.



Show code
def Rx(t):
    c, s = math.cos(t), math.sin(t); return np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, c, -s], [0, s, c]])
def Ry(t):
    c, s = math.cos(t), math.sin(t); return np.array([[c, 0, s], [0, 1, 0], [-s, 0, c]])
def Rz(t):
    c, s = math.cos(t), math.sin(t); return np.array([[c, -s, 0], [s, c, 0], [0, 0, 1]])

R = Rz(0.7) @ Ry(-0.4) @ Rx(1.1)
print("R^T R = I:", np.allclose(R.T @ R, np.eye(3)), "  det R =", round(np.linalg.det(R), 12))
print("Ry(30 deg) applied to the x-axis:", np.round(Ry(math.radians(30)) @ [1, 0, 0], 3))
print("order matters: |Ry Rz - Rz Ry| =", round(np.abs(Ry(0.5) @ Rz(0.8) - Rz(0.8) @ Ry(0.5)).max(), 3))


R^T R = I: True   det R = 1.0
Ry(30 deg) applied to the x-axis: [ 0.866  0.    -0.5  ]
order matters: |Ry Rz - Rz Ry| = 0.344

title: Forward Kinematics: Where Is the Foot?
text:
Homogeneous transforms
A rigid motion is a rotation followed by a translation, \(\mathbf x \mapsto R\mathbf x + \mathbf t\). Writing points as \((\mathbf x, 1)\) turns this into a single matrix product:
\[
T = \begin{pmatrix} R & \mathbf t \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad
T\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf x\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}R\mathbf x + \mathbf t\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
These \(4\times 4\) matrices form the special Euclidean group \(SE(3)\). Read \({}^{A}T_{B}\) as “the pose of frame \(B\) in frame \(A\)”. Poses then chain like fractions cancelling,
\[
{}^{A}T_{C} = {}^{A}T_{B}\;{}^{B}T_{C},
\]
and the inverse is cheap: \({}^{B}T_{A} = \begin{pmatrix}R^\top & -R^\top\mathbf t\\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1\end{pmatrix}\).
That chain rule is all of forward kinematics. Give every link a frame and write each frame’s pose relative to its parent. That pose is a fixed offset (the link’s geometry) times a rotation by the joint angle. Then multiply down the chain.

title: Forward Kinematics: Where Is the Foot?
text:
One leg, link by link
Each leg hangs from the underside of the hood. Its chain, from the hood’s centre to the foot, is:








Step
Transform
Meaning




hood → mount
\(\operatorname{Trans}(\mathbf m_i)\,\operatorname{Rot}_z(a_i)\)
hip mount on a 2.6 m circle, 2 m down; frame turned to face outward at azimuth \(a_i\)


yaw joint
\(\operatorname{Rot}_z(\psi)\)
swings the leg’s plane left and right


hip pitch
\(\operatorname{Rot}_y(q_h)\)
raises and lowers the thigh


thigh
\(\operatorname{Trans}(L_1, 0, 0)\)
16 m along the thigh to the knee


knee
\(\operatorname{Rot}_y(q_k)\)
bends the shin relative to the thigh


shin
\(\operatorname{Trans}(L_2, 0, 0)\)
28 m along the shin to the foot



Multiplying them out:
\[
{}^{W}T_\text{foot} = {}^{W}T_\text{hood}\;
\operatorname{Trans}(\mathbf m_i)\operatorname{Rot}_z(a_i)\;
\operatorname{Rot}_z(\psi)\operatorname{Rot}_y(q_h)\operatorname{Trans}(L_1)\operatorname{Rot}_y(q_k)\operatorname{Trans}(L_2).
\]
Because the hip and knee both turn about the same \(y\) axis, their angles add. The thigh’s direction is set by \(q_h\) and the shin’s by \(q_h + q_k\). In terms of elevation angles above the horizontal, \(\phi_1 = -q_h\) for the thigh and \(\phi_2 = -(q_h + q_k)\) for the shin. The foot, in the leg’s own vertical plane, is then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\rho &= L_1\cos\phi_1 + L_2\cos\phi_2 && \text{(horizontal reach from the hip)}\\
z &= L_1\sin\phi_1 + L_2\sin\phi_2 && \text{(height relative to the hip)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and the yaw turns that plane round the vertical:
\[
\mathbf p_\text{foot} = \mathbf p_\text{hood} + R_\text{hood}\Big(\mathbf m_i + R_z(a_i + \psi)\,(\rho,\ 0,\ z)^\top\Big).
\]
This closed form is what the project’s kinematics.foot_fk computes. Below, the same thing is built by brute-force matrix multiplication, so the two can be checked against each other.


Show code
def T(R=np.eye(3), t=(0, 0, 0)):
    M = np.eye(4); M[:3, :3] = R; M[:3, 3] = t; return M

def leg_chain(i, q, T_hood=np.eye(4)):
    """All the frames along leg i, as a list of 4x4 poses in the world."""
    psi, qh, qk = q
    az = math.radians(P.leg_azimuths_deg[i])
    m = (P.hip_radius*math.cos(az), P.hip_radius*math.sin(az), -P.hip_drop)
    frames = [T_hood]
    for step in (T(Rz(az), m), T(Rz(psi)), T(Ry(qh)), T(t=(L1, 0, 0)), T(Ry(qk)), T(t=(L2, 0, 0))):
        frames.append(frames[-1] @ step)
    return frames

q_stand = (0.0, *leg_ik(P))
foot_h = leg_chain(0, q_stand)[-1][:3, 3]
foot_c = foot_fk(P, 0, np.zeros(3), np.eye(3), q_stand)
print("standing angles: yaw 0, hip {:.1f} deg, knee {:.1f} deg".format(*map(math.degrees, q_stand[1:])))
print("foot from the transform chain:", np.round(foot_h, 6))
print("foot from the closed form:    ", np.round(foot_c, 6))


standing angles: yaw 0, hip -3.2 deg, knee 86.2 deg
foot from the transform chain: [ 22.    0.  -28.9]
foot from the closed form:     [ 22.    0.  -28.9]


With the hood at the origin, the standing foot sits 22 m out and 28.9 m down, in the foot sphere’s centre. The hip angle is slightly negative: the thigh points 3° above horizontal, and the knee folds the shin down through 86° to stand almost vertical.


Show code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.6))
configs = [(q_stand, "-", "standing"), ((0, 0.5, 0.6), "--", "q_h = 0.5, q_k = 0.6"),
           ((0, -0.6, 1.9), ":", "q_h = -0.6, q_k = 1.9")]
for q, ls, lab in configs:
    fr = leg_chain(0, q)
    pts = np.array([f[:3, 3] for f in fr])[1:]
    ax.plot(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 2], ls, color=STEEL, lw=2.5, label=lab)
    for f in (fr[1], fr[4], fr[6]):
        o = f[:3, 3]
        for col, axis in ((RED, 0), (BLUE, 2)):
            d = f[:3, axis]*3
            ax.annotate("", xy=(o[0] + d[0], o[2] + d[2]), xytext=(o[0], o[2]),
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=col, lw=1.2))
ax.add_patch(plt.matplotlib.patches.Ellipse((0, 0), 2*P.hood_radius, 2*P.hood_height, color=BRASS, alpha=0.7))
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("x: outward from the body axis (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("z: relative to hood centre (m)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower left"); plt.show()








Figure 1: The leg in its own plane, drawn by the transform chain for three configurations. Small arrows are each frame’s x (red) and z (blue) axes. The hip angle tilts the whole leg; the knee angle bends only the shin. Both rotate about the y axis, which points into the page.

title: Forward Kinematics: Where Is the Foot?
text:
The workspace
The workspace is the set of all points the foot can reach. In the leg plane, with no joint limits, the two-link arm reaches exactly the annulus
\[
|L_1 - L_2| \le \sqrt{\rho^2 + z^2} \le L_1 + L_2,
\]
which for the tripod is between 12 m and 44 m from the hip. The outer rim is the leg fully straight, and the inner rim fully folded. Real joints have limits, though: in the MuJoCo model the hip pitch is limited to \([-1.2, 1.4]\) rad and the knee to \([-0.3, 2.6]\) rad, and the limits carve pieces out of the annulus. The quickest way to see the workspace is to sample joint space and push every sample through FK.


Show code
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
lim = {j: model.jnt_range[model.joint(f"leg0_{j}").id] for j in ("yaw", "hip", "knee")}
qh = rng.uniform(*lim["hip"], 20000); qk = rng.uniform(*lim["knee"], 20000)
rho = L1*np.cos(-qh) + L2*np.cos(-(qh + qk)); zz = L1*np.sin(-qh) + L2*np.sin(-(qh + qk))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
th = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 400)
ax.fill((L1 + L2)*np.cos(th), (L1 + L2)*np.sin(th), color="#eef2f5", zorder=0)
ax.fill((L2 - L1)*np.cos(th), (L2 - L1)*np.sin(th), color="white", zorder=0)
sc = ax.scatter(rho, zz, c=qk, s=1, cmap="viridis")
plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, label="knee angle q_k (rad)")
foot0 = np.array([P.stance_radius - P.hip_radius, -(P.stance_height - P.hip_drop - P.leg.foot_radius)])
ax.plot(*foot0, "kx", ms=10, mew=2)
ax.axhline(foot0[1] - P.leg.foot_radius, color="#7a6a4f", ls="--")
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("ρ: horizontal reach from hip (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("z: height from hip (m)")
plt.show()
for j, r in lim.items():
    print(f"{j:5s} limits {r[0]:+.1f} .. {r[1]:+.1f} rad  ({math.degrees(r[0]):+.0f} .. {math.degrees(r[1]):+.0f} deg)")








Figure 2: The leg’s workspace in its own plane (hip at the origin). Grey: the ideal annulus. Coloured dots: 20,000 configurations sampled within the model’s joint limits, coloured by knee angle. The black cross is the standing foot; the dashed line is the ground in the standing pose.





yaw   limits -0.8 .. +0.8 rad  (-46 .. +46 deg)
hip   limits -1.2 .. +1.4 rad  (-69 .. +80 deg)
knee  limits -0.3 .. +2.6 rad  (-17 .. +149 deg)


Three features of the picture matter later.

The workspace is a crescent, not the annulus. The knee limit of 2.6 rad (149°) stops the leg folding completely, so the inner rim is never reached. The hip limits stop the leg swinging right round, so the crescent runs from the leg pointing nearly straight up to the foot curled in under the body.
The knee almost never bends backwards. Its range is \([-0.3, 2.6]\), so it can only overextend by 17°. Positive knee angles are the knee-up shape. A point in the workspace can usually be reached by a knee-up and a knee-down configuration, but here the knee-down one only exists in a thin sliver along the outer rim. The joint limits have nearly removed the ambiguity that part 2 has to resolve.
The stance sits well inside the workspace, with margin in every direction. That margin is what lets the hood rise, sway and tilt while the feet stay planted.

Adding the yaw sweeps this plane through \(\pm 0.8\) rad (\(\pm 46^\circ\)) about the vertical through the hip. The 3-D workspace is a thick wedge of a spherical shell. Three such wedges, one per leg at 120° apart, overlap only a little. Each foot has its own patch of ground, and a gait has to keep every foot inside its own patch.

title: Forward Kinematics: Where Is the Foot?
text:
Checking against MuJoCo
MuJoCo builds the same chain from the model file. Each <body> has a position and orientation relative to its parent, and each <joint> adds a rotation about its axis. mj_kinematics multiplies everything down the tree and stores every body’s world pose in data.xpos and data.xmat.
There is one subtlety in the configuration vector. The hood is attached to the world by a free joint: three translations and an orientation stored as a unit quaternion \((w, x, y, z)\). A quaternion has four numbers but only three degrees of freedom, so qpos (the positions) has one more entry than qvel (the velocities).


Show code
print(f"model: nq = {model.nq} position coordinates, nv = {model.nv} velocity coordinates")
print("free joint qpos (x, y, z, qw, qx, qy, qz):", np.round(data.qpos[:7], 3))

qadr = [model.joint(f"leg{i}_yaw").qposadr[0] for i in range(3)]
hood = model.body("hood").id
errs = {0: [], 1: [], 2: []}
for trial in range(300):
    data.qpos[:3] = rng.uniform(-20, 20, 3) + [0, 0, 30]
    quat = rng.normal(size=4); data.qpos[3:7] = quat/np.linalg.norm(quat)   # random hood orientation
    for i in range(3):
        data.qpos[qadr[i]:qadr[i] + 3] = [rng.uniform(*lim[j]) for j in ("yaw", "hip", "knee")]
    mujoco.mj_kinematics(model, data)
    T_hood = T(data.xmat[hood].reshape(3, 3), data.xpos[hood])
    for i in range(3):
        mine = leg_chain(i, data.qpos[qadr[i]:qadr[i] + 3], T_hood)[-1][:3, 3]
        errs[i].append(np.linalg.norm(mine - data.site_xpos[model.site(f"foot{i}").id]))
for i in range(3):
    print(f"leg {i} (azimuth {P.leg_azimuths_deg[i]:3.0f} deg): max |FK - MuJoCo| over 300 random poses = {max(errs[i]):.1e} m")


model: nq = 58 position coordinates, nv = 57 velocity coordinates
free joint qpos (x, y, z, qw, qx, qy, qz): [ 0.  0. 30.  1.  0.  0.  0.]
leg 0 (azimuth   0 deg): max |FK - MuJoCo| over 300 random poses = 2.8e-14 m
leg 1 (azimuth 120 deg): max |FK - MuJoCo| over 300 random poses = 2.1e-04 m
leg 2 (azimuth 240 deg): max |FK - MuJoCo| over 300 random poses = 1.0e-05 m


The transform chain agrees with MuJoCo to within a fraction of a millimetre across 300 random poses, with the hood flung about at random orientations. Leg 0 agrees to machine precision. The tiny residual on legs 1 and 2 is not a kinematics error: the model file writes each mount’s azimuth with six significant figures (2.0944 rad for 120°). A rounding error of a few millionths of a radian, swung through a 44 m leg, moves the foot a tenth of a millimetre.

title: Forward Kinematics: Where Is the Foot?
section: Another way to write it: the product of exponentials
text:
Another way to write it: the product of exponentials
The link-by-link chain needs a frame on every link. A more modern formulation, the product of exponentials (Brockett, 1984; the standard form in Lynch & Park’s Modern Robotics), needs only two things:

the home pose \(M\) of the foot when every joint is at zero;
for each joint, its screw axis \(\mathcal S_j = (\boldsymbol\omega_j, \mathbf v_j)\) in the home configuration. For a hinge, \(\boldsymbol\omega_j\) is the unit axis direction and \(\mathbf v_j = -\boldsymbol\omega_j\times\mathbf r_j\), where \(\mathbf r_j\) is any point on the axis.

Then
\[
T(\mathbf q) = e^{[\mathcal S_1]q_1}\,e^{[\mathcal S_2]q_2}\,e^{[\mathcal S_3]q_3}\,M,
\qquad
[\mathcal S] = \begin{pmatrix}[\boldsymbol\omega] & \mathbf v\\ \mathbf 0^\top & 0\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \([\boldsymbol\omega]\) is the skew-symmetric matrix with \([\boldsymbol\omega]\mathbf x = \boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf x\), and the exponential is the matrix exponential. Each factor is “rotate everything beyond joint \(j\) about joint \(j\)’s axis by \(q_j\)”, applied from the tip backwards. No intermediate frames are needed. The screw axes are also exactly the columns of the Jacobian at the home pose, which part 3 builds on.
For leg 0 the axes are simple. The yaw is a vertical axis through the hip at \(\mathbf r = (2.6, 0, -2)\). At home, the hip and knee are horizontal \(y\)-axes through the hip and through the point 16 m further out.


Show code
def skew(w):
    return np.array([[0, -w[2], w[1]], [w[2], 0, -w[0]], [-w[1], w[0], 0]])
def screw(w, r):
    w = np.asarray(w, float); v = -np.cross(w, r)
    S = np.zeros((4, 4)); S[:3, :3] = skew(w); S[:3, 3] = v
    return S

hip = np.array([P.hip_radius, 0, -P.hip_drop])
axes = [screw((0, 0, 1), hip), screw((0, 1, 0), hip), screw((0, 1, 0), hip + [L1, 0, 0])]
M_home = T(t=hip + [L1 + L2, 0, 0])

def fk_poe(q):
    out = np.eye(4)
    for S, qj in zip(axes, q):
        out = out @ expm(S*qj)
    return out @ M_home

worst = 0.0
for trial in range(300):
    q = [rng.uniform(*lim[j]) for j in ("yaw", "hip", "knee")]
    worst = max(worst, np.linalg.norm(fk_poe(q)[:3, 3] - leg_chain(0, q)[-1][:3, 3]))
print(f"product of exponentials vs transform chain, 300 random configurations: max difference {worst:.1e} m")


product of exponentials vs transform chain, 300 random configurations: max difference 9.3e-14 m


The two formulations agree to rounding error. The PoE form is popular for exactly this reason: it is defined by physical axes you can point at on the machine, it has no special-case conventions, and its Jacobian falls straight out of it.






What about Denavit–Hartenberg parameters?





Older textbooks and many industrial controllers describe chains with Denavit–Hartenberg (DH) parameters. That is four numbers per joint \((a, \alpha, d, \theta)\), which fix each link’s frame by a strict convention: \(z\) along the joint axis, \(x\) along the common normal to the next axis. DH is compact, but the conventions (there are two incompatible ones, “standard” and “modified”) are a famous source of errors. MuJoCo, URDF and most modern software instead give each link an arbitrary pose relative to its parent, as in the table above. The PoE form avoids link frames altogether.

title: Forward Kinematics: Where Is the Foot?
text:
Velocities: a look ahead
Differentiate the foot position with respect to time and every term picks up a joint velocity:
\[
\dot{\mathbf p} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial q_1}\dot q_1 + \frac{\partial f}{\partial q_2}\dot q_2 + \frac{\partial f}{\partial q_3}\dot q_3 = J(\mathbf q)\,\dot{\mathbf q}.
\]
The matrix \(J\) of partial derivatives is the Jacobian. It turns joint speeds into foot speed and, by a duality explained in part 3, foot forces into joint torques. It is also the engine of numerical inverse kinematics in part 2. Each column is “the foot’s velocity if only this joint moves”. For a hinge, that is \(\boldsymbol\omega_j \times (\mathbf p - \mathbf r_j)\): the foot circles the joint’s axis. A finite-difference check on the standing pose shows the idea:


Show code
q0 = np.array(q_stand); eps = 1e-6
p0 = leg_chain(0, q0)[-1][:3, 3]
J_fd = np.column_stack([(leg_chain(0, q0 + eps*np.eye(3)[j])[-1][:3, 3] - p0)/eps for j in range(3)])
fr = leg_chain(0, q0)
r = [fr[1][:3, 3], fr[3][:3, 3], fr[5][:3, 3]]                  # points on the yaw, hip and knee axes
w = [fr[1][:3, 2], fr[3][:3, 1], fr[5][:3, 1]]                  # their axis directions
J_geo = np.column_stack([np.cross(w[j], p0 - r[j]) for j in range(3)])
np.set_printoptions(precision=2, suppress=True)
print("finite differences (m/rad):\n", J_fd)
print("axis x lever, column by column:\n", J_geo)
print(f"max difference {np.abs(J_fd - J_geo).max():.1e}")


finite differences (m/rad):
 [[ -0.   -26.9  -27.79]
 [ 19.4    0.     0.  ]
 [  0.   -19.4   -3.42]]
axis x lever, column by column:
 [[ -0.   -26.9  -27.79]
 [ 19.4    0.     0.  ]
 [  0.   -19.4   -3.42]]
max difference 1.4e-05


Read the columns of \(J\) one at a time.

Yaw moves the foot purely sideways (\(y\)), at 19.4 m/rad. That is its horizontal distance from the yaw axis.
Hip moves the foot inward (26.9 m/rad) and down (19.4 m/rad). Positive \(q_h\) swings the whole leg downward round the hip. The foot is far below the hip, so it swings back towards the body as well as dropping. The downward part equals the foot’s horizontal reach from the hip, the lever arm.
Knee moves the foot almost purely horizontally. The shin hangs nearly vertically below the knee, so turning the knee swings the foot sideways along a near-horizontal arc.

That last point has consequences. Raising or lowering the foot with the knee is very inefficient, while pushing it outward is easy. In part 3 the same structure explains why the hip, not the knee, carries the machine’s weight.

title: Forward Kinematics: Where Is the Foot?
text:
Summary

A configuration is a vector of joint angles; forward kinematics maps it to the pose of a point of interest by composing one rigid transform per link.
Rotations live in \(SO(3)\) (\(R^\top R = I\), \(\det R = 1\)); poses live in \(SE(3)\) and chain by matrix multiplication.
The tripod’s leg is yaw–pitch–pitch: a yaw that turns a vertical plane, inside which a two-link arm reaches an annulus between 12 m and 44 m, trimmed by joint limits.
The hand-built chain, the closed form and the product of exponentials all agree with MuJoCo to within the precision of the model file.
Differentiating FK gives the Jacobian, which the next three parts lean on heavily.

Next: Inverse kinematics, turning a desired foot position back into joint angles.
