title: Ray Tracing a Black Hole
text:
This is the second of four explainers behind Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole:
Part 1 found how far a non-spinning hole bends a ray from infinity. A picture needs more than that. It needs a camera at a definite place, which in Interstellar is a few dozen \(M\) from the hole and sometimes moving at half the speed of light, and a sky for the rays to land on. This post builds both, for the non-spinning (Schwarzschild) case, where the symmetry makes everything checkable.
Show code
import sys, math, time, warnings
from pathlib import Path
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve().parents[1] / "gargantua"
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from blackhole import schwarzschild as S, kerr, render as R, sky as SK
from blackhole.colour import tonemap, bloom

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})

def show(ax, img, title=None):
    ax.imshow(np.clip(img, 0, 1), interpolation="lanczos")
    ax.set_axis_off()
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)

checker = SK.Sky(SK.checkerboard(1024, n_lat=12, n_lon=24))
milky = SK.Sky(SK.milky_way(2048))
stars = SK.star_catalogue()

title: Ray Tracing a Black Hole
Ray Tracing a Black Hole
text:
What a static observer sees
A pixel’s direction is measured in the camera’s own frame, not in the coordinates \((t, r, \theta, \phi)\). Start with a static camera, hovering at fixed \(r\) by firing rockets. Its local, orthonormal frame has basis vectors along \(\hat r\), \(\hat\theta\) and \(\hat\phi\), scaled so that lengths and times are the ones it actually measures:
\[
\mathbf e_{\hat t} = \frac{\partial_t}{\sqrt{1 - 2/r}}, \qquad
\mathbf e_{\hat r} = \sqrt{1 - 2/r}\;\partial_r, \qquad
\mathbf e_{\hat\phi} = \frac{1}{r}\,\partial_\phi .
\]
A photon with conserved energy \(E\) and angular momentum \(L\) (in its orbital plane) has, in this frame, energy and momentum components
\[
E_\text{loc} = -\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf e_{\hat t} = \frac{E}{\sqrt{1 - 2/r}}, \qquad
p^{\hat\phi} = \frac{L}{r}.
\]
If the ray makes an angle \(\delta\) with the outward radial direction, then \(\sin\delta = p^{\hat\phi}/E_\text{loc}\), so
\[
\boxed{\; b = \frac{L}{E} = \frac{r\,\sin\delta}{\sqrt{1 - 2/r}} \;}
\]
This one line connects a pixel to the theory in part 1. Note the factor \(1/\sqrt{1 - 2/r}\): near the hole, a given viewing angle corresponds to a larger impact parameter than flat space would suggest.

The size of the shadow
A ray looking inwards (\(\delta > \pi/2\)) escapes only if \(b > 3\sqrt3\). The edge of the shadow is therefore where \(b = 3\sqrt 3\), and its angular radius \(\psi\), measured from the direction of the hole, satisfies
\[
\sin\psi = \frac{3\sqrt3\,\sqrt{1 - 2/r}}{r}
\]
(Synge 1966). For \(r \gg 1\) this is just \(3\sqrt3/r\), the angular size of a disk of radius \(b_c\). Close in, it grows fast: at the photon sphere, \(r = 3\), the shadow fills exactly half the sky, and inside it the shadow covers more than half.


Show code
rr = np.geomspace(2.05, 1000, 400)
psi = np.degrees([S.shadow_angle(x) for x in rr])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.4))
ax.loglog(rr, psi, "k", lw=2, label="exact (Synge)")
ax.loglog(rr[rr > 4], np.degrees(S.B_CRIT / rr[rr > 4]), "C0--", label="3√3 / r")
ax.axvline(3, color="0.6", lw=0.8)
ax.axhline(90, color="0.6", lw=0.8)
ax.text(3.2, 100, "photon sphere: shadow = half the sky", fontsize=8, color="0.3")
for x in [30, 74.1]:
    ax.plot(x, math.degrees(S.shadow_angle(x)), "o", color="C3", ms=4)
    ax.annotate(f"r = {x:g}: {math.degrees(S.shadow_angle(x)):.1f}°", (x, math.degrees(S.shadow_angle(x))),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(6, 6), fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("camera radius r / M")
ax.set_ylabel("shadow radius (degrees)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 1: Angular radius of the shadow seen by a static observer, against distance from the hole. The dashed line is the far-field approximation 3√3/r. At the photon sphere (r = 3) the shadow is a hemisphere.

title: Ray Tracing a Black Hole
section: One function renders the whole image
text:
One function renders the whole image
Spherical symmetry does the rest. Every ray stays in the plane containing the hole, the camera and the ray’s initial direction. Within that plane, the only thing that matters is \(\delta\). So the whole image is determined by one function of one variable: the total angle \(\Phi(\delta)\) swept round the hole by the backward ray before it reaches infinity.
From part 1, with \(u_c = 1/r\) for the camera:

a ray heading outwards (\(\delta \le \pi/2\)) sweeps \(\displaystyle\Phi = \int_0^{u_c}\frac{du}{\sqrt{P(u)}}\);
a ray heading inwards with \(b > 3\sqrt3\) first falls to its turning point and then climbs out, so \(\displaystyle\Phi = \int_{u_c}^{u_0}\frac{du}{\sqrt{P(u)}} + \int_0^{u_0}\frac{du}{\sqrt{P(u)}}\), both elliptic integrals.

The pixel then shows the point of the sky at angle \(\Phi\) from the camera’s outward radial direction, rotated towards the ray’s own direction. With no hole at all, \(\Phi = \delta\) and the camera sees the sky undistorted.


Show code
r_cam = 30.0
tab = S.sky_angle_table(r_cam)
d, P = tab
psi_shadow = S.shadow_angle(r_cam)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8))
ax.plot(np.degrees(d), np.degrees(P), "k", lw=2)
ax.plot([0, 180], [0, 180], "k:", lw=0.8)
ax.axvspan(180 - math.degrees(psi_shadow), 180, color="k", alpha=0.8)
for n, lab in [(1, "π: Einstein ring"), (2, "2π"), (3, "3π")]:
    ax.axhline(180 * n, color="C3", lw=0.7, ls="--")
    ax.text(3, 180 * n + 8, lab, color="C3", fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 180)
ax.set_ylim(0, 640)
ax.set_xlabel("viewing angle δ from outward radial (degrees)")
ax.set_ylabel("sky angle Φ (degrees)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 2: The lensing map of a static camera at r = 30 M: the sky angle Φ against the viewing angle δ (both from the outward radial direction). The dotted line is flat space. Where the curve crosses Φ = π (the point directly behind the hole) is the Einstein ring. It crosses 2π and 3π ever closer to the shadow’s edge (shaded), where Φ diverges.





Tabulating \(\Phi(\delta)\) once, on a grid packed geometrically towards the shadow’s edge where it diverges, takes a fraction of a second. After that, every pixel is an interpolation. As an independent check, the same image can be traced the slow way, integrating every ray through the full spinning-hole equations of part 3 with the spin set to zero:


Show code
cam = kerr.Camera(r_cam, math.radians(80), 0.0, fov=60)
N = cam.directions(400, 300)
t0 = time.time()
v_lut, cap_lut = S.lens_directions(N, r_cam, cam.theta, tab)
t_lut = time.time() - t0
tr = R.trace_image(r_cam, 80, 0.0, 400, 300, 60, ss=1, disk=False, tol=1e-10)
esc = (tr["outcome"] == kerr.ESCAPED) & ~cap_lut
ang = np.arccos(np.clip((v_lut * tr["sky"]).sum(-1), -1, 1))
n_disagree = int(((tr["outcome"] == kerr.CAPTURED) != cap_lut).sum())
max_ang = ang[esc].max()
print(f"lookup table: {t_lut*1e3:.0f} ms for {N.shape[0]*N.shape[1]} pixels")
print(f"full geodesic integration: {float(tr['seconds']):.2f} s")
print(f"pixels classified differently (shadow or sky): {n_disagree}")
print(f"largest difference in sky direction: {max_ang:.1e} rad")


lookup table: 7 ms for 120000 pixels
full geodesic integration: 0.98 s
pixels classified differently (shadow or sky): 0
largest difference in sky direction: 2.2e-05 rad


The two methods agree on which pixels are shadow, and the sky directions differ by at most 2e-05 radians, about 5 arcseconds. About half of that residual comes from stopping the integrated rays at \(r = 1000\,M\) rather than infinity. The rest comes from interpolating the 4,000-point table close to the shadow’s edge, where \(\Phi\) changes fastest. A finer table and a more distant stopping radius bring it below \(10^{-6}\).

title: Ray Tracing a Black Hole
text:
The lensed sky
The test pattern used in the DNGR paper is a celestial sphere painted with a checkerboard, coloured by quadrant, so that every patch of the image can be traced back to where it came from. Here a static camera at \(r = 30\,M\) looks at the hole with a 90° field of view:


Show code
cam = kerr.Camera(r_cam, math.radians(90), 0.0, fov=90)
N = cam.directions(640, 640)
# flat space: the pixel sees the sky straight ahead; at theta = 90 the camera's
# (forward, right, up) are (-x, +y, +z) in the hole's frame
v_flat = np.stack([-N[..., 0], N[..., 1], N[..., 2]], -1)
v, cap = S.lens_directions(N, r_cam, cam.theta, tab)
flat = checker.sample(v_flat)
fp = SK.footprint(v, ~cap)
lensed = np.where(cap[..., None], 0.0, checker.sample(v, fp))
psiE = S.einstein_ring(r_cam, tab)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5))
show(ax[0], flat, "no black hole")
show(ax[1], lensed, f"black hole, camera at r = {r_cam:g} M")
t = math.tan(math.radians(45))
R_E = math.tan(psiE) / t * 320
ax[1].add_patch(plt.Circle((320, 320), R_E, fill=False, ec="w", lw=0.8, ls="--"))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 3: A checkerboard celestial sphere seen by a static camera 30 M from the hole: left, with the hole removed; right, lensed. The far side of the sky is magnified into a ring (the Einstein ring is where the quadrant directly behind the hole is stretched round the whole circle), and inside it a second, inverted image of the entire sky is squeezed against the shadow.





The dashed circle is the Einstein ring, where \(\Phi(\delta) = \pi\). It is the image of the single point of the sky directly behind the hole, smeared round a circle by symmetry. For a camera far from the hole, the ring’s angular radius approaches the weak-field value \(\sqrt{4M/r}\):

Show code
print(f"{'r/M':>6} {'ring (exact)':>13} {'sqrt(4M/r)':>11} {'shadow':>8}")
for x in [10, 30, 74.1, 100, 1000]:
    tb = S.sky_angle_table(x)
    print(f"{x:6g} {math.degrees(S.einstein_ring(x, tb)):12.2f}° {math.degrees(math.sqrt(4/x)):10.2f}° "
          f"{math.degrees(S.shadow_angle(x)):7.2f}°")




Table 1: Angular radius of the Einstein ring and of the shadow, for a static camera at radius r.



   r/M  ring (exact)  sqrt(4M/r)   shadow
    10        44.87°      36.24°   27.69°
    30        23.71°      20.92°    9.63°
  74.1        14.44°      13.31°    3.97°
   100        12.29°      11.46°    2.95°
  1000         3.71°       3.62°    0.30°




Inside the ring is a second image of the whole sky, inverted and compressed: the light that went round the “wrong” side of the hole. Inside that, too thin to see here, is a third, and so on, the sequence of part 1 shrinking by \(e^{-\pi}\) per half-turn.

title: Ray Tracing a Black Hole
text:
Point stars, images and magnification
A real sky is mostly point stars. Each star has a primary image outside the Einstein ring and a secondary image inside it, on the opposite side of the hole, plus fainter higher-order images hugging the shadow.
Because \(\Phi\) is monotonic, all of a star’s images can be found directly. If the star lies at angle \(\Psi\) from the camera’s outward direction, its images sit at
\[
\Phi(\delta) = \Psi + 2\pi k \quad\text{(same side)}, \qquad \Phi(\delta) = 2\pi(k+1) - \Psi \quad\text{(opposite side)}.
\]
How bright is each image? Lensing does not create or destroy light, and it conserves surface brightness (specific intensity). This is Liouville’s theorem: the phase-space density of photons is constant along a ray. So an image is brighter in proportion to how much solid angle it occupies on the camera’s sky compared with the star’s true solid angle. That ratio is the magnification:
\[
\mu = \frac{d\Omega_\text{camera}}{d\Omega_\text{sky}} = \frac{\sin\delta\,d\delta}{\sin\Psi\,d\Psi}
= \frac{\sin\delta}{\sin\Psi\,\left|d\Phi/d\delta\right|},
\]
(the azimuthal factor \(d\varphi\) is the same on both sides and cancels). Near the Einstein ring \(\sin\Psi \to 0\), so \(\mu\) diverges. A star passing behind the hole flares enormously as its two images stretch round the ring.
The renderer cannot use that formula once the hole spins, because there is no single function \(\Phi(\delta)\). The general method works for any ray map. Cut the camera’s sky into small triangles, two per cell of the ray grid. Each one maps to a spherical triangle on the celestial sphere. A star that falls inside a sky triangle has an image inside the matching camera triangle, at the same barycentric position. Its magnification is the ratio of the two triangles’ solid angles, with a negative sign if the triangle’s orientation is reversed, meaning the image is mirror-flipped. Here the two methods are compared, for 60,000 stars and a camera at \(30\,M\):


Show code
cam = kerr.Camera(r_cam, math.radians(90), 0.0, fov=60)
NX = NY = 900
N = cam.directions(NX, NY)
v, cap = S.lens_directions(N, r_cam, cam.theta, tab)
idx, x, y, mu, om = SK.lensed_stars(kerr.Camera.right_handed(N), v, ~cap, stars)
# exact images from the inverse of Phi
eidx, eN, emu, order = S.point_images(stars["v"], r_cam, cam.theta, tab, n_max=1)
t = math.tan(math.radians(30))
ex = (eN[:, 1] / eN[:, 0] / t + 1) / 2 * NX - 0.5
ey = (-eN[:, 2] / eN[:, 0] / t + 1) / 2 * NY - 0.5
inview = (eN[:, 0] > 0) & (ex > 2) & (ex < NX - 3) & (ey > 2) & (ey < NY - 3)
# match triangle-method images to exact ones (same star, same position)
from scipy.spatial import cKDTree
key = cKDTree(np.c_[ex[inview], ey[inview], 1e4 * eidx[inview]])
dist, j = key.query(np.c_[x, y, 1e4 * idx])
good = dist < 0.05
ratio = mu[good] / emu[inview][j[good]]
print(f"images found by the triangle method:       {len(idx)}")
print(f"primary + secondary images (exact, in view): {inview.sum()}")
print(f"matched to within 0.05 px:                 {good.sum()}")
for o, name in [(1, "primary"), (2, "secondary")]:
    m = order[inview][j[good]] == o
    q = np.percentile(ratio[m], [1, 50, 99])
    print(f"{name:9s}: magnification ratio, 1/50/99th percentile {q[0]:.4f} {q[1]:.4f} {q[2]:.4f};"
          f"  parity {'+' if np.median(mu[good][m]) > 0 else '-'}")
med_ratio = np.median(ratio)


images found by the triangle method:       34169
primary + secondary images (exact, in view): 31018
matched to within 0.05 px:                 30012
primary  : magnification ratio, 1/50/99th percentile 0.9853 1.0001 1.0175;  parity +
secondary: magnification ratio, 1/50/99th percentile 0.8547 0.9996 1.1440;  parity -


96.8% of the exact primary and secondary images in view are matched by a triangle-method image within 0.05 pixels, and the two magnifications agree with a median ratio of 0.9997. Almost all of the unmatched few are secondary images within a degree of the shadow’s edge, where the map is so compressed that interpolating inside one cell misplaces an image by a tenth of a pixel or so. The spread comes from interpolating inside triangles where the map curves. Secondary images come out with negative parity: they are mirror images. The triangle method also finds images the exact calculation above didn’t look for (third and higher orders, packed against the shadow), each with a tiny magnification.

Why not paint the stars on the sky?
The obvious alternative is to paint the stars into the celestial-sphere texture as small dots and let the lookup sample them. The DNGR paper explains why that fails. Near a critical curve such as the Einstein ring, the map magnifies hugely in one direction, so a painted dot becomes a long luminous streak whose length depends on the dot’s size, which is an artefact of the texture. A real star, smaller than any pixel, stays a point. It just gets brighter. DNGR solved this by tracing ray bundles (narrow beams whose cross-section is evolved with the equation of geodesic deviation) and feeding each star’s light into every beam it falls in. The triangle method above does the same job with differences between neighbouring rays.


Show code
cam = kerr.Camera(r_cam, math.radians(90), 0.0, fov=24)
NX, NY = 720, 480
centre = (-14.0, 12.0)
N = cam.directions(NX, NY, centre=centre)
v, cap = S.lens_directions(N, r_cam, cam.theta, tab)
painted = SK.Sky(SK.splat_stars(np.zeros((2048, 4096, 3), np.float32), stars))
fp = SK.footprint(v, ~cap)
img_tex = painted.sample(v, fp)
idx, x, y, mu, om = SK.lensed_stars(kerr.Camera.right_handed(N), v, ~cap, stars)
img_pts = SK.paint_stars((NY, NX), stars, idx, x, y, mu, 2 * np.abs(om))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.9))
show(ax[0], tonemap(img_tex, 6), "stars painted on the sky texture")
show(ax[1], tonemap(img_pts, 6), "point stars through the ray map")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 4: Close to the Einstein ring (upper left of the hole, camera at 30 M). Left: stars painted onto the sky texture and looked up through the lensing map: near the ring they smear into arcs whose length is an artefact of the painted dot size. Right: the same stars as point sources, each image placed and brightened by its exact position and magnification.





For extended light, such as the glow of the galaxy or nebulae, painting into a texture is exactly right. Since surface brightness is conserved, a pixel should show the average brightness of the patch of sky it sees. Where the map shrinks the sky (towards the shadow, where one pixel can cover square degrees of sky), the lookup averages over the pixel’s footprint using a mip-map pyramid of pre-averaged textures. The renderer here uses both methods: a mip-mapped texture for the diffuse Milky Way, and the triangle method for the stars.

title: Ray Tracing a Black Hole
text:
A moving camera: aberration
A camera hovering near a black hole is a rocket burning hard. The camera in Interstellar is on board a ship in orbit, and an orbiting camera moves through the static frame at high speed. At radius \(r\) a circular orbit has speed \(v = 1/\sqrt{r - 2}\) relative to the static observer, which is half the speed of light at \(r = 6\).
Motion changes the directions from which light arrives, which is relativistic aberration. A photon arriving along direction \(\mathbf n\) in the static frame arrives, for a camera moving at speed \(\beta\) along \(\hat{\mathbf x}\), from
\[
n'_x = \frac{n_x - \beta}{1 - \beta n_x}, \qquad
\mathbf n'_\perp = \frac{\mathbf n_\perp}{\gamma\,(1 - \beta n_x)}.
\]
This is the velocity-addition law applied to light. It crowds the sky towards the direction of motion, and in the full renderer it is the first step: map each pixel from the moving camera’s frame into the static frame, then trace. For a non-spinning hole that means aberration followed by the same \(\Phi(\delta)\) lookup:


Show code
r6 = 6.0
tab6 = S.sky_angle_table(r6)
cam6 = kerr.Camera(r6, math.pi / 2, 0.0, beta="orbit")
NX, NY = 960, 480
Np = cam6.panorama(NX, NY)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 9))
for k, (beta, title) in enumerate([(0.0, "static camera"), (cam6.beta, f"orbiting camera, v = {cam6.beta:.2f}c")]):
    v, cap = S.lens_directions(S.aberrate(Np, beta), r6, cam6.theta, tab6)
    fp = SK.footprint(v, ~cap)
    show(ax[k], np.where(cap[..., None], 0, checker.sample(v, fp)), title)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
tr6 = R.trace_image(r6, 90, 0.0, 300, 150, 0, ss=1, beta="orbit", disk=False, projection="panorama", tol=1e-10)
v6, cap6 = S.lens_directions(S.aberrate(cam6.panorama(300, 150), cam6.beta), r6, cam6.theta, tab6)
ok6 = (tr6["outcome"] == kerr.ESCAPED) & ~cap6
ab_err = np.arccos(np.clip((v6 * tr6["sky"]).sum(-1), -1, 1))[ok6].max()








Figure 5: The whole sky seen from r = 6 M, as an equirectangular panorama with the hole at the centre and the direction of motion to the right. Top: a static camera. Bottom: a camera in circular orbit, moving at 0.5c through the same point. Aberration shrinks the shadow and the sky behind it and spreads out the sky ahead. The lensing itself, which rays reach which star, is unchanged.





Aberration followed by lookup agrees with the full geodesic tracer, which applies the boost to the ray’s initial momentum instead, to 2e-05 radians. A moving camera also sees light Doppler shifted, blue ahead and red behind. That matters for the accretion disk and is the subject of part 4.

title: Ray Tracing a Black Hole
text:
The warped star field
Put together, these give the classic image: the night sky seen from a ship orbiting a black hole. Here the camera orbits at \(30\,M\), as in the film clip by Alain Riazuelo that the DNGR paper uses to introduce lensing. The Milky Way is a texture, and 60,000 stars are lensed as points.


Show code
cam = kerr.Camera(r_cam, math.radians(90), 0.0, beta="orbit", fov=90)
NX, NY = 1200, 720
ss = 2
N = cam.directions(NX * ss, NY * ss)
v, cap = S.lens_directions(S.aberrate(N, cam.beta), r_cam, cam.theta, tab)
fp = SK.footprint(v, ~cap)
diffuse = np.where(cap[..., None], 0, milky.sample(v, fp))
diffuse = R.downsample(diffuse, ss)
idx, x, y, mu, om = SK.lensed_stars(kerr.Camera.right_handed(N), v, ~cap, stars)
pts = SK.paint_stars((NY, NX), stars, idx, (x + 0.5) / ss - 0.5, (y + 0.5) / ss - 0.5, mu, 2 * np.abs(om) * ss * ss)
img = tonemap(bloom(diffuse + pts, weights=(0.03, 0.02, 0.01)), 2.0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
show(ax, img)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("thumbnail.png", dpi=80, bbox_inches="tight", pad_inches=0)
plt.show()








Figure 6: The star field seen from a camera in circular orbit at r = 30 M around a non-spinning black hole, looking at the hole (90° field of view). The band of the Milky Way is split and wrapped round the Einstein ring, and the secondary image of the whole sky is squeezed into the thin annulus around the shadow.





Everything here came from the single function \(\Phi(\delta)\), which is possible only because a non-spinning hole is spherically symmetric. Spin breaks that symmetry: there is no longer one plane per ray or one function for the whole image. Every ray must be integrated through the full equations. Part 3 does that.

title: Planning the Falling Walk
text:
Last of four explainers behind The Martian Tripod. Parts 1 and 2 covered geometry: where the feet are and how to put them there. Part 3 covered force, and ended on an awkward discovery. With a foot in the air, the tripod’s grasp matrix loses a rank: nothing the legs do can resist a tip about the line through the two planted feet. A walking tripod is never in static equilibrium. It is always falling, and each footfall catches it.
There are two ways to walk like that. The static way, the project’s first gait, carries the centre of mass to the edge of the next two-foot support, stops, lifts the foot, lets the body topple onto the new foot, and settles. It works at about 1.1 mph. The dynamic way, which reaches 5.6 mph, plans the fall in advance and keeps the body moving throughout. This post builds that planner from the ground up.
Show code
import sys, math, warnings
from pathlib import Path
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve().parents[1] / "martian-tripod"
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy.sparse as sp
import osqp
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

from tripod.params import DEFAULT as P
from tripod.planner import Schedule, COMPlanner
from tripod.kinematics import slot

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.25,
                     "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
BRASS, STEEL, RED, BLUE, GREEN, GREY = "#b8860b", "#4a5a6a", "#c0392b", "#2c7fb8", "#2ca25f", "#7f8c8d"

g = 9.81
h = 27.2                       # centre-of-mass height of the standing machine (m)
w = math.sqrt(g/h)
print(f"COM height h = {h} m:  omega = sqrt(g/h) = {w:.3f} 1/s,  time constant 1/omega = {1/w:.2f} s")


COM height h = 27.2 m:  omega = sqrt(g/h) = 0.601 1/s,  time constant 1/omega = 1.67 s

title: Planning the Falling Walk
section: From a falling pole to a linear model
text:
From a falling pole to a linear model
Picture the machine’s whole mass \(m\) at its centre of mass \(\mathbf c\), held at height \(h\) above the ground by massless legs. The ground pushes on the feet, and the net ground force \(\mathbf F\) acts through some point \(\mathbf z\) on the ground. Two conditions fix everything.

Vertical: if the height is held constant, the vertical force just carries the weight: \(F_z = mg\).
Rotational: a point mass has no angular momentum about itself, so the net force on it must point through it. The force’s line of action runs from \(\mathbf z\) on the ground to \(\mathbf c\) in the air, so its horizontal and vertical components are in the ratio of the horizontal and vertical offsets: \[\frac{F_x}{F_z} = \frac{c_x - z_x}{h}.\]

Newton’s second law horizontally, \(m\ddot c_x = F_x\), then gives the linear inverted pendulum model (LIPM; Kajita and colleagues, 2001):
\[
\boxed{\;\ddot{\mathbf c} = \omega^2(\mathbf c - \mathbf z), \qquad \omega = \sqrt{g/h}\;}
\]
with the same equation in \(x\) and \(y\), independently. It is linear, which is the whole point: an inverted pendulum with a fixed-length leg is nonlinear, but holding the height constant makes the dynamics exactly linear.
The point \(\mathbf z\) is the zero-moment point (ZMP, Vukobratović, 1972). It is the point on the ground about which the ground forces have no horizontal moment. When every foot is on flat ground, it is simply the centre of pressure, the load-weighted average of the foot positions:
\[
\mathbf z = \frac{\sum_i f_{i,z}\,\mathbf p_i}{\sum_i f_{i,z}} .
\]
Since every \(f_{i,z} \ge 0\) (the ground can only push), \(\mathbf z\) is a convex combination of the feet. It must lie inside the support polygon, their convex hull. This is the barycentric-coordinate result from part 3 read backwards. There, the centre of mass’s position fixed the foot loads. Here, choosing the foot loads places the ZMP anywhere in the polygon, and the ZMP steers the centre of mass.
That is the planner’s whole control authority. The legs choose where the ZMP is, within the support polygon, and the centre of mass falls away from it.

title: Planning the Falling Walk
text:
What the pendulum does
With \(\mathbf z\) held still, write \(x = c - z\) for one axis. The solution of \(\ddot x = \omega^2 x\) is
\[
x(t) = x_0\cosh\omega t + \frac{\dot x_0}{\omega}\sinh\omega t .
\]
The quantity
\[
E = \tfrac12\dot x^2 - \tfrac12\omega^2x^2
\]
is conserved, so trajectories in the \((x, \dot x)\) plane are hyperbolas. This is the LIPM’s orbital energy (Kajita & Tani, 1991). If \(E > 0\), the centre of mass has enough speed to pass over the ZMP and carry on. If \(E < 0\), it falls back the way it came. The boundary lines \(\dot x = \pm\omega x\) are the eigenvectors of the dynamics. Along \(\dot x = -\omega x\) the body glides in and stops exactly above the ZMP. Along \(\dot x = +\omega x\) it falls away exponentially.


Show code
xs = np.linspace(-12, 12, 41); vs = np.linspace(-7, 7, 41)
X, V = np.meshgrid(xs, vs)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5))
ax.streamplot(X, V, V, w*w*X, color=GREY, density=1.1, linewidth=0.7, arrowsize=0.8)
ax.plot(xs, w*xs, color=RED, lw=2.2, label="unstable: ẋ = +ωx")
ax.plot(xs, -w*xs, color=BLUE, lw=2.2, label="stable: ẋ = −ωx")
v_walk = 2.5
ax.axhline(v_walk, color=BRASS, ls="--", lw=1.2); ax.text(-11.6, v_walk + 0.25, "walking speed 2.5 m/s", color=BRASS)
ax.plot(-v_walk/w, v_walk, "o", color=BLUE, ms=7)
ax.set_xlim(-12, 12); ax.set_ylim(-7, 7)
ax.set_xlabel("x = c − z  (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("ẋ  (m/s)"); ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.show()
print(f"to coast to a stop over the ZMP from {v_walk} m/s, start {v_walk/w:.2f} m short of it")








Figure 1: Phase portrait of the linear inverted pendulum with the ZMP fixed at x = 0. Hyperbolas are lines of constant orbital energy. Red: the unstable direction, where the body falls away. Blue: the stable direction, where it comes to rest exactly over the ZMP. The tripod’s walking speed is marked: to stop dead over a point, the body has to start 4 m short of it.





to coast to a stop over the ZMP from 2.5 m/s, start 4.16 m short of it



The divergent component and the capture point
Change variables to split the stable and unstable parts. Define the divergent component of motion (DCM)
\[
\boldsymbol\xi = \mathbf c + \frac{\dot{\mathbf c}}{\omega}.
\]
Differentiating and substituting the LIPM gives two first-order equations:
\[
\dot{\boldsymbol\xi} = \omega(\boldsymbol\xi - \mathbf z), \qquad \dot{\mathbf c} = \omega(\boldsymbol\xi - \mathbf c).
\]
The second equation is stable: the centre of mass simply chases \(\boldsymbol\xi\) with time constant \(1/\omega\). All the instability is in the first. \(\boldsymbol\xi\) runs away from the ZMP exponentially. The control problem has halved in size: keep \(\boldsymbol\xi\) under control, and the centre of mass looks after itself.
There is a striking special case. Put the ZMP exactly at \(\boldsymbol\xi\) and hold it there. Then \(\dot{\boldsymbol\xi} = 0\), and the centre of mass coasts to a halt directly above the ZMP. So \(\boldsymbol\xi\) is the point on the ground where you must step, or put the centre of pressure, to stop. That is why it is also called the capture point (Pratt and colleagues, 2006). If the capture point leaves the region where any future support polygon could reach it, the fall can no longer be stopped.
There is another way to read the equation for \(\boldsymbol\xi\). Solving it forward from time \(t\) and asking that \(\boldsymbol\xi\) stays bounded (the robot does not fall over) forces
\[
\boldsymbol\xi(t) = \omega\int_t^\infty e^{-\omega(s - t)}\,\mathbf z(s)\,ds .
\]
The DCM now is a discounted average of all future ZMPs, with a discount time of \(1/\omega = 1.67\) s. A walk that doesn’t fall must therefore be planned with the future in view: where the ZMP will be over the next few seconds determines what the body must do now. That one equation is why the tripod needs a predictive planner, and how far ahead it must look.

title: Planning the Falling Walk
text:
The hinge, in pendulum terms
On three feet the ZMP can go anywhere in the triangle. On two feet the support polygon collapses to the line segment between them. Resolve the motion along and across that line. Along it, the ZMP can still slide, so that component is controlled. Across it, the ZMP is pinned at zero offset, and the equation becomes
\[
\ddot y = \omega^2 y ,
\]
a pure, uncontrolled fall: part 3’s hinge again. The tripod spends 60% of its walking time on two feet, so 60% of the time it is free-falling sideways. The fall is slow, because \(1/\omega = 1.67\) s for a 27 m pendulum, but it cannot be stopped from two feet. The planner’s job on three feet is to set up the state so that the coming fall lands the body where the next footfall will catch it.


Show code
for y0, v0 in ((1.0, 0.0), (1.0, 0.5), (-1.0, 1.0)):
    y12 = y0*math.cosh(w*1.2) + v0/w*math.sinh(w*1.2)
    xi = y0 + v0/w
    print(f"start {y0:+.1f} m from the hinge moving {v0:+.1f} m/s: after a 1.2 s swing {y12:+.2f} m  (DCM {xi:+.2f} m)")


start +1.0 m from the hinge moving +0.0 m/s: after a 1.2 s swing +1.27 m  (DCM +1.00 m)
start +1.0 m from the hinge moving +0.5 m/s: after a 1.2 s swing +1.92 m  (DCM +1.83 m)
start -1.0 m from the hinge moving +1.0 m/s: after a 1.2 s swing +0.04 m  (DCM +0.67 m)


The last line shows the DCM’s predictive power. The body starts 1 m on one side of the hinge but moving towards it fast enough that its DCM is on the other side, so it crosses over. Where it ends up is decided by the side of the line the DCM is on, not the side the body is on.

title: Planning the Falling Walk
text:
Discretising exactly
The planner works on a time grid of \(\Delta t = 0.1\) s, with the ZMP held constant during each interval. Because the LIPM is linear with constant coefficients, the state after one interval is exact, not an approximation like Euler’s method:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}c\\ \dot c\end{pmatrix}_{k+1} =
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}\cosh\omega\Delta t & \omega^{-1}\sinh\omega\Delta t\\ \omega\sinh\omega\Delta t & \cosh\omega\Delta t\end{pmatrix}}_{A}
\begin{pmatrix}c\\ \dot c\end{pmatrix}_k +
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}1 - \cosh\omega\Delta t\\ -\omega\sinh\omega\Delta t\end{pmatrix}}_{B} z_k .
\]


Show code
dt = 0.1
Ch, Sh = math.cosh(w*dt), math.sinh(w*dt)
A = np.array([[Ch, Sh/w], [w*Sh, Ch]]); B = np.array([1 - Ch, -w*Sh])
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
zs = rng.uniform(-3, 3, 40); x = np.array([0.0, 1.0]); traj = [x]
for z in zs:
    x = A @ x + B*z; traj.append(x)
sol_c, sol_v = 0.0, 1.0                                 # integrate the ODE numerically, piece by piece
for z in zs:
    s = solve_ivp(lambda t, y: [y[1], w*w*(y[0] - z)], (0, dt), [sol_c, sol_v], rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12)
    sol_c, sol_v = s.y[:, -1]
print(f"after 4 s of random ZMP moves: exact map {traj[-1].round(9)}, ODE solver {np.round([sol_c, sol_v], 9)}")
print(f"eigenvalues of A: {np.linalg.eigvals(A).round(4)}  = exp(+-omega dt) = {math.exp(w*dt):.4f}, {math.exp(-w*dt):.4f}")


after 4 s of random ZMP moves: exact map [10.72000848  6.53920555], ODE solver [10.72000848  6.53920555]
eigenvalues of A: [1.0619 0.9417]  = exp(+-omega dt) = 1.0619, 0.9417


The eigenvalues \(e^{\pm\omega\Delta t}\) are the discrete version of the stable/unstable split. One mode shrinks by 6% per step, the other grows by 6%.

title: Planning the Falling Walk
section: The ZMP planner as a quadratic programme
text:
The ZMP planner as a quadratic programme
Now set up the planning problem. Stack everything over a horizon of \(N\) steps into one vector of decision variables: the states \(\mathbf x_0, \dots, \mathbf x_N\) (position and velocity, in \(x\) and \(y\)) and the ZMPs \(\mathbf z_0, \dots, \mathbf z_{N-1}\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\mathbf x, \mathbf z}\quad & \sum_{k=1}^{N}\Big( w_v\|\dot{\mathbf c}_k - \mathbf v_\text{ref}\|^2 + w_p\|\mathbf c_k - \mathbf c^\text{nom}_k\|^2 \Big)
+ \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Big( w_{\Delta z}\|\mathbf z_k - \mathbf z_{k-1}\|^2 + w_z\|\mathbf z_k - \bar{\mathbf p}_k\|^2\Big)\\
\text{subject to}\quad & \mathbf x_0 = \text{measured state},\\
& \mathbf x_{k+1} = A\,\mathbf x_k + B\,\mathbf z_k \quad\text{(exact pendulum dynamics)},\\
& \mathbf z_k \in \text{support polygon at step } k \quad\text{(linear inequalities)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The cost asks for four things:

keep the walking speed;
keep up with the footstep timeline;
move the ZMP smoothly;
keep the ZMP near the middle of the support (around the centroid \(\bar{\mathbf p}_k\) of the planted feet).

The constraints are all linear. A triangle is three half-planes, \(\mathbf n_e^\top\mathbf z \le \mathbf n_e^\top\mathbf a_e - \text{margin}\) for each edge \(e\) with outward normal \(\mathbf n_e\). A two-foot line is an equality across it plus two bounds along it. A quadratic cost with linear constraints is a quadratic programme (QP). It is convex, so there is one global optimum and fast, reliable solvers find it. The tripod uses OSQP, an operator-splitting solver designed for exactly this kind of sparse, repeated problem.

A one-dimensional warm-up
Before the full planar version, here is the same QP stripped to one dimension, written out from scratch: a walker on a line. The footsteps advance 7.33 m every 2 s. For 0.8 s of each step the ZMP may be anywhere between the rear and front feet; for the next 1.2 s it is confined to a 1 m patch around the front foot, the 1-D stand-in for the hinge.


Show code
L, T_ds, T_ss, T_start = 22.0/3, 0.8, 1.2, 2.0
N = 240; tk = np.arange(N)*dt + dt/2               # plan 24 s, show the first 20
def bounds(t):
    if t < T_start:                                # standing start: feet at -L and +L
        return (-L, L)
    k, tau = divmod(t - T_start, T_ds + T_ss); k = int(k)
    rear, front = k*L, (k + 1)*L
    return (rear, front) if tau < T_ds else (front - 0.5, front + 0.5)
lo_hi = np.array([bounds(t) for t in tk])
v_ref = L/(T_ds + T_ss)

nx, nz = 2*(N + 1), N                              # variables: (c, v) at each knot, then z
iC = lambda k: 2*k; iV = lambda k: 2*k + 1; iZ = lambda k: nx + k
Pm = sp.lil_matrix((nx + nz, nx + nz)); q = np.zeros(nx + nz)
for k in range(1, N + 1):                          # speed tracking
    Pm[iV(k), iV(k)] += 1.0; q[iV(k)] -= v_ref
for k in range(N):                                 # ZMP smoothness and centring
    mid = lo_hi[k].mean()
    Pm[iZ(k), iZ(k)] += 0.01; q[iZ(k)] -= 0.01*mid
    if k > 0:
        Pm[iZ(k), iZ(k)] += 30; Pm[iZ(k - 1), iZ(k - 1)] += 30
        Pm[iZ(k), iZ(k - 1)] -= 30; Pm[iZ(k - 1), iZ(k)] -= 30
rows, lo, hi = [], [], []
def con(coef, l, u): rows.append(coef); lo.append(l); hi.append(u)
con({iC(0): 1}, 0.0, 0.0); con({iV(0): 1}, 0.0, 0.0)              # start at rest at x = 0, between the feet
for k in range(N):
    con({iC(k + 1): 1, iC(k): -A[0, 0], iV(k): -A[0, 1], iZ(k): -B[0]}, 0, 0)
    con({iV(k + 1): 1, iC(k): -A[1, 0], iV(k): -A[1, 1], iZ(k): -B[1]}, 0, 0)
    con({iZ(k): 1}, *lo_hi[k])
Am = sp.lil_matrix((len(rows), nx + nz))
for r, coef in enumerate(rows):
    for c_, v_ in coef.items(): Am[r, c_] = v_
solver = osqp.OSQP()
solver.setup(sp.csc_matrix(2*Pm), 2*q, sp.csc_matrix(Am), np.array(lo), np.array(hi),
             verbose=False, eps_abs=1e-6, eps_rel=1e-6, max_iter=20000, polishing=True)
res = solver.solve()
xsol = res.x[:nx].reshape(N + 1, 2); zsol = res.x[nx:]
c, v = xsol[:, 0], xsol[:, 1]; xi = c + v/w
print(f"OSQP status: {res.info.status}, {res.info.iter} iterations, {res.info.run_time*1e3:.1f} ms;"
      f" {nx + nz} variables, {len(rows)} constraints")

t_knots = np.arange(N + 1)*dt
show = t_knots <= 20; show_z = tk <= 20
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 5.6), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2, 1]})
a1.fill_between(tk[show_z], lo_hi[show_z, 0], lo_hi[show_z, 1], step="mid", color=GREY, alpha=0.2, label="allowed ZMP")
a1.step(tk[show_z], zsol[show_z], where="mid", color=RED, lw=1.5, label="ZMP")
a1.plot(t_knots[show], c[show], color=BLUE, lw=2, label="centre of mass")
a1.plot(t_knots[show], xi[show], color=BRASS, lw=1.5, ls="--", label="DCM ξ")
a1.set_ylabel("position (m)"); a1.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left", ncol=2)
a2.plot(t_knots[show], v[show], color=BLUE, lw=2); a2.axhline(v_ref, color=GREY, ls=":")
a2.set_ylabel("speed (m/s)"); a2.set_xlabel("time (s)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# the DCM really is the discounted future ZMP (check at t = 6 s, ignoring the horizon's end)
k0 = 60; s_ = np.arange(k0, N)
xi_future = np.sum(np.exp(-w*(s_ - k0)*dt)*(1 - math.exp(-w*dt))*zsol[s_])
print(f"DCM at t = 6 s: from the state {xi[k0]:.2f} m; as the discounted sum of future ZMPs {xi_future:.2f} m")


OSQP status: solved, 175 iterations, 2.9 ms; 722 variables, 722 constraints








Figure 2: A one-dimensional ZMP plan for the first 20 s of walking from a standing start (feet 7.3 m either side of the body for the first 2 s). Shaded: where the ZMP is allowed. Red: the planned ZMP. Blue: the centre of mass. Brass: the DCM (capture point), which always runs ahead of the body. Bottom: forward speed. The body never stops. Each time the support narrows to the front foot, the body vaults over it like an inverted pendulum, slowing as it approaches the foot and speeding up as it falls past: the ripple in the speed.





DCM at t = 6 s: from the state 23.01 m; as the discounted sum of future ZMPs 23.01 m


Read the picture from left to right. To get going from rest, the planner first puts the ZMP well behind the body: the only way to accelerate forward is to fall forward. Once walking, each three-foot phase sweeps the ZMP forward from the rear foot to the front one. In the narrow phase the ZMP is pinned at the front foot while the body vaults over it, slowing as it climbs towards the foot and speeding up as it falls past. That is the steady ripple in the speed. The capture point \(\xi\) always leads the body by \(\dot c/\omega\), about 6 m at this speed, and keeps ahead of the footsteps. The body has always just enough momentum to reach the next support. The last line confirms the integral formula: the DCM computed from the state equals the discounted sum of the planned future ZMPs. (The discrete version of the weight \(\omega\,dt\,e^{-\omega s}\) is \((1 - e^{-\omega\Delta t})e^{-\omega s}\).)


The real thing: the tripod in the plane
The tripod’s planner (tripod/planner.py) is the same QP in two dimensions with the real support polygons. A footstep schedule says which leg swings when and where it lands. Steps take 2.0 s: 0.8 s on three feet, then 1.2 s with one leg in the air. Each step moves one foot by a 22 m stride, in the order 1, 2, 0. Over a 14 s horizon at 0.1 s resolution there are 140 ZMP knots and 141 states, about 850 variables, solved in roughly 10 ms.


Show code
feet0 = [slot(P, i) for i in range(3)]
sched = Schedule(P, [f.copy() for f in feet0], t0=0.6, ds_time=0.8, ss_time=1.2, stride=22.0)
plan = COMPlanner(sched, h, horizon=14.0, margin=1.5, w_pos=0.05)
import time
t0 = time.perf_counter(); ok = plan.solve(0.0, np.array([-0.24, 0.0]), np.zeros(2)); t_solve = time.perf_counter() - t0
X, Z = plan.X, plan.Z
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.6))
seen = set()
for j in range(plan.N):
    feet, swing = sched.feet_at(j*dt + dt/2)
    pts = [f for f in feet if f is not None]
    key = tuple(np.round(np.concatenate(pts), 2))
    if key in seen: continue
    seen.add(key)
    poly = np.array(pts + [pts[0]])
    ax.plot(poly[:, 0], poly[:, 1], color=GREY, lw=0.8 if len(pts) == 3 else 2.2, alpha=0.6)
    if len(pts) == 3: ax.fill(poly[:, 0], poly[:, 1], color=GREY, alpha=0.05)
ax.plot(Z[:, 0], Z[:, 1], ".", color=RED, ms=4, label="ZMP")
ax.plot(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], color=BLUE, lw=2, label="centre of mass")
ax.plot(X[:, 0] + X[:, 2]/w, X[:, 1] + X[:, 3]/w, "--", color=BRASS, lw=1.3, label="DCM")
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("x (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("y (m)"); ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left", ncol=3)
plt.show()
print(f"solved: {ok} in {t_solve*1e3:.0f} ms; {plan.N} ZMP knots; schedule speed {sched.speed:.2f} m/s")








Figure 3: One solve of the tripod’s planner from standing still, seen from above. Grey triangles and lines: the support polygon over time (three-foot triangles and two-foot hinge lines). Red: the planned ZMP, which hops between hinge lines and sweeps across triangles. Blue: the planned centre of mass, weaving from side to side as each new hinge appears in a different direction. Brass: the DCM. The far end of the plan is the least constrained part, and it curls away; it is never executed, because the plan is re-solved long before the body gets there.





solved: True in 12 ms; 140 ZMP knots; schedule speed 3.67 m/s

title: Planning the Falling Walk
section: How far ahead must it look?
text:
How far ahead must it look?
The DCM integral says the present depends on the future ZMP, discounted with a 1.67 s time constant. A planner that looks only a second or two ahead cannot see the supports it will need, so it plans motions that look fine within its horizon and are doomed just beyond it. It has no notion that the body must still be catchable when the horizon ends. This is easy to test: run the receding-horizon loop on the pendulum with different horizons.


Show code
def walk(horizon, T=30.0, push=None, replan=True, sim_dt=0.01):
    s = Schedule(P, [f.copy() for f in feet0], 0.6, 0.8, 1.2, 22.0)
    pl = COMPlanner(s, h, horizon=horizon, margin=1.5, w_pos=0.05)
    c, v, t, last, last_sup, out = np.array([-0.24, 0.0]), np.zeros(2), 0.0, -1e9, None, []
    Cs, Ss = math.cosh(w*sim_dt), math.sinh(w*sim_dt)
    while t < T:
        k, _ = s.step_of(t); _, sw = s.feet_at(t); sup = (k, sw)
        may_replan = replan or (push is not None and t < push[0])
        if pl.X is None or (may_replan and (sup != last_sup or t - last >= 0.4)):
            pl.solve(t, c, v); last, last_sup = t, sup
        z = pl.reference(t)[3]
        c, v = z + (c - z)*Cs + v*Ss/w, (c - z)*w*Ss + v*Cs      # the exact pendulum, ZMP held over the step
        if push is not None and abs(t - push[0]) < sim_dt/2:
            v = v + np.array([0.0, push[1]])
        t += sim_dt; out.append((t, *c, *v))
        if np.linalg.norm(c - s.nominal(t)) > 40: break           # fallen over
    return np.array(out), s

print("horizon   outcome")
for H in (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 14):
    tr, s = walk(H)
    fell = tr[-1, 0] < 29.9
    print(f"{H:5.0f} s   " + (f"falls after {tr[-1, 0]:.1f} s" if fell else
                              f"walks 30 s: {tr[-1, 1] - tr[0, 1]:.0f} m at {(tr[-1, 1] - tr[0, 1])/30:.2f} m/s"))


horizon   outcome
    1 s   falls after 5.7 s
    2 s   falls after 4.6 s
    3 s   falls after 8.0 s
    4 s   falls after 22.5 s
    6 s   walks 30 s: 102 m at 3.42 m/s
    8 s   walks 30 s: 105 m at 3.49 m/s
   14 s   walks 30 s: 105 m at 3.49 m/s


Horizons of four seconds or less fail. Every individual QP is feasible, and the planner never reports a problem, yet the walk diverges: within a few steps for horizons of 1–3 s, after about ten steps at 4 s. From six seconds on, one full gait cycle (three steps of 2 s), the walk is stable and longer horizons change little. The rule of thumb in humanoid robotics is a preview of one to two steps; for this slow, tall pendulum on a three-step cycle, that means a whole cycle. The project uses 14 s for margin.

title: Planning the Falling Walk
section: Model-predictive control: replanning from what actually happened
text:
Model-predictive control: replanning from what actually happened
A plan computed once and followed blindly is open-loop. The pendulum is unstable, so any error — a gust, a misplaced foot, a modelling error — grows like \(e^{\omega t}\), doubling every 1.15 s. The cure is to re-solve the QP frequently from the measured state. Execute only the first part of each plan, then plan again. This is receding-horizon or model-predictive control (MPC). The tripod re-plans at every change of support and every 0.4 s in between.
To see the difference, push the walking pendulum sideways at \(t = 10\) s, and compare the MPC loop with one that stops re-planning at the moment of the push.


Show code
base, _ = walk(14.0, T=24.0)
mpc, _ = walk(14.0, T=24.0, push=(10.0, 2.0))
frozen, _ = walk(14.0, T=15.0, push=(10.0, 2.0), replan=False)
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 3.8))
a1.plot(base[:, 1], base[:, 2], color=GREY, lw=2, label="no push")
a1.plot(mpc[:, 1], mpc[:, 2], color=BLUE, lw=1.5, label="pushed, MPC")
a1.plot(frozen[:, 1], frozen[:, 2], color=RED, lw=1.5, label="pushed, plan frozen")
a1.set_xlabel("x (m)"); a1.set_ylabel("y (m)"); a1.set_ylim(-15, 30); a1.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")
dev_m = np.linalg.norm(mpc[:, 1:3] - base[:len(mpc), 1:3], axis=1)
dev_f = np.linalg.norm(frozen[:, 1:3] - base[:len(frozen), 1:3], axis=1)
a2.semilogy(mpc[:, 0], np.maximum(dev_m, 1e-3), color=BLUE, lw=2, label="MPC")
a2.semilogy(frozen[:, 0], np.maximum(dev_f, 1e-3), color=RED, lw=2, label="plan frozen")
a2.axvline(10, color=GREY, ls=":"); a2.set_xlabel("time (s)"); a2.set_ylabel("distance from unpushed path (m)")
a2.legend(frameon=False); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
i = lambda tr, t: np.searchsorted(tr[:, 0], t)
print(f"MPC: peak deviation {dev_m.max():.2f} m; {dev_m[i(mpc, 15)]:.2f} m at 15 s; {dev_m[i(mpc, 20)]:.2f} m at 20 s; {dev_m[-1]:.2f} m at 24 s")
print(f"frozen plan: {dev_f[i(frozen, 12)]:.1f} m at 12 s, {dev_f[-1]:.1f} m at 15 s")








Figure 4: Recovery from a sideways push at t = 10 s (a sudden 2 m/s change in lateral velocity, the equivalent of a 514 kN·s impulse on the 257-tonne machine). Grey: the unpushed walk. Blue: MPC, re-planning from the measured state; the deviation peaks at about 2 m and has shrunk to about 10 cm seven steps later. Red: the same push with the plan frozen at the moment of impact; the body falls away exponentially.





MPC: peak deviation 2.34 m; 1.15 m at 15 s; 0.28 m at 20 s; 0.12 m at 24 s
frozen plan: 3.8 m at 12 s, 31.7 m at 15 s


The frozen plan does not merely drift. Its error grows exponentially, the straight line on the log scale, because the push has moved the DCM and the old plan’s ZMP no longer contains it. MPC sees the new state at the next re-plan and moves the ZMP to absorb the push over the following steps. The deviation decays steadily, and the robot rejoins its path.






In the full MuJoCo simulation



The tripod model has extra machinery on top of this. Its whole-body controller adds a spring-damper pulling the centre of mass towards the plan. While three feet are down, friction at the feet can resist sideways forces directly. In the full simulation, a 2 m/s lateral push of 0.5 s duration during the walk hardly disturbs it. The pure pendulum above, with nothing but the ZMP to steer with, shows the planner’s contribution on its own.

title: Planning the Falling Walk
text:
From plan to torques
The planner outputs a centre-of-mass trajectory and a ZMP. Turning those into motor commands uses everything from the earlier parts, about 500 times a second.

Desired force. Compute the force that keeps the centre of mass on the plan: the planned acceleration \(m\ddot{\mathbf c}_\text{plan}\) as feedforward, plus a spring-damper on the tracking error, plus the weight. Compute a moment that keeps the hood level.
Share it among the planted feet. Solve the grasp-matrix least-squares problem from part 3, with every foot pushing and inside its friction cone. On two feet, drop the moment component about the hinge, which can’t be produced.
Torques. Map each foot force through \(\boldsymbol\tau = \mathbf g(\mathbf q) - J^\top\mathbf f\), the virtual-work law of part 3.
Swing leg. Move the lifted foot along its task-space arc using closed-form IK (part 2) and a joint servo, landing on the next scheduled foothold.

The result in MuJoCo, from the main post:

15 steps in 30.6 s, covering 77 m at 5.6 mph;
59% of the time on two feet;
the hood never tilting more than 2.7°.

That is five times the speed of the wait-and-topple gait, with a sixth of its tilt.

title: Planning the Falling Walk
text:
What this planner leaves out
The LIPM and a fixed footstep schedule are the classic starting point, not the state of the art. Some refinements, roughly in order of how much they would help the tripod:

Footstep optimisation. Here the footholds are fixed in advance and only the ZMP moves. Letting the QP also choose where the feet land, as a capture-point stepping strategy does, gives far more authority against pushes. That matters on two feet, where the ZMP has no sideways authority at all.
Height and angular momentum. Holding the height constant is what made the model linear. Allowing the body to bob, or the hood to pitch, adds more ways to control the body. The usual tool is the centroidal dynamics model, solved by nonlinear MPC.
Leg dynamics. Each 28 t leg weighs a ninth of the machine, and swinging it shoves the body. The LIPM ignores this; whole-body MPC includes it.
Learning. Much of modern legged locomotion is trained by reinforcement learning in simulators like MuJoCo, often with a model-based planner like this one providing structure or reference motions. The main post discusses why MuJoCo became the standard simulator for that work.

title: Planning the Falling Walk
text:
Summary

Holding the centre of mass at constant height gives the linear inverted pendulum \(\ddot{\mathbf c} = \omega^2(\mathbf c - \mathbf z)\). The ZMP \(\mathbf z\) is the centre of pressure and must stay in the support polygon.
The divergent component \(\boldsymbol\xi = \mathbf c + \dot{\mathbf c}/\omega\) carries all the instability. It equals the discounted future ZMP, so walking must be planned ahead. It is also the capture point: put the ZMP there to stop.
On two feet the support polygon is a line, and the motion across it is a pure fall. A walking tripod is falling sideways 60% of the time.
Exact discretisation plus linear support constraints make ZMP planning a convex QP, solved by OSQP in about 10 ms.
The horizon must cover about one gait cycle; shorter horizons produce feasible plans that still fall.
Re-planning from the measured state (MPC) turns an exponentially unstable open-loop plan into a robust walk.

title: The Kerr Black Hole
text:
This is the third of four explainers behind Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole:
Gargantua spins. In the story it spins within a whisker of the maximum, which is what makes an hour on Miller’s planet cost seven years on Earth. Spin breaks the spherical symmetry that made part 2 so economical: a ray no longer stays in one plane, and no single function of one angle describes the image. This post sets up the equations that DNGR, the code behind Interstellar, actually integrated, builds a ray tracer from them, and checks it against the few results for a spinning hole that are known exactly.
Show code
import sys, math, time, warnings
from pathlib import Path
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve().parents[1] / "gargantua"
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from blackhole import kerr, render as R, sky as SK, disk as D, schwarzschild as S
from blackhole.colour import tonemap, bloom

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})

def show(ax, img, title=None):
    ax.imshow(np.clip(img, 0, 1), interpolation="lanczos")
    ax.set_axis_off()
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)

title: The Kerr Black Hole
text:
The Kerr metric
Roy Kerr found the spacetime of a spinning black hole in 1963. In Boyer–Lindquist coordinates \((t, r, \theta, \phi)\), with \(G = c = M = 1\) and spin parameter \(a = J/M\) (the angular momentum per unit mass, \(0 \le a < 1\)), it can be written, as in the DNGR paper, in a form that exposes its meaning:
\[
ds^2 = -\alpha^2\,dt^2 + \frac{\rho^2}{\Delta}\,dr^2 + \rho^2\,d\theta^2 + \varpi^2\left(d\phi - \omega\,dt\right)^2,
\]
with
\[
\rho^2 = r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta, \quad \Delta = r^2 - 2r + a^2, \quad \Sigma^2 = (r^2 + a^2)^2 - a^2\Delta\sin^2\theta,
\] \[
\alpha = \frac{\rho\sqrt\Delta}{\Sigma}, \qquad \omega = \frac{2ar}{\Sigma^2}, \qquad \varpi = \frac{\Sigma\sin\theta}{\rho}.
\]
Each function has a job:

\(\alpha\) is the lapse: how fast a local clock ticks relative to \(t\). It vanishes at the horizon.
\(\varpi\) is the circumferential radius: a ring at fixed \(r, \theta\) has circumference \(2\pi\varpi\).
\(\omega\) is the frame-dragging angular velocity. The combination \(d\phi - \omega\,dt\) means that “not rotating” near the hole means rotating at \(d\phi/dt = \omega\) relative to the distant stars.

Setting \(a = 0\) gives \(\omega = 0\), \(\rho = \varpi/\sin\theta = r\), \(\alpha^2 = 1 - 2/r\), and the Schwarzschild metric of parts 1 and 2.
The horizon is where \(\Delta = 0\), at \(r_+ = 1 + \sqrt{1 - a^2}\), which shrinks from \(2\) to \(1\) as the spin rises to its maximum. Outside it is the ergosphere, where \(g_{tt} > 0\), out to \(r = 1 + \sqrt{1 - a^2\cos^2\theta}\). Inside the ergosphere frame dragging is so strong that nothing can stay still relative to the distant stars. Everything there is swept round with the hole.


Show code
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(12, 3.4))
th = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 400)
for ax, a in zip(axs, [0.0, 0.6, 0.9, 0.999]):
    rp = kerr.horizon(a)
    rerg = 1 + np.sqrt(1 - a**2 * np.cos(th) ** 2)
    ax.fill(rerg * np.sin(th), rerg * np.cos(th), color="0.8")
    if a > 0:
        r1, r2 = kerr.photon_orbit_radii(a)
    else:
        r1 = r2 = 3.0
    # photon region: where spherical orbits exist at this theta
    rr = np.linspace(r1, r2, 300)
    if a > 0:
        b, q = kerr.spherical_photon_constants(rr, a)
    for t in np.linspace(0, np.pi, 181):
        if a > 0:
            ok = q + a * a * np.cos(t) ** 2 - b * b / np.tan(t + 1e-12) ** 2 >= 0
            ax.plot(rr[ok] * np.sin(t), rr[ok] * np.cos(t), ".", color="C1", ms=0.6)
            ax.plot(-rr[ok] * np.sin(t), rr[ok] * np.cos(t), ".", color="C1", ms=0.6)
    if a == 0:
        ax.plot(3 * np.sin(th), 3 * np.cos(th), color="C1", lw=2)
    ax.fill(rp * np.sin(th), rp * np.cos(th), color="k")
    ri = D.isco(a)
    ax.plot(ri * np.sin(th), ri * np.cos(th), "k--", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlim(-6.5, 6.5)
    ax.set_ylim(-5, 5)
    ax.set_title(f"a = {a}", fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"{'a':>6} {'horizon':>8} {'prograde photon':>16} {'retrograde photon':>18} {'ISCO':>7}")
for a in [0.0, 0.6, 0.9, 0.999]:
    r1, r2 = kerr.photon_orbit_radii(a) if a > 0 else (3.0, 3.0)
    print(f"{a:6g} {kerr.horizon(a):8.4f} {r1:16.4f} {r2:18.4f} {D.isco(a):7.4f}")








Figure 1: Cross-sections through Kerr holes of increasing spin, the spin axis vertical (Boyer-Lindquist r and θ drawn as if they were polar coordinates). Black: horizon. Grey: the ergosphere. Orange: the region swept by spherical photon orbits, between the prograde and retrograde circular photon orbits in the equator. Dashed: the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) for matter. As the spin rises, prograde orbits move in towards the horizon.





     a  horizon  prograde photon  retrograde photon    ISCO
     0   2.0000           3.0000             3.0000  6.0000
   0.6   1.8000           2.1889             3.6298  3.8291
   0.9   1.4359           1.5579             3.9103  2.3209
 0.999   1.0447           1.0521             3.9991  1.1818



Observers who do not rotate
Which observer should hold the camera? Near a spinning hole there are no static observers inside the ergosphere, and outside it they are not the natural choice either. The natural one is the zero-angular-momentum observer (ZAMO), the “fiducial observer” or FIDO of the DNGR paper. It moves on the line \(\phi = \omega t + \text{const}\), carried round by frame dragging but with no angular momentum of its own. Its orthonormal basis vectors point along the coordinate lines:
\[
\mathbf e_{\hat r} = \frac{\sqrt\Delta}{\rho}\,\partial_r, \qquad
\mathbf e_{\hat\theta} = \frac{1}{\rho}\,\partial_\theta, \qquad
\mathbf e_{\hat\phi} = \frac{1}{\varpi}\,\partial_\phi .
\]
Any real camera moves relative to the local ZAMO with some velocity \(\beta\), and its view is the ZAMO’s view, aberrated as in part 2.

title: The Kerr Black Hole
section: Three constants for a light ray
text:
Three constants for a light ray
In Schwarzschild spacetime a ray has energy \(E\) and angular momentum \(L\), and spherical symmetry supplies the rest. The Kerr metric is independent of \(t\) and \(\phi\), which again gives \(E = -p_t\) and \(L_z = p_\phi\). But it is only axially symmetric, so total angular momentum is no longer conserved, and two constants are not enough to determine a path in three dimensions.
In 1968 Brandon Carter found a third. Write the Hamilton–Jacobi equation for null geodesics,
\[
g^{\mu\nu}\,\frac{\partial S}{\partial x^\mu}\frac{\partial S}{\partial x^\nu} = 0,
\]
and try \(S = -Et + L_z\phi + S_r(r) + S_\theta(\theta)\). With \(E = 1\) (so that \(b = L_z/E\) is the axial impact parameter), the inverse Kerr metric turns the equation into
\[
\Delta\,S_r'^2 - \frac{P^2}{\Delta} + (b - a)^2 \;=\; -\,S_\theta'^2 - \cos^2\theta\left(\frac{b^2}{\sin^2\theta} - a^2\right),
\qquad P = r^2 + a^2 - ab .
\]
The left side depends only on \(r\) and the right side only on \(\theta\), so both equal a constant, \(-q\). That separability is the hidden symmetry of the Kerr metric, and \(q\) is the Carter constant (divided by \(E^2\)). The radial and polar motions then decouple:
\[
p_r^2\,\Delta^2 = R(r) \equiv P^2 - \Delta\left[(b - a)^2 + q\right],
\qquad
p_\theta^2 = \Theta(\theta) \equiv q - \cos^2\theta\left(\frac{b^2}{\sin^2\theta} - a^2\right).
\]
A ray can only be where \(R \ge 0\) and \(\Theta \ge 0\). A ray that crosses the equator has \(q \ge 0\), and \(q = 0\) means a ray confined to the equatorial plane.

title: The Kerr Black Hole
text:
The ray equations
Integrating \(p_r = \pm\sqrt R/\Delta\) directly runs into trouble at every turning point, where the square root changes sign. DNGR instead integrated Hamilton’s equations for the super-Hamiltonian \(H = \tfrac12 g^{\mu\nu}p_\mu p_\nu\), which handle turning points smoothly. With \(p_t = -1\) and \(p_\phi = b\) fixed,
\[
H = \frac{\Delta}{2\rho^2}\,p_r^2 + \frac{1}{2\rho^2}\,p_\theta^2 - \frac{R + \Delta\Theta}{2\Delta\rho^2} = 0,
\]
and Hamilton’s equations, \(\dot x = \partial H/\partial p\) and \(\dot p = -\partial H/\partial x\), give the five equations that are the heart of the renderer:
\[
\frac{dr}{d\zeta} = \frac{\Delta}{\rho^2}\,p_r, \qquad
\frac{d\theta}{d\zeta} = \frac{p_\theta}{\rho^2}, \qquad
\frac{d\phi}{d\zeta} = -\frac{\partial}{\partial b}\left(\frac{R + \Delta\Theta}{2\Delta\rho^2}\right),
\] \[
\frac{dp_r}{d\zeta} = \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left[-\frac{\Delta}{2\rho^2}p_r^2 - \frac{p_\theta^2}{2\rho^2} + \frac{R + \Delta\Theta}{2\Delta\rho^2}\right], \qquad
\frac{dp_\theta}{d\zeta} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\left[\;\cdots\;\right].
\]
These are equations (A.15) of the DNGR paper. The combination \((R + \Delta\Theta)/\Delta = P^2/\Delta - (b-a)^2 - \cos^2\theta\,(b^2/\sin^2\theta - a^2)\) does not involve \(q\) at all, so \(q\) is never used during integration. Its conservation is therefore a genuine test of the integrator. Working out the derivatives,
\[
\frac{d\phi}{d\zeta} = \frac{1}{\rho^2}\left(\frac{aP}{\Delta} + \frac{b}{\sin^2\theta} - a\right),
\]
which for \(a = 0\) is the familiar \(b/(r^2\sin^2\theta)\).

Initial conditions from a pixel
The camera supplies a direction. A pixel’s unit vector \(\mathbf N\) (from camera to sky) in the camera frame becomes, for the arriving photon, a propagation direction \(\mathbf n = -\mathbf N\). Aberration converts it to the ZAMO frame, giving \(\mathbf n_F\). The photon’s energy measured by the ZAMO is then
\[
E_F = \frac{1}{\alpha + \omega\varpi\,n_{F\hat\phi}},
\]
and its covariant momenta are
\[
p_r = E_F\frac{\rho}{\sqrt\Delta}\,n_{F\hat r}, \qquad
p_\theta = E_F\,\rho\,n_{F\hat\theta}, \qquad
b = p_\phi = E_F\,\varpi\,n_{F\hat\phi}.
\]
These satisfy \(H = 0\) automatically. The ray is then integrated backwards, \(\zeta \to -\infty\), until it escapes, reaches the horizon, or hits the disk.


The integrator
The tracer (kerr.trace) is a Dormand–Prince 5(4) Runge–Kutta integrator with adaptive steps. It is compiled with numba and runs one ray per thread. Steps are small where the ray bends sharply near the hole and long far away. A ray that crosses the equator inside the disk’s radius is stopped there, the crossing located to \(10^{-10}\) in \(\theta\) by secant iteration (part 4). Here it traces the rays of one image of a fast-spinning hole and checks the constants it is not told about:


Show code
a = 0.999
cam = kerr.Camera(6.03, math.pi / 2, a, beta="orbit", fov=90)
N = cam.directions(480, 480)
Y0, B, E_cam = cam.initial_conditions(N)
q0 = kerr.carter_q(Y0[:, 0], Y0[:, 1], Y0[:, 4], B, a)
H0 = kerr.hamiltonian(Y0[:, 0], Y0[:, 1], Y0[:, 3], Y0[:, 4], B, a)
t0 = time.time()
Y, oc, ns = kerr.trace(Y0, B, a, tol=1e-9)
secs = time.time() - t0
q1 = kerr.carter_q(Y[:, 0], Y[:, 1], Y[:, 4], B, a)
H1 = kerr.hamiltonian(Y[:, 0], Y[:, 1], Y[:, 3], Y[:, 4], B, a)
esc = oc == kerr.ESCAPED
dq = np.abs(q1 - q0)[esc] / np.maximum(1, np.abs(q0[esc]))
print(f"{len(Y)} rays in {secs:.2f} s: {esc.sum()} escaped, {(oc == kerr.CAPTURED).sum()} captured")
print(f"steps per ray: median {np.median(ns):.0f}, max {ns.max()}")
print(f"|H| at the camera:   max {np.abs(H0).max():.1e}")
print(f"|H| at the end:      max {np.abs(H1[esc]).max():.1e}")
print(f"Carter constant drift (relative): median {np.median(dq):.1e}, max {dq.max():.1e}")
dq_max = dq.max()


230400 rays in 7.01 s: 153574 escaped, 76826 captured
steps per ray: median 154, max 2581
|H| at the camera:   max 9.8e-16
|H| at the end:      max 4.4e-08
Carter constant drift (relative): median 1.8e-10, max 3.1e-08


The Carter constant, which the equations never use, is conserved to 3e-08 or better along every ray, through every turning point.

title: The Kerr Black Hole
text:
Photon orbits
A Schwarzschild hole has one photon sphere. A Kerr hole has a whole shell of spherical photon orbits: rays that stay at constant \(r\) while oscillating in \(\theta\) and winding round the axis. They exist where \(R(r) = 0\) and \(R'(r) = 0\) at once, which fixes the two constants as functions of the radius (Bardeen 1973; equations (A.5) of DNGR):
\[
b(r) = -\frac{r^3 - 3r^2 + a^2 r + a^2}{a\,(r - 1)}, \qquad
q(r) = -\frac{r^3\left(r^3 - 6r^2 + 9r - 4a^2\right)}{a^2\,(r - 1)^2},
\]
for \(r\) between the prograde and retrograde equatorial photon orbits,
\[
r_{1,2} = 2\left\{1 + \cos\!\left[\tfrac23\arccos(\mp a)\right]\right\}.
\]
These orbits are all unstable. A ray launched exactly onto one stays there only as long as rounding error allows, and then peels off exponentially. The tracer shows both behaviours:


Show code
a = 0.999
r_o = 2.0
b_o, q_o = kerr.spherical_photon_constants(r_o, a)
path, outcome = kerr.trace_path([r_o, math.pi / 2, 0.0, 0.0, math.sqrt(q_o)], b_o, a,
                                r_esc=30, tol=1e-12, n=200000, sgn=1.0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4))
turns = path[:, 2] / (2 * np.pi)
dev = np.abs(path[:, 0] - r_o)
k = np.argmax(dev > 1e-3)
ax[0].plot(turns[:k], np.degrees(path[:k, 1]), "C1", lw=0.8)
ax[0].set_xlabel("turns round the axis, φ/2π")
ax[0].set_ylabel("θ (degrees)")
ax[0].invert_yaxis()
ax[1].semilogy(turns, np.maximum(dev, 1e-16), "k", lw=1)
ax[1].set_xlabel("turns round the axis, φ/2π")
ax[1].set_ylabel("|r - 2| / M")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
th_range = np.degrees([path[:k, 1].min(), path[:k, 1].max()])
# growth rate of the deviation, fitted between 1e-11 and 1e-2
fit = (dev > 1e-11) & (dev < 1e-2)
growth = 10 ** np.polyfit(turns[fit], np.log10(dev[fit]), 1)[0]
print(f"b = {b_o:.4f}, q = {q_o:.4f}; latitude range {th_range[0]:.1f}° to {th_range[1]:.1f}°; "
      f"{turns[k]:.1f} turns before |r - 2| > 1e-3")
print(f"the deviation grows by a factor of {growth:.1f} per turn")








Figure 2: A spherical photon orbit at r = 2 M around a hole with a = 0.999, launched from the equator with the b and q of the formula above. Left: its path on the sphere (θ against φ, unrolled) is a steady oscillation between two latitudes while it winds round the axis. Right: the radius starts at 2 to within rounding error, and the instability amplifies that error exponentially, by a constant factor per turn, until the ray leaves the orbit and escapes.





b = 1.0070, q = 15.9680; latitude range 13.8° to 166.2°; 9.5 turns before |r - 2| > 1e-3
the deviation grows by a factor of 11.9 per turn


The deviation from the orbit grows by a factor of about 12 with every turn round the axis. This is the Kerr version of the winding rays of part 1, and the DNGR paper pictures one such orbit (their Figure 11). Rays that pass close to this shell are what pile up the multiple images near the shadow’s edge.

title: The Kerr Black Hole
text:
The shadow
The edge of the shadow is made of rays that, followed backwards, approach a spherical photon orbit asymptotically. For a distant observer at inclination \(\theta_o\) from the spin axis, each orbit radius \(r\) gives two points on the observer’s sky (Bardeen 1973):
\[
x = -\frac{b(r)}{\sin\theta_o}, \qquad
y = \pm\sqrt{q(r) + a^2\cos^2\theta_o - b(r)^2\cot^2\theta_o},
\]
in units of \(M\). Here \(x\) runs in the direction of the hole’s rotation and \(y\) along the projected spin axis. This curve is an exact, independent result, so it is the natural test of the ray tracer. The test is to place a camera very far away (\(r = 10^5 M\)) and bisect, along rays out from the shadow’s centre, for the boundary between captured and escaping rays:


Show code
def traced_edge(a, theta_o, n_ang=120, r_cam=1e5):
    cam = kerr.Camera(r_cam, theta_o, a)
    xb, yb = kerr.shadow_edge(a, theta_o)
    cx = 0.5 * (xb.max() + xb.min())
    ang = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, n_ang, endpoint=False)
    lo, hi = np.full(n_ang, 0.5), np.full(n_ang, 12.0)
    for _ in range(40):
        mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
        X, Yy = cx + mid * np.cos(ang), mid * np.sin(ang)
        Nv = np.stack([np.ones(n_ang), X / r_cam, Yy / r_cam], -1)
        Nv /= np.linalg.norm(Nv, axis=1, keepdims=True)
        Y0, B, _ = cam.initial_conditions(Nv)
        _, o, _ = kerr.trace(Y0, B, a, r_esc=2 * r_cam, tol=1e-11)
        cap = o == kerr.CAPTURED
        lo, hi = np.where(cap, mid, lo), np.where(cap, hi, mid)
    return cx + lo * np.cos(ang), lo * np.sin(ang), cx

worst = 0.0
for a, inc in [(0.999, 90), (0.999, 60), (0.6, 86.56)]:
    xt, yt, cx = traced_edge(a, math.radians(inc))
    xb, yb = kerr.shadow_edge(a, math.radians(inc), n=4000)
    # distance from each traced point to the nearest segment of Bardeen's curve
    P0 = np.c_[xb[:-1], yb[:-1]]
    dP = np.c_[np.diff(xb), np.diff(yb)]
    pts = np.c_[xt, yt]
    tpar = np.clip(((pts[:, None, :] - P0[None]) * dP[None]).sum(-1) / (dP ** 2).sum(-1)[None], 0, 1)
    dmin = np.linalg.norm(pts[:, None, :] - (P0[None] + tpar[..., None] * dP[None]), axis=-1).min(1)
    worst = max(worst, dmin.max())
    print(f"a = {a:5g}, inclination {inc:5.2f}°: largest distance from Bardeen's curve {dmin.max():.1e} M")


a = 0.999, inclination 90.00°: largest distance from Bardeen's curve 7.0e-05 M
a = 0.999, inclination 60.00°: largest distance from Bardeen's curve 6.7e-05 M
a =   0.6, inclination 86.56°: largest distance from Bardeen's curve 6.3e-05 M


The traced shadow lies on Bardeen’s curve to within 7e-05 \(M\) at every inclination tested. That is the size of error expected from putting the camera at \(10^5 M\) rather than at infinity: corrections of relative order \(M/r\) applied to a shadow about \(5\,M\) across.


Show code
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.6))
for ax, inc in zip(axs, [90, 60]):
    t = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 300)
    ax.fill(S.B_CRIT * np.cos(t), S.B_CRIT * np.sin(t), color="0.9")
    for a, col in [(0.3, "C0"), (0.6, "C2"), (0.9, "C1"), (0.999, "C3")]:
        xb, yb = kerr.shadow_edge(a, math.radians(inc), n=4000)
        ax.plot(xb, yb, color=col, lw=1.5, label=f"a = {a}")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axhline(0, color="0.7", lw=0.5)
    ax.axvline(0, color="0.7", lw=0.5)
    ax.set_xlabel("x / M (direction of rotation)")
    ax.set_ylabel("y / M")
    ax.set_title(f"inclination {inc}°", fontsize=10)
axs[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 3: Shadows of black holes of increasing spin, seen from the equatorial plane (left) and from 60° (right). The hole rotates so that its left side (x < 0) moves towards the viewer. The shadow is pushed sideways and flattened on the approaching side, where prograde photons can orbit closer to the hole, and bulges on the receding side. The grey circle is the Schwarzschild shadow, radius 3√3 M.





This flattened edge is why Interstellar did not show Gargantua at its story spin. Christopher Nolan and Paul Franklin judged that the flattened shadow, with the multiple disk images along it and an off-centre disk, would confuse a mass audience. For the pictures they turned the spin down to \(a = 0.6\), where the shadow is still almost round (part 4 and the main post).

title: The Kerr Black Hole
section: The camera’s motion matters as much as the spin
text:
The camera’s motion matters as much as the spin
Close to a fast-spinning hole, the choice of camera changes the picture more than anything else. The DNGR paper makes this point with a checkerboard sky seen from \(r = 2.6\,M\) around a hole with \(a = 0.999\), inside the photon region and just outside the ergosphere, by three cameras at the same point:

one on a prograde circular orbit;
one at rest relative to the local ZAMO;
one static relative to the distant stars, which takes a rocket working very hard against frame dragging.



Show code
a, r26 = 0.999, 2.6
cam0 = kerr.Camera(r26, math.pi / 2, a)
beta_static = -cam0.omega * cam0.varpi / cam0.alpha
checker = SK.Sky(SK.checkerboard(1024, n_lat=12, n_lon=24))
fig, axs = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(9, 13))
betas = {}
for ax, (beta, name) in zip(axs, [("orbit", "prograde circular orbit"), (0.0, "zero-angular-momentum observer"),
                                  (beta_static, "static camera")]):
    tr = R.trace_image(r26, 90, a, 720, 360, 0, ss=1, beta=beta, disk=False, projection="panorama")
    lin = np.where((tr["outcome"] == kerr.ESCAPED)[..., None], checker.sample(tr["sky"], SK.footprint(tr["sky"], tr["outcome"] == kerr.ESCAPED)), 0)
    show(ax, lin, f"{name}: β = {float(tr['beta']):+.3f} relative to the ZAMO")
    betas[name] = float(tr["beta"])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
b_orb, b_st = betas["prograde circular orbit"], betas["static camera"]
rel_static = (b_orb - b_st) / (1 - b_orb * b_st)
print(f"ZAMO relative to orbiting camera: {-b_orb:.3f}c;  static relative to orbiting camera: {-rel_static:.3f}c")








Figure 4: The whole sky seen from r = 2.6 M around a hole with a = 0.999, for three cameras at the same point: (top) on a prograde circular geodesic orbit; (middle) a ZAMO; (bottom) static relative to the distant stars. The hole’s centre is in the middle of each panorama. The rays and the multiplicity of images are the same in all three; only aberration differs. Compare Figure 12 of James et al. (2015).





ZAMO relative to orbiting camera: -0.546c;  static relative to orbiting camera: -0.813c


The speeds match the DNGR paper’s figures exactly: relative to the orbiting camera, the ZAMO moves at 0.546c and the static camera at 0.813c (the paper gives 0.546c and 0.813c). The static camera, racing backwards against the hole’s rotation, sees the shadow swell to cover more than half its sky. The orbiting camera sees it shrink. Yet the pattern of images, how many copies of each piece of sky appear and where the critical curves fall, is the same for all three. The caustics belong to the light cone at that point, not to whoever is looking.

title: The Kerr Black Hole
text:
Stars round a spinning hole
The DNGR paper’s first image of a spinning hole (their Figure 4) is a star field seen from a camera in a circular equatorial orbit at \(r_c = 6.03\,M\) around a hole with \(a = 0.999\). Here is the same configuration, with this renderer’s synthetic sky: a mip-mapped Milky Way and 30,000 point stars lensed by the triangle method of part 2.


Show code
a, r603 = 0.999, 6.03
milky = SK.Sky(SK.milky_way(2048))
stars = SK.star_catalogue()
ss = 2
tr = R.trace_image(r603, 90, a, 1200, 600, 0, ss=ss, beta="orbit", disk=False, projection="panorama")
img, lin = R.compose(tr, a, ss, sky=milky, stars=stars, star_gain=1.0, exposure=2.0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5.6))
show(ax, img)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("thumbnail.png", dpi=70, bbox_inches="tight", pad_inches=0)
plt.show()
print(f"{tr['outcome'].size} rays traced in {float(tr['seconds']):.1f} s; median {np.median(tr['steps']):.0f} steps per ray")








Figure 5: The whole sky from a camera in a circular equatorial orbit at r = 6.03 M around a hole with a = 0.999 (equirectangular panorama, hole at the centre, direction of motion to the right). The shadow is flattened on its left, the side where the hole’s rotation carries light towards the camera. Around it the Milky Way and the stars are repeated in nested, distorted copies between the critical curves.





2880000 rays traced in 17.5 s; median 107 steps per ray


With a spinning hole there is nothing left to tabulate, so every pixel is a full geodesic integration. On a laptop with numba that takes seconds for an image of a few million rays. DNGR rendered 23-million-pixel IMAX frames with ray bundles, at 30 minutes to several hours per frame on 10 cores. The last ingredient is the light source Interstellar is remembered for, the accretion disk. That is part 4.
