title: Markov Chains
text: This is the first of three short refreshers behind two earlier posts — Reproducing a Phase Transition in Diffusion Models and Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models — both of which lean on ideas from Sclocchi, Favero & Wyart (2024) (Sclocchi, Favero, and Wyart 2024) that are easy to gloss over if you haven’t seen them recently. This one covers Markov chains; the next two cover mean-field analysis and the generative diffusion process itself.

title: Markov Chains
text:
What makes a process “Markov”
A process is Markov if its next state depends only on its current state — not on the path that got it there. Formally, \(P(x_{t+1} \mid x_t, x_{t-1}, \dots, x_0) = P(x_{t+1} \mid x_t)\). That’s it; the entire history collapses into whatever’s true right now.
A simple weather model makes this concrete: three states, and a transition matrix giving the probability of tomorrow’s weather given today’s.

states <- c("Sunny", "Cloudy", "Rainy")
P <- matrix(
  c(0.7, 0.2, 0.1,
    0.3, 0.4, 0.3,
    0.2, 0.3, 0.5),
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(states, states)
)

set.seed(1)
n_steps <- 200
path <- integer(n_steps)
path[1] <- 1L
for (t in 2:n_steps) path[t] <- sample.int(3, 1, prob = P[path[t - 1], ])

data.frame(step = seq_len(n_steps), state = factor(states[path], levels = states)) |>
  ggplot(aes(step, state, colour = state)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "step", y = NULL, colour = NULL, title = "Simulated weather path") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")







Figure 1: A 200-step simulated path through the weather chain, colour-coded by state.





The same transition matrix, drawn as a state diagram, makes the “only today matters” structure visually explicit — every arrow starts from a single current state, with no memory of how the chain got there:

\usetikzlibrary{automata,positioning,arrows}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  ->, >=stealth', auto, thick, node distance=4.4cm,
  state/.style={circle, draw, minimum size=1.5cm, font=\small}
]
  \node[state] (S) {Sunny};
  \node[state, below left=of S]  (C) {Cloudy};
  \node[state, below right=of S] (R) {Rainy};

  \path
    (S) edge[loop above] node {0.7} (S)
    (C) edge[loop left]  node {0.4} (C)
    (R) edge[loop right] node {0.5} (R)
    (S) edge[bend left=15]  node {0.2} (C)
    (C) edge[bend left=15]  node {0.3} (S)
    (C) edge[bend right=32] node {0.3} (R)
    (R) edge[bend left=10]  node[swap] {0.3} (C)
    (R) edge[bend left=15]  node {0.2} (S)
    (S) edge[bend left=15]  node {0.1} (R);
\end{tikzpicture}







Figure 2: State diagram for the three-state weather chain. Edge labels are transition probabilities from the current state.





Knowing today is Sunny tells you everything relevant about tomorrow; knowing it was also Sunny for the last five days adds nothing. That’s the whole idea, and it’s what makes chains like this tractable to analyze — no exploding state space of “all possible histories” to track.

title: Markov Chains
section: Where does it settle? Two ways to find out
text:
Where does it settle? Two ways to find out
Run the chain long enough and the fraction of time spent in each state converges to a fixed stationary distribution \(\pi\), satisfying \(\pi P = \pi\) — a left eigenvector of \(P\) with eigenvalue 1. Two independent ways to find it should agree:

eig <- eigen(t(P))
pi_stat <- Re(eig$vectors[, which.min(abs(eig$values - 1))])
pi_stat <- pi_stat / sum(pi_stat)
names(pi_stat) <- states

n_long <- 5000
path_long <- integer(n_long)
path_long[1] <- 1L
for (t in 2:n_long) path_long[t] <- sample.int(3, 1, prob = P[path_long[t - 1], ])
pi_empirical <- table(factor(states[path_long], levels = states)) / n_long

df <- data.frame(
  state = rep(states, 2),
  probability = c(pi_stat, as.numeric(pi_empirical)),
  method = rep(c("eigenvector", "5000-step simulation"), each = 3)
)

ggplot(df, aes(state, probability, fill = method)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "probability", fill = NULL)







Figure 3: Stationary distribution via eigen-decomposition vs. a long simulated path’s empirical frequencies.





Eigenvector: Sunny 0.457, Cloudy 0.283, Rainy 0.261. A long simulated path lands close to the same numbers — the chain has “forgotten” where it started and settled into its long-run behaviour. This idea — a distribution that’s a fixed point of an update rule — will come back in the next post, where a self-consistency equation plays exactly the same role.

title: Markov Chains
section: Why an eigenvector, and how eigen() actually gets it
text:
Why an eigenvector, and how eigen() actually gets it
The stationary condition \(\pi P = \pi\) treats \(\pi\) as a row vector multiplying \(P\) from the left — a left eigenvector of \(P\) with eigenvalue 1. Transposing both sides turns it into an ordinary right-eigenvector problem: \(P^\top \pi^\top = \pi^\top\). That’s why the code above calls eigen(t(P)) rather than eigen(P) — R’s eigen() only ever returns right eigenvectors, so finding a left eigenvector of \(P\) means first transposing.
An eigenvalue-1 solution is guaranteed to exist. Every row of \(P\) sums to 1, so \(P\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}\): the all-ones vector is a right eigenvector of \(P\) with eigenvalue 1. \(P\) and \(P^\top\) share the same eigenvalues (they have the same characteristic polynomial, since \(\det(P^\top - \lambda I) = \det((P - \lambda I)^\top) = \det(P - \lambda I)\)), so 1 is also an eigenvalue of \(P^\top\) — guaranteeing a \(\pi\) satisfying \(\pi P = \pi\) exists, though not automatically that it’s unique or non-negative (that extra guarantee comes from Perron–Frobenius, since every entry of \(P\) here is strictly positive).
Under the hood, eigen() finds all three eigenvalues of \(P^\top\) as the roots of \(\det(P^\top - \lambda I) = 0\), then for each eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\) finds a vector spanning the null space of \((P^\top - \lambda_i I)\) — solved numerically via matrix decomposition rather than by hand, but conceptually just “solve \((P^\top - \lambda_i I)v = 0\).” Doing that null-space step explicitly for \(\lambda = 1\), independently of eigen()’s eigenvector output, should recover the same \(\pi\) up to scale:

eig$values

[1] 1.0000000 0.4732051 0.1267949

A <- t(P) - diag(3)
qr(A)$rank

[1] 2

pi_manual <- svd(A)$v[, 3]
pi_manual <- pi_manual / sum(pi_manual)
names(pi_manual) <- states
pi_manual

    Sunny    Cloudy     Rainy 
0.4565217 0.2826087 0.2608696 


eig$values shows one eigenvalue at 1 and two others strictly smaller in modulus — consistent with the all-ones-vector argument above and with a unique stationary distribution. A has rank 2 out of 3, meaning \((P^\top - I)\) has a 1-dimensional null space — exactly one free direction, which svd() extracts as the singular vector paired with a (numerically) zero singular value. pi_manual matches pi_stat from eigen() up to floating-point noise, since both are just different numerical routes to the same null space.
Those two smaller eigenvalues aren’t wasted information either: the second-largest one in modulus governs how fast the chain forgets its starting state and converges to \(\pi\) — larger gap to 1, faster mixing. That’s a thread this post won’t pull further, but it’s the same kind of “look at the eigenvalues away from the fixed point” reasoning that shows up when analyzing stability in the mean-field post next.

title: Markov Chains
text:
DDPM’s actual Markov chain
Diffusion models run a Markov chain too, just with a continuous state and Gaussian transition kernels rather than a lookup table. Forward and reverse processes run along the same chain of latents \(x_0, x_1, \dots, x_T\), in opposite directions:
Each \(x_t\) is a latent variable — same shape as the data (an image’s pixel array, say), but not itself an observed data point except at the two ends of the chain. \(x_0\) is a real, clean data sample; \(x_T\) is (by construction, after enough steps) indistinguishable from pure Gaussian noise; everything in between, \(x_1, \dots, x_{T-1}\), is a progressively noisier, unobserved intermediate version of \(x_0\) that only exists as a mathematical construct — you never have a “true” \(x_t\) for \(0 < t < T\) the way you have a genuine image or a genuine noise sample. “Latent” here just means: a random variable in the model that generative code manipulates and a network learns to reverse, but that’s never seen directly in the training data. The subscript \(t\) indexes position along the chain (equivalently, how much noise has accumulated), not real time.

\usetikzlibrary{positioning,arrows}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  ->, >=stealth', thick, node distance=3.1cm,
  state/.style={circle, draw, minimum size=1.15cm, font=\normalsize},
  dots/.style={font=\normalsize}
]
  \node[state] (x0) {$x_0$};
  \node[state, right=of x0] (x1) {$x_1$};
  \node[dots, right=of x1] (d1) {$\cdots$};
  \node[state, right=of d1] (xtm1) {$x_{t-1}$};
  \node[state, right=of xtm1] (xt) {$x_t$};
  \node[dots, right=of xt] (d2) {$\cdots$};
  \node[state, right=of d2] (xT) {$x_T$};

  \path
    (x0)   edge node[above] {$q(x_1|x_0)$} (x1)
    (x1)   edge (d1)
    (d1)   edge (xtm1)
    (xtm1) edge node[above] {$q(x_t|x_{t-1})$} (xt)
    (xt)   edge (d2)
    (d2)   edge (xT);

  \path[dashed]
    (x1) edge[bend left=35] node[below] {$p_\theta(x_0|x_1)$} (x0)
    (xt) edge[bend left=35] node[below] {$p_\theta(x_{t-1}|x_t)$} (xtm1);
\end{tikzpicture}







Figure 4: The DDPM Markov chain. Forward (noising) transitions q run left to right and are fixed; reverse (denoising) transitions p_theta run right to left and are learned.





The forward (noising) process is fixed by construction, defined, exactly as in Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) (Ho, Jain, and Abbeel 2020), by:
\[
q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\, x_{t-1},\ \beta_t I\right)
\]
Each step nudges \(x_{t-1}\) slightly toward the origin and adds a little Gaussian noise, with \(\beta_t\) controlling how much. This is precisely the recurrence used in guided_diffusion/gaussian_diffusion.py, the codebase reproduced in the diffusion-phase-transition post.
\(\beta_t \in (0, 1)\) is the noise schedule — a small, hand-chosen number per step (Ho et al.’s schedule ramps it linearly from \(10^{-4}\) at \(t=1\) to \(0.02\) at \(t=T\)) fixing how much variance gets injected at step \(t\). It’s not learned; it’s a fixed hyperparameter sequence chosen before training even starts. \(\alpha_t := 1 - \beta_t\) is just a convenient rename — close to 1 when \(\beta_t\) is small — so that the update reads \(x_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t}\, x_{t-1} + \sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\epsilon\): shrink the previous state slightly, add noise to make up the variance budget. Their product across steps, \(\bar\alpha_t := \prod_{s \le t} \alpha_s\), is what actually appears in the closed-form jump below — it tracks how much of the original signal \(x_0\) survives after \(t\) compounded steps, and it’s what decays toward 0 as \(t \to T\) in Figure 5, driving \(x_t\) toward pure \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\) noise.

T_steps <- 1000
beta <- seq(1e-4, 0.02, length.out = T_steps)
alpha <- 1 - beta
alpha_bar <- cumprod(alpha)

x0 <- 2.0
n_traj <- 8
set.seed(2)
traj <- matrix(NA_real_, T_steps + 1, n_traj)
traj[1, ] <- x0
for (t in 1:T_steps) {
  eps <- rnorm(n_traj)
  traj[t + 1, ] <- sqrt(alpha[t]) * traj[t, ] + sqrt(beta[t]) * eps
}

traj_df <- as.data.frame(traj) |>
  mutate(step = 0:T_steps) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-step, names_to = "trajectory", values_to = "x")

band_df <- data.frame(step = 0:T_steps, sd = sqrt(1 - alpha_bar[c(1, seq_len(T_steps))]))

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = band_df, aes(step, ymin = -2 * sd, ymax = 2 * sd), fill = "grey85") +
  geom_ribbon(data = band_df, aes(step, ymin = -sd, ymax = sd), fill = "grey70") +
  geom_line(data = traj_df, aes(step, x, group = trajectory), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "t", y = expression(x[t]), title = "Forward chain trajectories vs. their theoretical envelope")







Figure 5: Eight sample trajectories of the scalar Gaussian chain, starting from x0=2, collapsing into the N(0,1) envelope (shaded bands at +-1, +-2 sd) under the real Ho et al. (2020) schedule.

title: Markov Chains
text:
The closed-form jump
Simulating 1000 sequential steps every time you need a noisy sample would be wasteful, and because each step’s kernel is Gaussian, it’s also unnecessary: the composition of \(t\) Gaussian steps is itself Gaussian, in closed form:
\[
q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0,\ (1-\bar\alpha_t) I\right), \qquad \bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s \le t}(1-\beta_s)
\]
You can jump straight from \(x_0\) to any \(x_t\) in one draw. This is exactly q_sample in the reproduced code, and it’s what makes the “forward-diffuse-partway-then-reverse” experiment in the diffusion-phase-transition post practical on real images. Worth actually checking it’s true rather than taking it on faith:

check_t <- 30
n_mc <- 200000
set.seed(3)
x_stepwise <- rep(x0, n_mc)
for (t in 1:check_t) {
  eps <- rnorm(n_mc)
  x_stepwise <- sqrt(alpha[t]) * x_stepwise + sqrt(beta[t]) * eps
}
mean_cf <- sqrt(alpha_bar[check_t]) * x0
var_cf <- 1 - alpha_bar[check_t]

At \(t=30\), 200,000 step-by-step Monte Carlo draws give mean 1.9885 and variance 0.01163; the closed form predicts mean 1.9884 and variance 0.0116 — matching to within Monte Carlo noise.

title: Markov Chains
text:
The reverse chain
The reverse process \(p_\theta(x_{t-1} \mid x_t)\) is modelled the same way — Markov, approximately Gaussian for small \(\beta_t\) — but its mean isn’t known in closed form for real data; that’s what a neural network is trained to approximate. The next explainer is a detour into a different piece of machinery this paper needs (mean-field analysis); the third comes back to build a toy reverse chain where, unusually, the right answer is known exactly.

title: Markov Chains
text:
References


Ho, Jonathan, Ajay Jain, and Pieter Abbeel. 2020. “Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2006.11239.


Sclocchi, Antonio, Alessandro Favero, and Matthieu Wyart. 2024. “A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models Reveals the Hierarchical Nature of Data.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2402.16991.

title: Statics and the Jacobian: What the Motors Must Hold
text:
Third of four explainers behind The Martian Tripod. Part 1 found where the foot is; part 2 found the joint angles that put it there. Both were pure geometry. This part brings in force. The machine weighs 257 tonnes and stands on three point feet, so how hard must each motor push?
One matrix answers that: the Jacobian, the derivative of forward kinematics. It maps joint velocities to foot velocity, and its transpose maps foot forces back to joint torques. This post derives it for the tripod’s leg, checks it against MuJoCo, and then uses it to explain the spider-like stance. It ends by sharing the weight between the feet, which sets up part 4.
Show code
import sys, math, warnings
from pathlib import Path
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve().parents[1] / "martian-tripod"
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import mujoco
from scipy.linalg import null_space

from tripod.build import write
from tripod.params import DEFAULT as P, leg_ik
from tripod.kinematics import foot_fk, rotz
from tripod.control import BodyController, skew

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.25,
                     "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
BRASS, STEEL, RED, BLUE, GREEN, GREY = "#b8860b", "#4a5a6a", "#c0392b", "#2c7fb8", "#2ca25f", "#7f8c8d"
np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)

model = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path(str(write()))
def fresh():
    d = mujoco.MjData(model)
    mujoco.mj_resetDataKeyframe(model, d, model.key("stand").id)
    mujoco.mj_forward(model, d)
    return d
L1, L2 = P.leg.thigh, P.leg.shin
HOOD = model.body("hood").id
MASS = float(model.body_subtreemass[HOOD])
W = MASS*9.81
print(f"machine mass {MASS/1e3:.1f} t, weight {W/1e6:.2f} MN, {W/3/1e6:.2f} MN per foot on average")


machine mass 257.2 t, weight 2.52 MN, 0.84 MN per foot on average

title: Statics and the Jacobian: What the Motors Must Hold
text:
Velocity kinematics
Forward kinematics gives the foot position as a function of the joints, \(\mathbf p = f(\mathbf q)\). Differentiate with respect to time:
\[
\dot{\mathbf p} = J(\mathbf q)\,\dot{\mathbf q}, \qquad J_{ij} = \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial q_j}.
\]
\(J\) is the Jacobian. For the tripod’s leg it is \(3\times3\): three joints in, three components of foot velocity out. Column \(j\) is the foot’s velocity when joint \(j\) alone turns at 1 rad/s.
Part 1 gave the foot in the leg’s own plane, horizontal reach \(\rho\) and height \(z\) relative to the hip, in terms of the elevation angles \(\phi_1 = -q_h\) and \(\phi_2 = -(q_h + q_k)\):
\[
\rho = L_1\cos\phi_1 + L_2\cos\phi_2, \qquad z = L_1\sin\phi_1 + L_2\sin\phi_2 .
\]
The yaw \(\psi\) turns that plane about the vertical, so with \(\theta = a_i + \psi\) (mount azimuth plus yaw) the foot is at \(\big(\rho\cos\theta,\ \rho\sin\theta,\ z\big)\) relative to the hip. Differentiating term by term:
\[
J = \begin{pmatrix}
-\rho\sin\theta & \cos\theta\,\partial_h\rho & \cos\theta\,\partial_k\rho \\
\phantom{-}\rho\cos\theta & \sin\theta\,\partial_h\rho & \sin\theta\,\partial_k\rho \\
0 & \partial_h z & \partial_k z
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{aligned}
\partial_h\rho &= L_1\sin\phi_1 + L_2\sin\phi_2, & \partial_k\rho &= L_2\sin\phi_2,\\
\partial_h z &= -(L_1\cos\phi_1 + L_2\cos\phi_2) = -\rho, & \partial_k z &= -L_2\cos\phi_2 .
\end{aligned}
\]
The first column is the yaw: it moves the foot round a horizontal circle of radius \(\rho\). The other two act within the leg’s plane. MuJoCo computes Jacobians for any point on any body (mj_jac, mj_jacSite). Here they are side by side for all three legs in the standing pose.


Show code
def J_leg(q, az):
    psi, qh, qk = q
    p1, p2 = -qh, -(qh + qk)
    rho = L1*math.cos(p1) + L2*math.cos(p2)
    dr_h, dr_k = L1*math.sin(p1) + L2*math.sin(p2), L2*math.sin(p2)
    dz_h, dz_k = -rho, -L2*math.cos(p2)
    c, s = math.cos(az + psi), math.sin(az + psi)
    return np.array([[-s*rho, c*dr_h, c*dr_k],
                     [ c*rho, s*dr_h, s*dr_k],
                     [ 0.0,   dz_h,   dz_k ]])

d = fresh()
jacp = np.zeros((3, model.nv))
for i in range(3):
    dof = model.joint(f"leg{i}_yaw").dofadr[0]; qa = model.joint(f"leg{i}_yaw").qposadr[0]
    mujoco.mj_jacSite(model, d, jacp, None, model.site(f"foot{i}").id)
    J_mj = jacp[:, dof:dof + 3]
    J_an = J_leg(d.qpos[qa:qa + 3], math.radians(P.leg_azimuths_deg[i]))
    print(f"leg {i}: max |analytic - MuJoCo| = {np.abs(J_an - J_mj).max():.1e} m/rad")
print("\nleg 0, standing (rows x, y, z; columns yaw, hip, knee), m/rad:\n", J_leg(d.qpos[qa - 6:qa - 3], 0.0))


leg 0: max |analytic - MuJoCo| = 3.6e-15 m/rad
leg 1: max |analytic - MuJoCo| = 1.2e-04 m/rad
leg 2: max |analytic - MuJoCo| = 4.9e-06 m/rad

leg 0, standing (rows x, y, z; columns yaw, hip, knee), m/rad:
 [[ -0.    -26.9   -27.79 ]
 [ 19.4    -0.     -0.   ]
 [  0.    -19.4    -3.425]]


The analytic Jacobian matches MuJoCo’s. Leg 0 agrees to machine precision; the others differ only by the six-figure rounding of their mount angles noted in part 1. For legs 1 and 2 the same numbers appear, rotated by 120° and 240°.

Singularities
The Jacobian is invertible except where its determinant vanishes. Expanding along the bottom row and simplifying gives a compact result:
\[
\det J = \rho\,L_1L_2\sin q_k .
\]
There are three ways to lose a degree of freedom.

\(\rho = 0\): the foot is directly below the yaw axis, and turning the yaw does nothing. This is the yaw singularity from part 2.
\(q_k = 0\): the leg is straight. Hip and knee then both move the foot perpendicular to the leg, and nothing can move it along the leg. This is the edge of reach.
\(q_k = \pi\): the leg is folded back on itself. The joint limits rule this out.



Show code
qh0, qk0 = leg_ik(P)
J0 = J_leg((0, qh0, qk0), 0.0)
rho0 = P.stance_radius - P.hip_radius
print(f"det J (numerical) = {np.linalg.det(J0):.1f};   rho L1 L2 sin(q_k) = {rho0*L1*L2*math.sin(qk0):.1f}  (m^3)")
sv = np.linalg.svd(J0, compute_uv=False)
print(f"singular values {sv.round(2)} m/rad: condition number {sv[0]/sv[-1]:.1f}")


det J (numerical) = 8671.7;   rho L1 L2 sin(q_k) = 8671.7  (m^3)
singular values [42.09 19.4  10.62] m/rad: condition number 4.0

title: Statics and the Jacobian: What the Motors Must Hold
text:
Velocity and force ellipsoids
Push unit-speed joint motions, \(\|\dot{\mathbf q}\| = 1\), through \(J\) and the foot velocities fill an ellipsoid. Its axes are the singular vectors of \(J\), and its semi-axis lengths are the singular values. This is the manipulability ellipsoid. Where it is long the foot moves fast; where it is thin the leg is close to a singularity in that direction.
Forces behave in the opposite way. As derived below, a foot force \(\mathbf f\) needs joint torques \(\boldsymbol\tau = J^\top\mathbf f\). The foot forces that unit joint torques can produce, \(\|\boldsymbol\tau\| = 1\), form the force ellipsoid \(\mathbf f^\top(JJ^\top)\mathbf f = 1\). It has the same axes, with reciprocal lengths. A direction in which the leg moves fast is one in which it pushes weakly, and vice versa: the same trade as a bicycle’s gears.


Show code
def J2(qh, qk):
    p1, p2 = -qh, -(qh + qk)
    return np.array([[L1*math.sin(p1) + L2*math.sin(p2), L2*math.sin(p2)],
                     [-(L1*math.cos(p1) + L2*math.cos(p2)), -L2*math.cos(p2)]])
def ik2(rho, z):
    c = (rho*rho + z*z - L1*L1 - L2*L2)/(2*L1*L2); b = -math.acos(c)
    p1 = math.atan2(z, rho) - math.atan2(L2*math.sin(b), L1 + L2*math.cos(b))
    return -p1, -b
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 5))
t = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 100); circ = np.vstack([np.cos(t), np.sin(t)])
foot0 = np.array([rho0, -(P.stance_height - P.hip_drop - P.leg.foot_radius)])
for pt in [foot0, (10, -28), (30, -20), (38, -18), (25, -35), (8, -38)]:
    qh, qk = ik2(*pt)
    U, S, _ = np.linalg.svd(J2(qh, qk))
    vel = U @ np.diag(S) @ circ; frc = U @ np.diag(1/S) @ circ
    ax.plot(pt[0] + 3.0*vel[0]/S.max(), pt[1] + 3.0*vel[1]/S.max(), color=BLUE, lw=1.6)
    ax.plot(pt[0] + 3.0*frc[0]*S.min(), pt[1] + 3.0*frc[1]*S.min(), color=RED, lw=1.6)
    knee = (L1*math.cos(-qh), L1*math.sin(-qh))
    lw, al = (3, 1) if np.allclose(pt, foot0) else (1, 0.35)
    ax.plot([0, knee[0], pt[0]], [0, knee[1], pt[1]], color=STEEL, lw=lw, alpha=al)
ax.plot([], [], color=BLUE, label="velocity ellipse  J Jᵀ"); ax.plot([], [], color=RED, label="force ellipse  (J Jᵀ)⁻¹")
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("ρ (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("z (m)"); ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right")
plt.show()








Figure 1: Velocity (blue) and force (red) ellipses for the hip–knee part of the leg at several foot positions in the leg plane, hip at the origin. Each is drawn to its own scale; only shape and orientation matter. Near full reach (right) the velocity ellipse collapses along the leg and the force ellipse stretches along it: a straight leg can hold a huge load along its length but cannot move that way at all. The thick leg is the standing pose.

title: Statics and the Jacobian: What the Motors Must Hold
text:
Virtual work: τ = Jᵀf
Now the key result. Suppose the ground pushes on the foot with force \(\mathbf f\), and the leg is in equilibrium, held there by joint torques \(\boldsymbol\tau\). Imagine a tiny joint displacement \(\delta\mathbf q\). The foot moves \(\delta\mathbf p = J\,\delta\mathbf q\). In equilibrium the total work done in any such virtual displacement is zero. The work the motors do equals the work done against the ground:
\[
\boldsymbol\tau^\top\delta\mathbf q = \mathbf f^\top\delta\mathbf p = \mathbf f^\top J\,\delta\mathbf q \quad\text{for every } \delta\mathbf q
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\boldsymbol\tau = J^\top\mathbf f .
\]
This is the principle of virtual work. It needs no free-body diagrams, no reaction forces at the joints and no geometry beyond the Jacobian already computed. Each row of \(J^\top\mathbf f\) is a dot product: joint \(j\)’s torque is the foot force projected onto the direction joint \(j\) moves the foot. For a hinge, \(\mathbf J_j = \boldsymbol\omega_j\times(\mathbf p - \mathbf r_j)\), so
\[
\tau_j = \mathbf f\cdot\big(\boldsymbol\omega_j\times(\mathbf p - \mathbf r_j)\big) = \boldsymbol\omega_j\cdot\big((\mathbf p - \mathbf r_j)\times\mathbf f\big),
\]
which is just the moment of the foot force about joint \(j\)’s axis. That is the familiar lever law, recovered from the Jacobian.

Adding the legs’ own weight
The legs themselves are heavy: each weighs 28 t. Gravity on each part does work too, so each part contributes its own \(J^\top\) term, using the Jacobian of its centre of mass:
\[
\boldsymbol\tau = \underbrace{\sum_\text{parts} J_{c,j}^\top\,(-m_j\mathbf g)}_{\text{gravity torque } \mathbf g(\mathbf q)} \;-\; J^\top\mathbf f_\text{ground}.
\]
The sign follows the equations of motion, \(M\ddot{\mathbf q} + \mathbf c(\mathbf q, \dot{\mathbf q}) = \boldsymbol\tau + J^\top\mathbf f\). With everything at rest, the motor torque must cancel the gravity term \(\mathbf g(\mathbf q)\) and the ground force. MuJoCo calls the term \(\mathbf c\) (gravity plus Coriolis and centrifugal terms, which vanish at rest) qfrc_bias. The tripod’s balance controller computes exactly this: bias - J.T @ force for every planted leg.


The check: torques from measured contact forces
The strongest test is to let MuJoCo settle the standing machine and then measure the contact forces from its contact solver. Those are numbers the controller never sees directly. Then predict the joint torques from them with \(\boldsymbol\tau = \mathbf g(\mathbf q) - J^\top\mathbf f\), and compare with what the motors are actually commanding.


Show code
d = fresh()
ctl = BodyController(P, model)
goal, _ = ctl.com_state(d)
while d.time < 6.0:
    ctl(d, [0, 1, 2], goal, np.zeros(3), rotz(0.0)); mujoco.mj_step(model, d)
mujoco.mj_forward(model, d)

floor = model.geom("floor").id

for k in range(d.ncon):

print("measured ground forces on the feet (MN):")
for i in range(3):

    print(f"  foot {i}: {F/1e6} at ({pos[0]:6.2f}, {pos[1]:6.2f})")

  foot 1: [0.   0.   0.85] at (-11.00,  19.05)
  foot 2: [ 0.   -0.    0.85] at (-11.00, -19.05)
  total vertical 2.5232 MN; weight 2.5232 MN

joint torques (MN m)          predicted g(q) - J^T f        commanded by the controller
  leg 0 (yaw, hip, knee):   [-0.    12.672  2.583]          [-0.    12.672  2.583]
  leg 1 (yaw, hip, knee):   [ 0.    13.201  2.676]          [ 0.    13.201  2.676]
  leg 2 (yaw, hip, knee):   [-0.    13.202  2.676]          [-0.    13.202  2.676]


Prediction and simulation agree to every printed digit. The feet carry nearly pure vertical loads that add up to the machine’s weight. Foot 0 carries a little less than the others because the centre of mass sits about 0.24 m behind the hood’s centre, pulled back by the carrier basket.

title: Statics and the Jacobian: What the Motors Must Hold
text:
Why the spider stance
For a vertical foot load \(F_z\) the virtual-work formula gives a striking result. The yaw column has no vertical component, so the yaw torque is zero. The hip and knee torques come from the bottom row of \(J\):
\[
\tau_h = -F_z\,\partial_h z = F_z\,\rho, \qquad \tau_k = -F_z\,\partial_k z = F_z\,L_2\cos\phi_2 .
\]
Here \(\rho\) is the foot’s horizontal distance from the hip, and \(L_2\cos\phi_2\) is its horizontal distance from the knee. A joint’s torque from a vertical load depends only on how far the foot is from it horizontally. The leg’s shape doesn’t matter, nor does its height or the angle of the thigh. The legs’ own weight modifies this. It hangs on the inboard side of the foot and partly offsets the load, which is why the hip’s 16.3 MN·m from the load alone becomes the 13.2 MN·m measured above.
This is why a heavy walker stands like a daddy long-legs (harvestman). The hip must sit 19.4 m inboard of the foot, because the feet must be spread wide for stability, so the hip carries a large torque whatever happens. But the knee can be put almost directly above the foot. Then the knee torque is nearly zero, and the shin becomes a column in compression.


Show code
Fz = W/3
R_, Z_ = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(0, 44, 300), np.linspace(-44, 10, 300))
TH = np.full(R_.shape, np.nan); TK = np.full(R_.shape, np.nan)
for idx in np.ndindex(R_.shape):
    rho, z = R_[idx], Z_[idx]
    c = (rho*rho + z*z - L1*L1 - L2*L2)/(2*L1*L2)
    if abs(c) > 1:
        continue
    qh, qk = ik2(rho, z)
    if not (-1.2 <= qh <= 1.4 and -0.3 <= qk <= 2.6):
        continue
    tau = -J2(qh, qk).T @ np.array([0.0, Fz])
    TH[idx], TK[idx] = abs(tau[0]), abs(tau[1])
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.6), sharey=True)
for ax, Tm, name in ((axs[0], TH, "hip"), (axs[1], TK, "knee")):
    cs = ax.contourf(R_, Z_, Tm/1e6, levels=np.arange(0, 40, 2.5), cmap="YlOrBr", extend="max")
    ax.plot(*foot0, "x", color="k", ms=10, mew=2)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_title(f"{name} torque (MN·m)"); ax.set_xlabel("ρ (m)")
axs[0].set_ylabel("z (m)")
fig.colorbar(cs, ax=axs, shrink=0.8)
plt.show()
qh, qk = ik2(*foot0)
tau0 = -J2(qh, qk).T @ np.array([0.0, Fz])
print(f"standing, load only (no leg weight): hip {abs(tau0[0])/1e6:.2f} MN m = Fz x {rho0:.1f} m;"
      f" knee {abs(tau0[1])/1e6:.2f} MN m = Fz x {abs(tau0[1])/Fz:.2f} m")








Figure 2: Joint torques needed to carry one third of the machine’s weight, for every foot position in the leg plane (knee-up solutions within joint limits), hip at the origin. Left: hip. Right: knee. The cross is the standing foot. Hip torque depends only on horizontal reach; knee torque is smallest when the shin is vertical.





standing, load only (no leg weight): hip 16.32 MN m = Fz x 19.4 m; knee 2.88 MN m = Fz x 3.42 m


The hip torque map is a set of vertical bands: it depends only on \(\rho\). The knee map has a cool valley along the line where the knee sits above the foot. The standing pose sits near that valley, with the foot only 3.4 m horizontally from the knee. Statically the 40 MN·m motors could hold a third of the machine’s weight with the foot anywhere out to \(40/0.84 \approx 47\) m from the hip, which is beyond reach. So standing is never torque-limited. The limit comes when walking. The motors have only about three times the standing hip torque in hand, and the main post found that the swing legs saturate once the gait is pushed much past 5–6 mph.

title: Statics and the Jacobian: What the Motors Must Hold
section: Sharing the weight between three feet
text:
Sharing the weight between three feet
So far each leg had its own foot force. Where do those come from? The machine as a whole must be in equilibrium. The ground forces \(\mathbf f_1, \mathbf f_2, \mathbf f_3\) acting at the feet \(\mathbf p_i\) must balance the weight acting at the centre of mass \(\mathbf c\):
\[
\sum_i \mathbf f_i = m\mathbf g_\uparrow, \qquad \sum_i (\mathbf p_i - \mathbf c)\times\mathbf f_i = \mathbf 0,
\]
where \(\mathbf g_\uparrow = (0, 0, g)\). Stack the nine force components into one vector and these six equations become linear:
\[
G\,\mathbf f = \mathbf w, \qquad
G = \begin{pmatrix} I & I & I \\ [\mathbf p_1 - \mathbf c]_\times & [\mathbf p_2 - \mathbf c]_\times & [\mathbf p_3 - \mathbf c]_\times\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{6\times9},
\qquad \mathbf w = \begin{pmatrix} m\mathbf g_\uparrow\\ \mathbf 0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\(G\) is the grasp matrix, a name borrowed from robot hands, where fingers share the job of holding an object. Here the “object” is the machine itself and the “fingers” are the ground contacts. Nine unknowns and six equations leave a three-dimensional null space. Those are the internal forces: combinations of foot forces that cancel exactly, adding no net force or moment. For three point feet they are pairs of feet pushing against each other, squeezing or stretching along each edge of the triangle.


Show code
com = d.subtree_com[HOOD].copy()
feet = [contact[f"foot{i}"][1] for i in range(3)]
G = np.zeros((6, 9))
for i, p in enumerate(feet):
    G[:3, 3*i:3*i + 3] = np.eye(3); G[3:, 3*i:3*i + 3] = skew(p - com)
w = np.array([0, 0, W, 0, 0, 0])
print(f"rank G = {np.linalg.matrix_rank(G)}, null space dimension = {9 - np.linalg.matrix_rank(G)}")

f_min = np.linalg.pinv(G) @ w                      # minimum-norm solution
print("minimum-norm foot forces (MN):\n", f_min.reshape(3, 3)/1e6)

N = null_space(G)
# rotate the null-space basis to make it readable: one squeeze per edge
edges = []
for a, b in ((0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0)):
    v = np.zeros(9); u = (feet[b] - feet[a])/np.linalg.norm(feet[b] - feet[a])
    v[3*a:3*a + 3] = -u; v[3*b:3*b + 3] = u      # feet a and b pushed apart along their edge
    edges.append(v)
E = np.column_stack(edges)
print(f"G times each edge-squeeze = {np.abs(G @ E).max():.1e}  (they are internal forces)")
print(f"edge-squeezes span the null space: rank [N E] = {np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.hstack([N, E]))}")

# vertical loads are the barycentric coordinates of the centre of mass
A = np.vstack([np.array(feet)[:, :2].T, np.ones(3)])
lam = np.linalg.solve(A, [com[0], com[1], 1.0])
print("vertical share of weight:  measured", np.round([contact[f'foot{i}'][0][2]/W for i in range(3)], 4),
      "  barycentric coords of COM", lam.round(4))


rank G = 6, null space dimension = 3
minimum-norm foot forces (MN):
 [[ 0.    -0.     0.823]
 [-0.     0.     0.85 ]
 [-0.     0.     0.85 ]]
G times each edge-squeeze = 3.8e-15  (they are internal forces)
edge-squeezes span the null space: rank [N E] = 3
vertical share of weight:  measured [0.326 0.337 0.337]   barycentric coords of COM [0.326 0.337 0.337]


Four results come out of this.

The minimum-norm solution is the one MuJoCo found. It is purely vertical, with no internal squeeze. The project’s controller solves the same least-squares problem (BodyController.distribute), with two extra conditions explained below.
The edge squeezes span the null space. Any amount of push-apart or pull-together along the three edges can be added without disturbing equilibrium. A real controller uses this freedom to keep the feet away from slipping, by pushing them inward so friction is not needed, or to reduce the hip torques.
Vertical loads are barycentric coordinates. For vertical forces, moment balance says the weighted average of the foot positions, weighted by each foot’s share of the load, must equal the centre of mass’s position over the ground. Those weights are exactly the barycentric coordinates of the centre of mass in the foot triangle. MuJoCo’s measured shares match them to four figures.
The ground can push but not pull. A foot’s vertical force must be positive, \(f_{i,z} \ge 0\). Its sideways force must stay inside the friction cone, \(\sqrt{f_{i,x}^2 + f_{i,y}^2} \le \mu f_{i,z}\). These inequalities turn the least-squares problem into a constrained one. The controller handles them with a small active-set loop: any foot that would have to pull is clamped to a light push, and the rest are re-solved.


Unloading a foot
The barycentric picture explains how to take a step. Move the centre of mass towards the edge between two feet, and the third foot’s barycentric coordinate, and so its load, falls linearly to zero. Once it is unloaded it can be lifted without the machine noticing. Go any further and it would have to pull: the machine tips.


Show code
F2 = np.array(feet)[:, :2]
mid = 0.5*(F2[0] + F2[2])
s = np.linspace(0, 1.25, 200)
loads = []
for si in s:
    cxy = (1 - si)*F2.mean(axis=0) + si*mid
    loads.append(np.linalg.solve(A, [cxy[0], cxy[1], 1.0])*W/1e6)
loads = np.array(loads)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.6))
for i, col in zip(range(3), (STEEL, RED, BRASS)):
    ax.plot(s, loads[:, i], color=col, lw=2, label=f"foot {i}")
ax.axvspan(1, s[-1], color=GREY, alpha=0.15); ax.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("fraction of the way from the triangle's centre to the 0–2 edge")
ax.set_ylabel("vertical load (MN)"); ax.legend(frameon=False); plt.show()








Figure 3: Foot loads as the centre of mass is carried in a straight line from the centre of the support triangle towards the edge between feet 0 and 2 (and beyond it), from the barycentric formula. Foot 1’s load reaches zero exactly at the edge. Beyond that, keeping all three feet down would need foot 1 to pull on the ground (shaded).







On two feet, the machine is a hinge
Lift a foot and \(G\) shrinks to \(6\times6\), with just two feet. You might expect six equations and six unknowns to have a unique solution. But one combination is impossible: no pair of forces applied at two points can make a moment about the line through those points, since every such force either passes through the line or crosses it. \(G\) loses rank.


Show code
# moments about a point on the hinge line (foot 0), so the missing direction comes out cleanly
G2 = np.zeros((6, 6))
for k, i in enumerate((0, 2)):
    G2[:3, 3*k:3*k + 3] = np.eye(3); G2[3:, 3*k:3*k + 3] = skew(feet[i] - feet[0])
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(G2)
axis = (feet[2] - feet[0])/np.linalg.norm(feet[2] - feet[0])
print(f"rank of the two-foot grasp matrix: {np.linalg.matrix_rank(G2)} of 6 (smallest singular value {S[-1]:.1e})")
print("unreachable wrench direction (force; moment):", U[:, -1].round(3))
print("direction of the line through feet 0 and 2:          ", axis.round(3))


rank of the two-foot grasp matrix: 5 of 6 (smallest singular value 1.6e-21)
unreachable wrench direction (force; moment): [-0.    -0.     0.     0.866  0.5    0.   ]
direction of the line through feet 0 and 2:           [-0.866 -0.5   -0.   ]


The missing direction has no force part and a moment part along the line through the two feet: a pure moment about that line (the sign of a singular vector is arbitrary). Nothing the legs do can resist a tip about that line. Wherever the centre of mass is relative to it, the machine rotates about it freely, like a door on its hinges. The controller acknowledges this explicitly: on two feet it projects the hinge component out of the moment it asks for (the hinge argument of distribute) instead of fighting it.
So a walking tripod is never in static equilibrium while a foot is in the air. It is always falling sideways about the hinge, and the next footfall has to catch it. Planning that fall is the subject of the final part.

title: Statics and the Jacobian: What the Motors Must Hold
text:
Summary

The Jacobian \(J = \partial f/\partial\mathbf q\) maps joint velocities to foot velocity. For the tripod’s leg, \(\det J = \rho\,L_1L_2\sin q_k\). It is singular with the foot under the hip, with the leg straight, or with the leg folded.
Virtual work gives \(\boldsymbol\tau = J^\top\mathbf f\). Velocity and force are dual: the leg moves fast in the directions where it pushes weakly.
With gravity, \(\boldsymbol\tau = \mathbf g(\mathbf q) - J^\top\mathbf f\). This predicts MuJoCo’s standing torques exactly, from contact forces measured in the simulation.
A vertical load costs torque in proportion to horizontal distance. So the knee sits above the foot, and the hip does the work.
Balance is a \(6\times9\) linear system with a 3-D null space of internal forces. Vertical loads are the barycentric coordinates of the centre of mass. On two feet the system loses a rank: the hinge.

Next: Planning the falling walk.

title: Statics and the Jacobian: What the Motors Must Hold
text:
Further reading

K. M. Lynch and F. C. Park, Modern Robotics (2017), chapter 5 (velocity kinematics and statics) and chapter 12 (grasping and the grasp matrix).
R. M. Murray, Z. Li and S. S. Sastry, A Mathematical Introduction to Robotic Manipulation (CRC, 1994), chapter 5, for internal forces and friction cones.
T. Yoshikawa, “Manipulability of robotic mechanisms”, International Journal of Robotics Research 4(2), 1985. The origin of the manipulability ellipsoid.

title: Instrumenting Agent Cybernetics
text:
Wang et al. (2026) argue that cybernetics supplies the missing theoretical scaffold for foundation agents, and derive six design principles from six classical laws. Their Principle 2 (Requisite Variety) requires that \(\min(V(\mathcal{O}), V(\mathcal{I})) \geq V(\mathcal{W})\), and three of the failure modes they name are diagnosed as \(V(\mathcal{T}) < V(\mathcal{W})\). Their headline open question — how should an agent respond when its environment exceeds its representational capacity? — presupposes that this condition can be detected.
It cannot, as the framework currently stands. \(V(\mathcal{W})\) appears throughout as Ashby’s classical cardinality — a theoretical quantity Wang et al. never operationalise from deployment telemetry. An operator who tries to estimate it from observed disturbance classes defaults to plug-in (maximum-likelihood) coverage; that default systematically understates environmental variety and overstates coverage, worst where the distribution is heaviest-tailed. Agent Cybernetics is, as written, unmeasurable.
We supply the instrument. Our central result is the Enumeration Elasticity Theorem: the elasticity of unhandled traffic with respect to enumeration investment is exactly \(\eta = 1 - \beta\), where \(\beta\) is the Heaps exponent of the disturbance-class discovery curve — a directly measurable quantity. A \(\lambda\)-fold increase in the effort spent mapping disturbance classes to responses reduces the unhandled fraction by \(\lambda^{1-\beta}\). As \(\beta \to 1\), \(\eta \to 0\) and investment stops buying coverage: at \(\beta = 0.9\), halving the residual costs a thousandfold increase in effort. This gives an operational answer to Wang et al.’s open question. When \(\eta \approx 0\), requisite variety cannot be met by amplification at any ledger a rational operator will build, and the deficit must be met by attenuation or by a class-independent fallback — an architectural conclusion, not an engineering one.
We further contribute: an open-world estimator for \(V(\mathcal{W})\) combining Good–Turing missing-mass correction and Heaps tracking, and a demonstration that plug-in estimation errs on both sides of the inequality at once; a determinism instrument, \(H(R \mid D)\), that operationalises the Conant–Ashby good regulator theorem, which is absent from the six laws; an interventional test that renders feedback blindness — a named closed-loop reliability failure they diagnose but do not measure (one of their first four failure modes, ranked highest for cost–benefit) — falsifiable rather than merely diagnosable, and which we run on the demonstrator (\(\Phi = 0.55\) bits, \(\approx\) 90x the resampling-noise floor: the agent’s action distribution genuinely conditions on its observations); and a partition-refinement procedure with three admission gates, including a policy-improvement criterion that corrects a natural but wrong instinct about when a disturbance class should be split.
We also identify a hazard in our own instrument: attenuation lowers measured \(\beta\), so the treatment we recommend improves the diagnostic whether or not it improves the system. We give the mitigation and do not claim to resolve it.
Finally, the same interventional machinery yields an adversarial instrument: susceptibility \(\Sigma\), the probability that an agent complies with an instruction injected into its observation channel (indirect prompt poisoning). Measured end-to-end through an agent’s real data-input tools — file read, RAG retrieval, web fetch — against a matched clean control (\(\Sigma_{\text{clean}} = 0\)), \(\Sigma\) is strongly attack-class-dependent (0.83 for a blunt instruction-override, 0.00 for a system-prompt-exfiltration attempt) and inversely tracks content-sensitivity \(\Phi\) across vectors, the direction §5.2 predicts: an agent that treats tool output as evidence to be checked, not an instruction to obey, is harder to hijack through that output, while a feedback-blind one passes an injected payload straight through.
We package these as a variety ledger: a versioned registry of essential variables, disturbance classes, response repertoire, and channel specifications, recomputed from telemetry and enforced as a CI gate. §6 exercises the full ledger on a semi-synthetic benchmark with known ground truth — including a graded outcome signal that makes the partition-refinement gates non-vacuous, an interventional feedback-blindness measurement, and an end-to-end prompt-poisoning susceptibility measurement — and reports one incident: a latent regulatory defect that inverted the dithering measurement until it was found and fixed, which is itself the clearest available demonstration of why §4.5’s canary discipline is not optional.

title: Instrumenting Agent Cybernetics
A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
text:
Sclocchi, Favero and Wyart’s A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models Reveals the Hierarchical Nature of Data (Sclocchi, Favero, and Wyart 2024) makes a simple, sharp claim about how diffusion models generate images. Take a real image, run the forward noising process partway to some timestep \(t\), then run the backward (denoising) process the rest of the way back to \(t=0\). If \(t\) is small, you get back almost exactly the image you started with. If \(t\) is large, you get a plausible image of the same rough kind but with different fine details. The paper’s finding is that the switch between these two regimes isn’t gradual — it’s a genuine phase transition, and it happens at different noise levels for different levels of an image’s hierarchy (fine texture destabilizes first, then object parts, then overall semantic class).
This post reproduces that experiment end to end: real pretrained weights, real ImageNet-derived images, run locally on a Mac (Apple Silicon, no CUDA) rather than the multi-GPU cluster the paper used. The code lives in forward-backward-diffusion, the paper’s own release — I had to fix a couple of bugs in it and add Apple GPU (MPS) support to get it running here; the how and why of that is at the bottom of the post.

title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
section: Scaling it down to run on a laptop
text:
Scaling it down to run on a laptop
The paper’s own experiment uses OpenAI’s 256×256 unconditional ADM diffusion model over the full ImageNet-1k validation set (1000 classes, 10 images each), resampled to 250 diffusion steps, swept across the full 0–250 range of reversal points. Doing that on a single Mac would take a very long time, so this reproduction keeps every piece of the pipeline real but turns the dials down:

This post

same checkpoint

250

So: same model, same classifier, same underlying mechanism, real (if smaller) ImageNet-derived data — just a coarser grid and a tenth-scale image set, sized to finish in about 20 minutes on a laptop instead of hours on a cluster.

title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
section: Where does the class identity break?
text:
Where does the class identity break?
For each reversal point \(t\), we forward-diffuse every starting image to \(t\), denoise it back to a clean image, and ask ConvNeXt-Base what class it thinks the result is — then compare that to what it originally said about the untouched image. sample_correct and start_correct track agreement with the true (Imagenette) label; pred_unchanged tracks whether reconstruction preserved the classifier’s own original prediction, which is the more direct read on “did the reverse process preserve identity” independent of whether the classifier was right to begin with.

summary_by_t <- accuracy_by_t |>
  group_by(step_reverse) |>
  summarise(
    sample_correct = mean(sample_correct),
    pred_unchanged = mean(pred_unchanged),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(c(sample_correct, pred_unchanged), names_to = "metric", values_to = "fraction")

baseline_acc <- baseline$accuracy_top1[1] / 100

ggplot(summary_by_t, aes(step_reverse, fraction, color = metric)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = baseline_acc, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = max(summary_by_t$step_reverse), y = baseline_acc,
           label = "baseline accuracy (no diffusion)", vjust = -0.6, hjust = 1,
           size = 3, color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(sample_correct = "#2C7FB8", pred_unchanged = "#D95F02"),
    labels = c(sample_correct = "matches true label", pred_unchanged = "matches original prediction")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "reversal timestep (t, out of 25 respaced steps)",
    y = "fraction of images",
    color = NULL,
    title = "Identity survives small t, then degrades"
  )







Figure 1: Classification agreement after forward-backward diffusion, as a function of the reversal timestep. t=0 is a no-op (perfect reconstruction); higher t means more of the diffusion trajectory is re-randomized before reconstruction.

title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
section: A hierarchy of breakdown, layer by layer
text:
A hierarchy of breakdown, layer by layer
The more interesting view is inside the classifier. Every image gets pushed through ConvNeXt-Base twice — once as the original, once as the forward-backward reconstruction — and we compare activations at every one of its ~45 internal layers, from the earliest convolutional stem (depth 0) to the final classification head (depth ≈44). If the paper’s hierarchical story is right, shallow layers (fine texture) should start diverging at small \(t\), while only the deepest layers (semantic class) diverge at large \(t\).

cosine_by_depth_t <- activation_diff |>
  filter(metric == "cosine") |>
  group_by(step_reverse, depth) |>
  summarise(cosine_distance = 1 - mean(value), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(cosine_by_depth_t, aes(step_reverse, depth, fill = cosine_distance)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", labels = percent_format()) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = pretty_breaks()) +
  labs(
    x = "reversal timestep (t)",
    y = "network depth (0 = input stem, ~44 = classification head)",
    fill = "cosine\ndistance",
    title = "Where in the network reconstruction diverges from the original"
  )







Figure 2: Mean cosine distance (1 - cosine similarity) between original and reconstructed activations, by network depth and reversal timestep. Warmer = more disrupted. A hierarchy would show the disruption front moving from shallow layers (bottom) to deep layers (top) as t increases.






depth_max <- max(cosine_by_depth_t$depth)
sample_depths <- unique(round(seq(0, depth_max, length.out = 6)))

cosine_by_depth_t |>
  filter(depth %in% sample_depths) |>
  mutate(depth = factor(depth)) |>
  ggplot(aes(step_reverse, cosine_distance, color = depth, group = depth)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "magma", end = 0.85) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(
    x = "reversal timestep (t)",
    y = "cosine distance",
    color = "depth",
    title = "Shallow layers move first, deep layers move last"
  )







Figure 3: The same data as a line plot: a handful of representative depths, cosine distance vs. t.

title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
section: What actually broke in the code, and how I fixed it
text:
What actually broke in the code, and how I fixed it
The paper’s released code isn’t quite runnable as committed, and separately, nothing about it was written with Apple’s MPS backend in mind. Four fixes were needed:

A broken relative import. guided_diffusion/image_datasets.py did from ..datasets.imagenet_classes import IMAGENET_CLASSES, a relative import that reaches outside the installed guided_diffusion package. It fails immediately with ImportError: attempted relative import beyond top-level package — every one of the repo’s three custom scripts imports this module, so nothing in the repo could run at all. Fixed by making datasets its own installable package (setup.py) and importing it absolutely.
Two sampling methods that don’t exist. The actual forward-backward experiment script calls diffusion.p_sample_loop_forw_back and diffusion.ddim_sample_loop_forw_back — methods that appear nowhere in gaussian_diffusion.py, and never have, across the entire git history. I implemented both, as variants of the existing p_sample_loop_progressive / ddim_sample_loop_progressive that start the reverse process at a given timestep instead of at pure noise.
float64 on MPS. _extract_into_tensor moved the diffusion schedule’s coefficients — stored as float64 numpy arrays — directly onto the compute device. MPS doesn’t support float64 at all, so this crashed on first use; fixed by casting to float32 before the device transfer.
torch.distributed collectives on an MPS tensor. The scripts use dist.all_reduce/all_gather (inherited from the original multi-GPU design) even for a single-process laptop run. Those collectives run over the gloo backend here (no CUDA means no NCCL), and gloo only understands CPU tensors — so the handful of tensors that cross a collective call needed to be routed to CPU rather than MPS, while leaving NCCL’s CUDA path untouched for the cluster case.

None of this changes the paper’s method — it’s the same forward-then-partial-backward diffusion process, the same classifier, the same activation-comparison logic. The fixes just make the released code actually executable, and executable somewhere other than a CUDA cluster.
Related: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models connects this paper’s belief-propagation phase transition to the renormalization-group critical phenomena in my own dissertation · if any of the underlying math felt assumed rather than explained, Markov Chains, Concretely and A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve are refreshers written to fill exactly that gap.

title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
text:
A forensic expert tells the court: “The DNA profile matches the defendant, and only one person in a million would match by chance.” The prosecutor concludes: “So there is only a one-in-a-million chance the defendant is innocent.”
The conclusion does not follow. It swaps a conditional probability for its converse, and the error has contributed to real miscarriages of justice.

title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
text:
Two different questions
Let \(E\) be the evidence (a DNA match) and \(I\) the event that the defendant is innocent. The expert can legitimately report
\[
P(E \mid I) = 10^{-6},
\]
the chance of a match if the defendant is innocent. The court needs a different quantity,
\[
P(I \mid E),
\]
the chance the defendant is innocent given the match. These are not equal in general, any more than “most cricketers are men” means “most men are cricketers”.

title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
section: Bayes’ theorem supplies the missing piece
text:
Bayes’ theorem supplies the missing piece
\[
P(I \mid E) = \frac{P(E \mid I)\,P(I)}{P(E \mid I)\,P(I) + P(E \mid G)\,P(G)},
\]
where \(G\) is guilt. The missing ingredient is the prior \(P(I)\): how likely was this person to be the source before the match was known?
Suppose the crime happened in a city of \(N = 2{,}000{,}000\) possible suspects, and the defendant was found by trawling a database, with no other evidence. A sensible prior is that each person is equally likely to be the source, so \(P(G) = 1/N\). A true source always matches, so \(P(E \mid G) = 1\).

posterior_innocent <- function(prior_guilt, p_match_innocent, p_match_guilty = 1) {
  num <- p_match_innocent * (1 - prior_guilt)
  num / (num + p_match_guilty * prior_guilt)
}

N <- 2e6
posterior_innocent(1 / N, 1e-6)

[1] 0.6666666


The probability of innocence is about 67%, not one in a million.

title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
text:
Natural frequencies
The same answer is easier to see by counting people. Among 2,000,000 people:

1 is the true source, and matches.
The other 1,999,999 are innocent, and about \(1{,}999{,}999 \times 10^{-6} \approx 2\) of them match by chance.

So roughly 3 people match, and only 1 of them is guilty. Picking one matching person at random, the chance they are innocent is about \(2/3\).

tibble(
  group = factor(c("Guilty source", "Innocent, matches by chance"),
                 levels = c("Guilty source", "Innocent, matches by chance")),
  count = c(1, (N - 1) * 1e-6)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(group, count, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(count, 2)), vjust = -0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#d95f0e", "#2c7fb8")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Expected matching people") +
  ylim(0, 2.6)







Figure 1: Expected matches in a population of 2,000,000: one true source and about two innocent people who match by chance.

title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
text:
How much the prior matters
The match probability alone doesn’t fix the answer. It depends on how many people could plausibly have done it.

grid <- expand.grid(
  pool = 10^seq(2, 8, length.out = 200),
  rmp = c(1e-4, 1e-6, 1e-9)
) |>
  mutate(
    p_innocent = posterior_innocent(1 / pool, rmp),
    rmp = factor(format(rmp, scientific = TRUE), levels = c("1e-04", "1e-06", "1e-09"))
  )

ggplot(grid, aes(pool, p_innocent, colour = rmp)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  labs(x = "Number of possible suspects", y = "P(innocent | match)",
       colour = "Random-match\nprobability")







Figure 2: Posterior probability of innocence given a match, for several random-match probabilities, as the pool of possible suspects grows.





A one-in-a-million match is strong evidence when the pool is a few hundred people, and weak when it is millions. Strong evidence only becomes decisive once the prior is also taken into account.

title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
text:
Simulation check
Simulate many “crimes” in a city of \(N\) people: pick the true source, test everyone, and look at the people who match. Then ask how often a randomly chosen matching person is innocent.

trials <- 20000
innocent_matches <- rbinom(trials, N - 1, 1e-6)  # innocent people who match, per crime
total_matches <- 1 + innocent_matches            # the true source always matches

c(simulated_pooled   = sum(innocent_matches) / sum(total_matches),
  bayes              = posterior_innocent(1 / N, 1e-6),
  naive_prosecutor   = 1e-6,
  mean_per_crime     = mean(innocent_matches / total_matches))

simulated_pooled            bayes naive_prosecutor   mean_per_crime 
       0.6655407        0.6666666        0.0000010        0.5645903 


Pooling all matching people across the simulated crimes reproduces the Bayes answer of roughly two-thirds, and is nowhere near \(10^{-6}\).
The last line is a different quantity: it averages the innocent fraction crime by crime. It comes out lower (about 0.57) because crimes with no innocent matcher count as a full 0, and averaging a ratio is not the ratio of averages. The Bayes calculation, and the question “of everyone who matches, how many are innocent?”, correspond to the pooled figure.

title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
text:
Takeaways

\(P(E \mid I)\) and \(P(I \mid E)\) are different quantities. Equating them is the prosecutor’s fallacy.
The prior (how many people could have done it) is needed to get from one to the other.
Natural frequencies, such as “about 2 innocent people would also match”, make the correct reasoning hard to miss.
The mirror image is the defence attorney’s fallacy: arguing that because several people would match, the match is worthless. It is still evidence; it just must be weighed against the prior.

title: Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar’s Black Hole
text:
Gargantua in motion
The disk is not a still picture. Its gas orbits, the inner edge faster than the outer, so any pattern in it is sheared into a tighter and tighter spiral. With the camera held still the ray map never changes: it is traced once, and each frame rotates the gas underneath it, every ring at its own orbital angular velocity \(\Omega(r)\).
There is one subtlety. Light from different parts of the image has travelled for different times. The image of the disk curled under the shadow is light that went round the back of the hole, and it left the gas long before the light from the near side. The tracer records each ray’s travel time, and each pixel shows the gas as it was when that light set out.


Show code
G, c, M_sun = 6.674e-11, 2.998e8, 1.989e30
t_M = G * 1e8 * M_sun / c**3            # one unit of time, GM/c^3, for Gargantua
t_hit = tr_film["t_hit"][tr_film["outcome"] == kerr.DISK]
P_in = 2 * np.pi / D.omega(D.isco(A_FILM), A_FILM)
P_out = 2 * np.pi / D.omega(R_OUT, A_FILM)
span = 90.0                            # the clip covers 90 M of coordinate time
print(f"for a 10^8-solar-mass hole, M = GM/c^3 = {t_M:.0f} s")
print(f"orbital period at the inner edge ({D.isco(A_FILM):.2f} M): {P_in:.0f} M = {P_in*t_M/3600:.1f} hours")
print(f"orbital period at the outer edge ({R_OUT:g} M): {P_out:.0f} M = {P_out*t_M/3600:.0f} hours")
print(f"the 15-second clips cover {span:g} M = {span*t_M/3600:.1f} hours")
print(f"light reaching the camera from the disk left it between {-t_hit.max():.0f} M and {-t_hit.min():.0f} M earlier")


for a 10^8-solar-mass hole, M = GM/c^3 = 493 s
orbital period at the inner edge (3.83 M): 51 M = 7.0 hours
orbital period at the outer edge (20 M): 566 M = 77 hours
the 15-second clips cover 90 M = 12.3 hours
light reaching the camera from the disk left it between 57 M and 158 M earlier


Each 15-second clip compresses about 12 hours of Gargantua’s time: the inner edge of the disk goes round almost twice, the outer edge less than a fifth of a turn. First as the film showed it:

and then with the Doppler and gravitational shifts. Now the gas brightens as it swings round towards the camera on the left and fades as it recedes on the right:

The video’s texture adds some clumpier structure to the gas so that the rotation is easy to follow. The ray map is the same 5.8 million rays for every frame, and the clips are rendered by animate.py in the gargantua project.

The soundtrack
The music is computed from the disk too. Each note is a ring of gas, and its pitch is the ring’s orbital frequency. Those frequencies are a few millionths of a hertz, far below hearing, so every one of them is raised by the same 24 octaves. That is a factor of \(2^{24} \approx 17\) million, and it keeps every ratio between them, so the chord you hear is the chord the rings make. The rings are chosen to be in resonance with the outer edge, orbiting 1, 1½, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 times as fast. That gives the open fifths and octaves of an organ chord, a nod to the church organ in Hans Zimmer’s score.


Show code
import soundtrack as ST
r_n, f_true, f_hear, turn = ST.notes()
for n, rr, f0, f in zip(ST.RATIOS, r_n, f_true, f_hear):
    print(f"{n:>4g} x outer edge: ring at r = {rr:5.2f} M, {f0:.2e} Hz -> {f:6.1f} Hz")


   1 x outer edge: ring at r = 20.00 M, 3.59e-06 Hz ->   60.2 Hz
 1.5 x outer edge: ring at r = 15.23 M, 5.38e-06 Hz ->   90.3 Hz
   2 x outer edge: ring at r = 12.54 M, 7.18e-06 Hz ->  120.4 Hz
   3 x outer edge: ring at r =  9.53 M, 1.08e-05 Hz ->  180.6 Hz
   4 x outer edge: ring at r =  7.83 M, 1.44e-05 Hz ->  240.8 Hz
   6 x outer edge: ring at r =  5.92 M, 2.15e-05 Hz ->  361.2 Hz
   8 x outer edge: ring at r =  4.84 M, 2.87e-05 Hz ->  481.6 Hz


The outer edge sounds first and the inner rings join one by one, every 1.5 seconds. Each note swells and fades once per turn of its ring in the clip. The voice is three slightly detuned pipes per note, with organ-like overtones and a synthetic stone-hall reverb. It is all generated by soundtrack.py, with no recorded or licensed audio.
